papers.summary: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.

authors.name: Xudi Ge, Yepeng Liu, Haifeng Liu, Enze Shi, Liangqi Zhang, Yongchao Xu

papers.title: Fast-JEPA: Advancing the Success-Latency Frontier for Latent World Models
papers.summary: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our project page is available at https://deepcybo-physai.github.io/Fast-JEPA.

authors.name: Yao Zhang, Bin Yu, Shijie Lian, Haishan Liu, Changti Wu, Yu Wu, Kai Chen

papers.title: C-LiTE: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Cellular feature learning in Histopathology
papers.summary: Characterising individual cells is fundamental to computational pathology, as cellular morphology informs tasks such as tumour grading, mitotic assessment and immune profiling. However, most pathology foundation models are trained on tissue patches and capture cellular features only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or rely on computationally expensive architectures with hundreds of millions of parameters. Applying ViTs directly to small cellular crops also presents an architectural challenge: upsampling increases computational cost without adding morphological information and may introduce interpolation artefacts. To address these limitations, we introduce C-LiTE, a lightweight foundation model for cellular representation learning in H&E-stained histopathology, with only 22 million parameters. C-LiTE employs a native-resolution tokenisation strategy tailored to cellular inputs, processing 64 x 64 px cell-centred crops using a 4 x 4 patch embedding to produce a 16 x 16 token grid without image upsampling. To transfer visual knowledge from large-scale pre-training, we adapt the patch embedding weights of a pre-trained ViT-5-S using a pseudoinverse-based transformation, enabling weight initialisation at the finer patch resolution. We further assemble a pre-training dataset of 60 million cell-centred crops from TCGA, balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types. To our knowledge, this represents the largest public dataset for self-supervised pre-training on H&E images at the cellular level. We evaluate C-LiTE on seven public datasets spanning mitotic figure recognition, nucleus and cell-type classification, and immune cell phenotyping. Under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30x fewer parameters.

authors.name: Esha Sadia Nasir, Jiaqi Lv, Gozde N. Gunesli, Shan E Ahmed Raza

papers.title: Non-Expanding Gated Continued Fraction Architecture for Feedforward Layers in Language Models
papers.summary: Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. We achieve this by two simple yet critical contributions: i) we propose a novel non-expanding gated continued fraction inspired architectural component to replace feedforward layers in established language model architectures that may use vanilla multilayer perceptrons or gated linear units or (vanilla/gated) experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) type architectures. ii) We propose a way to re-implement divisions -- the non-linearity in these architectures -- in terms of logarithms and exponentials. By experimenting on different language modeling architectures such as GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2 and (nano) Llama-MoE we find that our proposed architecture performs similarly or significantly better than the continued fraction architecture proposed in prior work along with having higher throughput. In addition, our re-implementation of divisions makes training of deeper CoFrGeNets stable without the need for incremental training which was proposed in prior work as a means to stabilize training, but added notable complexity to existing large language model training implementations. Code is available at http://github.com/IBM/CoFrNets

authors.name: Amit Dhurandhar, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy, Dennis Wei, Rahul Nair

papers.title: A Frugal AI Framework for India: Responsible and Right-sized AI
papers.summary: India's AI debate often swings between two insufficient options: replicating the compute-intensive, capital-heavy foundation-model programmes of the United States or China, or remaining a downstream adopter of foreign AI with localised interfaces and safeguards. Neither serves a country that must deliver AI to a very large, diverse population across uneven infrastructure and within constrained budgets. This white paper from the Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), IIT Madras, proposes a third path: Responsible Frugal AI, which applies principle-based frugal engineering alongside Responsible AI. Responsible Frugal AI is right-sized AI: it fixes the functional requirement first, asks whether AI is needed at all, and then chooses the smallest sufficient model, meeting the requirement with minimal resources while keeping a verified margin, robustness and responsible governance. The framework applies frugality across four dimensions (data, compute, model and operations) through seven levers spanning the AI lifecycle, each with practices and measures. It calls for public AI rails, vernacular-first design, measured resource use, human oversight for high-stakes decisions, and a cap on total resource consumption so that efficiency gains are not cancelled out by rising usage. We argue that India is resource-imbalanced rather than resource-poor, and that frugal principles offer the most viable route to population-scale deployment, fit naturally with India's digital public infrastructure, and make sovereignty operational by preserving India's capacity to specify, deploy, govern, inspect and adapt its AI systems. A seven-point adoption checklist and eleven policy statements translate the framework into practice, positioning AI in India as a responsible, frugal public-value system that maximises social value per rupee and per joule.

authors.name: Balaraman Ravindran, K. S. Venkataraghavan, Gokul S Krishnan, Balaji Srinivasan, Balkrishna C. Rao

papers.title: PaMuk-Bench: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Vision-Language Tasks
papers.summary: While vision-language models (VLMs) currently obtain notable results for highly-studied languages, e.g. English, they exhibit significant performance drops in certain low-resource languages, especially due to the lack of annotated datasets. To this end, we propose PaMuk-Bench, a novel parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language tasks. Our benchmark includes a set of over 10K curated English prompts that are translated into six languages: Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, Romanian. Parallel translations, which are obtained via a semi-automatic process, along with accompanying generated and retrieved images enable the comparative development and evaluation of VLMs across a wide range of tasks: text-to-image generation, image captioning, content-based image retrieval, image generation difficulty estimation, image retrieval difficulty estimation. We empirically show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs compare consistently worse than their fine-tuned counterparts, confirming that PaMuk-Bench is a valuable resource that can drastically reduce the language gap across a variety of VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is available at https://github.com/ghesil/pamuk_bench.

authors.name: Silviu-Florin Gheorghe, Radu-Stefan Popa, Adriana Valentina Costache, Adrian-Gabriel Chifu, Alessia Amelio, Paul Irofti, Anders Skaarup Johansen, Lallouani Bouchakour, Mohamed Lichouri, Khaled Lounnas, Neelu Madan, Yashvir Malik, Radu Tudor Ionescu

papers.title: Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and Practical Multilingual Translation Models in the Wild
papers.summary: Hy-MT3 is the third generation of the Hunyuan multilingual translation model family, including \textbf{Hy-MT3-1.8B}, \textbf{Hy-MT3-7B} and \textbf{Hy-MT3-30B-A3B (MoE)}. Compared with Hy-MT2, Hy-MT3 translates \textbf{more accurately, more completely and more faithfully to user constraints}: on real-world scenario data, the share of samples with mistranslations is reduced by \textbf{43\%}, omissions or additions by \textbf{74\%}, and instruction-following errors by \textbf{40\%}, while language coverage is expanded from \textbf{38 to 102} languages. With only 3B activated parameters, \textbf{Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models in non-thinking mode}, including flagship models such as Qwen3.8-Max, Kimi-K3.1-Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and approaches the strongest closed-source thinking models such as GPT-6.1-Sol and Gemini-4-Argon, while surpassing models that consume \textbf{more than 30$\times$} its inference compute. Beyond general translation, Hy-MT3 is optimized for two industrial scenarios. For \textbf{game localization}, built with high-quality game-domain data and a professional evaluation system from the Honor of Kings team, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B matches or outperforms strong closed-source models such as Gemini 3.1 Pro on all core metrics, and can be plugged into game development pipelines through an open-source toolchain. For \textbf{image translation}, Hy-MT3 improves context understanding and error correction to better tolerate OCR errors, achieving the best result among models of comparable size. Finally, we open-source \textbf{TransRubric}, a rubric-based automatic evaluation suite for translation, which outperforms other evaluation schemes on the WMT26 metrics shared task test set and is more stable with respect to human evaluation.

authors.name: Mao Zheng, Zheng Li, Fangxu Liu, Tao Chen, Bingxin Qu, Bo Lv, Mingrui Sun, Hongyu Li, Hong Huang, Jinlong Song, Decheng Wu, Guanghua Yu

papers.title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
papers.summary: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.

authors.name: Zhenxuan Fan, Zhuoya Wang, Yuqian Yuan, Wenqiao Zhang, Juncheng Li, Jun Xiao, Siliang Tang, Yueting Zhuang

papers.title: Search-RSI: Expanding Search Worlds Along Multimodal Agents' Capability Frontier
papers.summary: Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.

authors.name: Chengchao Lv, Yin Wang, Chunzheng Zhu, Wanli Chang

papers.title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($\delta_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

authors.name: Chi Yan, Guoyang Zhao, Wentao Yuan, Yixiao Ge, Yanning Zhou, Dan Xu

papers.title: WISP: Composable Representations for Wrist-Worn Activity Recognition
papers.summary: Smartwatches and fitness bands are among the most common wearable devices, and large national health studies record movement at the wrist. Yet existing human activity recognition benchmarks mix sensors worn on different parts of the body, so they do not show how well activities can be recognised from the wrist alone. We introduce WristHARBench, a benchmark that standardises participant-disjoint evaluation across nine wrist-acceleration datasets and two additional multichannel inertial datasets. We hypothesise that different human activities leave complementary patterns in wrist motion, such as local shape, rhythm, temporal order and cross-axis relationships, and propose WISP (Wrist-Informed Space of Predictive Representations), a composable representation space that combines representations of these patterns with compatible classifiers. Across the nine primary datasets, WISP with random search achieves 70.20% mean Macro-F1, compared with 59.62% for the strongest of 18 external baselines. Controlled ablations and baseline comparisons indicate that recognition improves mainly when a representation adds motion patterns that the others lack, rather than when it represents the same pattern in a different way.

authors.name: Zipeng Wu, Shiqiao Zhou, Fabian Spill, James Andrews

papers.title: RefineKV: Query-Adaptive KV Cache Compression via Attention-Error Bounds
papers.summary: Repeatedly accessing the full key--value (KV) cache is a major bottleneck in long-context language model decoding. We find that small query-specific subsets can accurately approximate full attention, yet their union covers nearly the entire cache, motivating query-adaptive access for the KV cache. A natural approach is to split the KV cache into clusters, using compact representatives for clusters that incur negligible error while expanding the rest to their original KV entries. We derive a selection criterion from an upper bound on attention-output error, which reveals two complementary factors governing the error: importance measures the impact of a cluster, while distortion measures how faithfully the cluster can be represented. Based on this criterion, we propose RefineKV, a decoding-time query-adaptive KV compression method. Experiments on two models and three benchmarks demonstrate that RefineKV retains near-full-attention quality while achieving up to 7.6x speedup in the attention phase and 1.66x faster decoding, establishing a new quality-latency Pareto frontier.

authors.name: Kewei Lian, Jiayi Zhai, Anji Liu

papers.title: Feedback Shortcut: Speculative Decoding for Latent Feedback Transformers
papers.summary: Feeding each position's top-layer hidden state back into the next position's input improves Transformer performance. However, this feedback breaks speculative decoding, since verifying a drafted token requires the top-layer state from its preceding position, which forces the draft to rely on an approximate stand-in. Training the model to adapt to this stand-in can lower the exact-decoding performance ceiling, while using it at inference time further introduces approximation error. We propose Feedback Shortcut to address both bottlenecks. First, state alignment trains a lightweight projection from multi-token prediction head states to stand-ins, leaving base model training untouched. Second, pipelined correction re-evaluates each draft using its predecessor's newly computed state, a much closer proxy to true feedback. Running this correction inside the verification pass of subsequent drafts improves accuracy with zero extra calls. Across 135M and 780M scales, Feedback Shortcut stays within $10^{-4}$ bits per byte of the exact-decoding ceiling on Paloma and accelerates decoding by 2.4-2.8x with about 2% more training compute than the latent feedback Transformer. At large batch sizes, skipping correction still preserves Transformer speed and over 80% of latent feedback's gains.

authors.name: Benhao Huang, Xuezhe Ma, Hector Liu

papers.title: Learning the Projection onto the Data Support: Distribution Learning that Avoids Memorization
papers.summary: We introduce a framework for learning distributions supported on manifolds based on estimating the nearest-point projection onto the data support. Specifically, we define an objective functional over a class of functions whose minimizer recovers this projection. The proposed framework automatically adapts to the intrinsic dimension and allows for data supported on unions of manifolds with varying dimensions. The resulting objective can be optimized using standard neural network architectures. We present population-level results establishing recovery of the manifold projection and prove finite-sample Wasserstein generalization bounds. Furthermore, we validate the approach empirically across a range of settings. In contrast to widely used generative models such as diffusion models, whose objectives can be minimized by memorizing training samples, our formulation excludes such behavior. We also introduce a direct memorization metric to verify that the learned projection generates new samples rather than reproducing the training set.

authors.name: Lin Chen, Dejan Slep\v{c}ev

papers.title: The Cross-Context Threshold Test: Detecting Discrimination Under Environmental Shifts
papers.summary: We study how threshold tests for detecting discrimination under environmental shifts, focusing on the Veil-of-Darkness (VoD) setting where visibility changes between daylight and darkness. We show that standard threshold tests, when applied separately to daylight and darkness data, violate key assumptions: risk distributions drift across contexts and thresholds fluctuate arbitrarily. We propose a cross-context threshold test that enforces distributional invariance and monotonic threshold decay. Using New York City stop-and-frisk data and synthetic experiments, we demonstrate that this model yields more reliable thresholds, improves bias detection, and aligns with the counterfactual logic of the VoD test. Our framework generalizes to fairness auditing whenever environmental context influences decisions.

authors.name: Jun Yuan, Xinyue Ye

papers.title: FoGConcept: Identifying Interpretable Movement Concepts for Freezing-of-Gait Detection from Multi-Scale IMU Signals
papers.summary: Freezing of gait (FoG) is a disabling motor symptom of Parkinson's disease, characterized by an episodic inability to initiate or sustain effective stepping. Current inertial measurement unit (IMU)-based models can detect FoG accurately, but they fail to explain their predictions in terms of human-understandable movement concepts. A major contribution of this work is to identify nine human-understandable movement concepts encoded by a multi-scale FoG model, including gait initiation, rhythmic bilateral gait, trembling in place, shuffling steps, and pivot turns. These concepts recur across subjects, are functionally linked to the model's FoG decisions, and exhibit emergent specialization across short and long temporal contexts. Repeating the concept-discovery procedure on a new FoG dataset, wider temporal contexts, and a deeper backbone recovers the same comparatively stable set of movement concepts. Accordingly, we propose FoGConcept, a mechanism-based interpretability framework for learning movement concepts from multi-scale IMU signals. Domain experts independently recognize 88.9% of the identified concepts, while the proposed model achieves an F1 score of 94.2% for FoG detection. Our findings show that accurate FoG detection can be understood through human-recognizable movement patterns, providing new insight into what a detection model learns to distinguish FoG from non-FoG movement.

authors.name: Chuntian Chi, John Clapham, GinaMari Blackwell, Leslie Cloud, Ingrid Pretzer-Aboff, Yanfu Zhang, Huajie Shao, Gang Zhou

papers.title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows
papers.summary: Fast and accurate prediction of viscoplastic flows remains a challenge in computational rheology due to yield surfaces, discontinuous gradients, and strongly nonlinear transitions between yielded and unyielded regions. Transformer-based neural operators such as RheOFormer have recently shown strong potential for surrogate modeling of non-Newtonian flows. However, their applicability to viscoplastic systems and their efficacy in recovering realistic flows remain poorly understood. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of RheOFormer applied to steady Bingham channel flow. By isolating the problem to a simple geometry and constitutive model, we examine how dataset structure, numerical value range, and input representation govern the model's ability to interpolate and extrapolate within the parameter space. The data regimes in which RheOFormer remains accurate and those in which errors emerge are identified, particularly for plug-dominated flows and for conditions outside the velocity scales or flow structures represented during training. Upon identifying these failure modes, targeted enhancements to the input representation and loss formulation are introduced to better predict low-gradient plug regions. Logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware loss formulations substantially improve accuracy in challenging regimes where the baseline formulation fails. In addition, extrapolation errors are reduced by augmenting the training set with only a few strategically selected cases spanning the missing physical regimes. Finally, a single partially developed snapshot suffices for an accurate steady-state prediction, and the model outperforms simply copying its input throughout flow development. These results highlight the importance of appropriate field representation and parameter-space coverage for data-efficient neural-operator prediction of viscoplastic flows.

authors.name: Maedeh Saberi, Hugo Franca, Maziyar Jalaal, Safa Jamali

papers.title: SONATI: Spatio-temporal ocean neighbourhood asymmetric transformer for imputation of sparse, tabular data with uncertainty
papers.summary: Missing value imputation is often a prerequisite for downstream analyses. In oceanography, observational data are frequently structured in a tabular manner, highly sparse and exhibit spatio-temporal structures that classical imputers such as k-nearest neighbours or MissForest are not suited to exploit. We present the Spatio-temporal Ocean Neighbourhood Asymmetric Transformer for Imputation (SONATI), a masked, factorised time-space transformer operating on pre-computed, local time and space neighbourhoods, which reduces computational complexity compared to global attention. SONATI is designed to work with tabular data and is thus in principle able to work on both gridded and unstructured data, though evaluation here was performed on gridded North Atlantic data only. It provides aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties through a negative log-likelihood loss and multiple forward passes with Monte Carlo dropout. Systematic ablations on attention type and masking strategies guided the final architecture design. The results showed that SONATI outperformed classical and transformer-based methods by at least 12.5% in terms of root mean squared error (RMSE) on a large observational oceanographic dataset with key biogeochemical and physical parameters in the North Atlantic (potential temperature, salinity, oxygen, nitrate, silicate and phosphate). Attention type and masking strategy strongly affected imputation accuracy and smoothness of the produced oceanographic fields. Best results were achieved by factorised time-space attention and combined geographic and per-sample masking. The combined masking strategy reduced the imputation error by 14.3% compared to per-sample masking only. Uncertainties were moderately well calibrated (miscalibration area at observed locations $0.074\pm0.012$) and moderately correlated with the imputation error.

authors.name: Yvonne Jenniges, Boris Peter Koch, Maike Sonnewald, Sebastian Maneth

papers.title: What Do Differentiable Rule Learners Need? FLARE: Fuzzy Rules with Additive Evidence
papers.summary: Rule learners are used where transparency and accountability are required, because they give practitioners patterns they can read. Learning rules is a discrete problem, so neurosymbolic pipelines that use rules as explanations rely on relaxations such as the straight-through estimator. However, these differentiable rule learners often lag behind both classical rule learners and black-box classifiers in terms of performance. We study which parts of a rule-based classifier affect performance, and how well gradient-based training learns each of them. We found that most of the performance comes from how the rules are weighted: random rules with learned weights are already more accurate than every published differentiable rule learner we tested. Based on our results, we propose FLARE (Fuzzy Learned-Antecedent Rule Evidence), a differentiable rule learner that learns simple rules that combine to make the final decision. We also propose a learned encoding for variables with thousands of categories. We test FLARE on tabular data, using 42 datasets of OpenML-CC18 and the 38 classification tasks of TabArena. On CC18, FLARE exceeds the compared rule learners by 7.69 to 12.38 macro-F1 points and performs comparably to random forests, while remaining 1.00 to 1.11 points below tuned gradient-boosted trees. On TabArena it ranks at the same level as random forests and ahead of the other rule learners. As the concept-to-label head of a concept bottleneck model, FLARE is the best rule-based head in five of six settings. On graphs, it is competitive on PubMed and EMOGI but falls behind graph neural networks on Cora and Citeseer. Our code is available at https://github.com/Fuminides/FLARE

authors.name: Javier Fumanal-Idocin, Javier Andreu-Perez

papers.title: Scalable Beckmann Maps Improve One-step Generation
papers.summary: Beckmann Transport Models (BTM) learn one-step generative maps end-to-end from data, without a teacher, a distillation stage, or pretrained features. We introduce Scalable Beckmann Maps (SBM), which bring to BTM the two ingredients behind the quality of modern multistep generators: classifier-free guidance (CFG) and a training recipe that scales, while keeping sampling at a single network evaluation. CFG combines conditional and unconditional velocity or score predictions, which a Beckmann map does not have. Our guidance rests on one observation: the BTM current is a positive multiple of an autonomous denoising field, to which CFG applies as it does to a velocity. With exact denoisers this gives guided BTM. In practice we substitute the map's own conditional and null predictions for the denoisers, which requires no additional network and introduces a bias that we characterize. We show that the guided update is consistent with a guided conservation equation, and that guidance can move the boundaries between basins, sending more noise to the modes a condition favors. Trained from scratch in the latent of a representation autoencoder, SBM reaches a one-step FID of 1.6 on ImageNet 256x256 without a teacher or a feature loss, outperforming the Improved-MeanFlow baseline with 3.2x fewer FLOPs. In text-to-image generation it reaches a GenEval score of 0.86 with one network evaluation. As a world model, where we train without guidance, the recipe alone outperforms DriftWorld on all five metrics of two robot-manipulation benchmarks, with 1.9-2.8x less training compute and no pretrained auxiliary feature encoder.

authors.name: Ulrik Unneberg, Shiyi Wang, Lee Cheuk-Kit, Felix Berg, Boris Kozinsky, Yilun Du, Michael S. Albergo, Eric Vanden-Eijnden

papers.title: Benchmarking EEG feature families for ADHD research in children and adolescents: performance and explainability across attention tasks
papers.summary: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder varies in presentation. Diagnosis requires clinical and developmental assessment. Reproducible electroencephalography measures may complement clinical and behavioural characterisation, but differing feature definitions and evaluation methods hinder comparison. We compared seven feature families and four combinations across attention tasks and assessed the stability of held-out explanations. Two serious games yielded four overlapping attention-task cohorts of 123-140 participants each. Repeated nested participant-held-out evaluation assessed recruitment-group discrimination. Exploratory paired participant-cluster bootstrap tests corrected for multiplicity in two separate families: 72 individual-task contrasts and 18 fusion contrasts. For eight configurations selected after inspecting predictive results, we explained held-out native probabilities before calibration. In the strongest task context, the highest configuration mean AUROC over three repetitions was 0.773, with a fixed-prediction 95% interval of 0.692-0.854 unadjusted for selecting the maximum. Precision, sensitivity and specificity were 0.740, 0.556 and 0.861. In that task, the paired AUROC difference for connectivity minus spectral features averaged +0.2083 across six classifiers and the common 8 s and 16 s durations, with pointwise 95% CI 0.1076-0.3072 and adjusted p = 0.0036. F4-AF4 beta-band coherence led repetition-level attribution summaries in five selected procedures and was selected in every fit. Other contexts showed weaker discrimination and less consistent retention of leading scientific inputs. No general classifier winner emerged. Connectivity and its recurring coherence input warrant independent replication, but do not justify a universal feature recommendation. These exploratory findings do not establish causal task effects, disease mechanisms or diagnostic validity.

authors.name: Javier Sanchis, Jorge Garc\'ia-Carrasco, \'Alvaro Navarro, Tahar Kechadi, Juan Trujillo

papers.title: AV-FLARE: Feature-Level Reliability Estimation for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.summary: Multimodal emotion recognition (MMER) systems typically rely on learned feature representations and attention mechanisms that implicitly weight information across time and modalities. However, these mechanisms do not explicitly incorporate input reliability, despite the presence of noise in audio, occlusions in visual data, and the sparse and event-driven nature of affective cues. We propose AV-FLARE, a framework that explicitly estimates fine-grained reliability scores across both temporal and feature dimensions prior to temporal modeling and uses them to modulate feature representations. Reliability is computed using two complementary components: (i) a supervised network trained jointly with the classification objective, and (ii) an unsupervised Gaussian Mixture Model that models global feature distributions. These signals are combined to provide both task-driven and distribution-aware reliability estimates. To integrate modalities, we introduce a hierarchical cross-modal attention mechanism in which textual features are used to guide audio-visual fusion as a semantic reference modality. Experiments on the IEMOCAP dataset show that AV-FLARE improves over a no-reliability baseline, achieving 90.81\% accuracy and 81.69\% F1-score, corresponding to gains of +4.41% and +8.56%, respectively. These results suggest that incorporating explicit input reliability estimation may improve robustness in multimodal emotion recognition under the evaluated setting.

authors.name: Ines Jemmali, Alaa Nfissi, Wassim Bouachir, Nizar Bouguila

papers.title: TabK: Amortized Bayesian Estimation of the Number of Clusters in Tabular Data
papers.summary: Estimating the number of clusters, $k$, is a fundamental prerequisite for most clustering algorithms. Traditionally, this estimation has relied on computationally expensive grid searches over internal cluster validity indices (CVIs) or adaptive clustering algorithms, both constrained by specific statistical assumptions. We introduce TabK, a zero-shot, permutation-invariant transformer architecture that frames the estimation of $k$ as an amortized Bayesian inference problem for tabular data. TabK leverages a novel Quantile Feature Encoder (QFE) to extract position-free, content-derived representations from empirical marginal distributions. By learning a generalized structural bias over a diverse synthetic prior, TabK estimates the number of clusters in a single forward pass per ensemble member. Evaluated across 50 diverse real-world benchmarks, TabK outperforms all competing methods, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) value of 1.04 compared to 2.14 for the closest competitor. TabK also achieves the lowest average inference time, producing estimates in less than one second on average and running $2\times$ faster than TabClustPFN and $30\times$ faster than traditional CVIs such as Silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz. Code is available at https://github.com/mrbakhtyari/TabK.

authors.name: Mohammadreza Bakhtyari, Bogdan Mazoure, Renato Cordeiro de Amorim, Guillaume Rabusseau, Vladimir Makarenkov

papers.title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
papers.summary: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.

authors.name: Xin Xu

papers.title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models
papers.summary: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.

authors.name: Ethan Rathbun, Jonathan N\"other, Christopher Amato, Alina Oprea, Goran Radanovi\'c

papers.title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
papers.summary: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices. We formalize this as the Co-Evolving Graph Game (CEGG), a setting that sits between facility location, interdependent-network analysis, and graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) but is not jointly addressed by any of them. We propose Cross-Graph Attention with Policy Mirror Descent (CGA-PMD), pairing cross-graph attention, which lets each agent read only the partner-graph nodes structurally coupled to its own, with a policy mirror descent update for stable training. Across three reward domains and a range of practical network scales, we find that the structure of the coupling selects which method wins: at small scale most methods are competitive, but as scale grows or coupling becomes irregular, CGA-PMD is the one method that stays reliable: it attains the highest success count on each of five real city networks, while own-only, unmasked-attention, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based variants degrade in distinct ways. Our theoretical analysis addresses the optimizer side: the Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized update admits an iteration-uniform cumulative drift bound, whereas the clip update admits no such bound on the iterations where the clip does not bind. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Mina-Kim-Github/cegg-cga-pmd.

authors.name: Mina Kim, Guanghui Lan, Benoit Montreuil

papers.title: Data-Dependent Probability Estimation via Sample Amplification
papers.summary: Can we estimate the probability of an event chosen after seeing the data, without using any fresh samples? Its empirical probability can be arbitrarily misleading, while learning the entire distribution to constant accuracy requires $\Theta(d)$ samples on a domain of size $d$. We show that $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d})$ samples suffice for constant mean squared error, provided the rule choosing the event is known. More generally, our estimator handles arbitrary $[0,1]$-valued queries and runs in polynomial time given evaluation access to the rule. This sample complexity matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors and resolves the open question posed by Feldman, Kale, Raman, Talwar, and Tewari (arXiv:2610.41244). Our estimation framework relies on a new combination of sample amplification (arXiv:1904.12053 and arXiv:2201.04315) with distribution learning via online optimization. Our estimator achieves mean squared error $O(d^{3/4}/n)$ when $d\leq n$ and $\widetilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$ when $d>n$. We complement this with a lower bound of $\Omega(\min\{1,\sqrt{d}/n\})$ on the mean squared error. Using our framework, we also design an efficient estimator for data-dependent queries on Gaussian distributions with unknown mean and identity covariance. Finally, we show that a smoothed variant of the problem is much (exponentially) easier. For discrete distributions, if the sample size is chosen uniformly from $\{n,\ldots,2n-1\}$, then $n=O(\log d)$ suffices for constant mean squared error.

authors.name: Vitaly Feldman, Satyen Kale, Mahbod Majid, Kunal Talwar

papers.title: PFN-Syn: Generating Synthetic Tabular Data with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
papers.summary: Synthetic tabular data can help enable data sharing and model development in privacy-sensitive domains, but existing generators often require dataset-specific training and substantial computation. We introduce PFN-Syn, a training-free framework for synthetic tabular data generation based on prior-data fitted networks. We evaluate PFN-Syn against training-based generators on eight binary classification datasets. PFN-Syn achieves the highest average downstream utility among evaluated synthetic generators, with higher generation throughput than training-based baselines, while maintaining competitive distributional similarity and distance-to-closest-record privacy behavior. Our results suggest that tabular foundation models can serve as useful building blocks for practical synthetic tabular data generation.

authors.name: Michael Zuo, Inwon Kang, Oshani Seneviratne, Stacy Patterson

papers.title: When a Permitted Action Completes a Forbidden Workflow: Designing Consequence-Oriented Approval for LLM Agents
papers.summary: Tool-using language-model agents increasingly ask people to approve consequential actions, yet an approval prompt shows only the next step. A request to send a file to an approved recipient can look harmless even when that file was assembled, several steps earlier, from data the user said must never leave. We call this a cumulative authorization failure and argue that it is an interaction design problem as much as a security problem. The evidence a reviewer needs is spread across the trajectory, and listing it in time order leaves the reviewer to reconstruct the causal chain. We present the Cumulative Consent Ledger (CCL), an approval interface built on four design principles that restate the user's intent, bind the review to the exact action, compose the cumulative consequence, and keep every claim checkable. A trusted monitor that tracks artifact lineage supplies the evidence. In a between-subjects study with 80 participants and 960 approval decisions, CCL was associated with fewer unsafe approvals than an evidence-matched chronological log (24.2% vs. 32.5%), higher comprehension, and faster decisions, although the adjusted difference in unsafe approvals remained uncertain (-7.9 points, 95% CrI [-19.7, 3.8]). In a system evaluation, the monitor detected 89.2% of 120 violating checkpoints and, used as an execution gate, reduced executed unsafe effects from 43.3% to 5.0% for one agent at a small cost to benign completion. We derive implications for designing consent around consequences rather than individual calls.

authors.name: S M Asif Hossain, Ruksat Khan Shayoni, Md Kishor Morol, M F Mridha

papers.title: Optimal User-Level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization and Mean Estimation with Heavy Tails
papers.summary: We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and $k$-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only $\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. (2022) and Zhao et al. (2024). Finally, for mean estimation under the directional-moment assumption of Agarwal et al. (2025), we close their remaining approximate-DP gap by removing the additional $d/\varepsilon$ user requirement and attaining the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

authors.name: Andrew Lowy

papers.title: AMP-OD: Active Model Probing for Unsupervised Outlier Model Selection--Extended Version
papers.summary: Outlier detection is often deployed in fully unsupervised settings, where labels are unavailable and practitioners must choose a detector without direct performance feedback. Existing unsupervised outlier model selection methods predict detector quality from static meta-features and historical performance on meta-datasets, but they commit before observing how any detector behaves on the target dataset. We propose AMP-OD, an execution-conditioned probe-then-commit framework. AMP-OD runs a small number of inexpensive probe detectors, uses their score patterns as target-dataset evidence, and then selects a final detector from a larger candidate pool. To interpret unlabeled probe responses, we introduce a Leave-One-Out Family Probe Posterior (LOO-FPP), which converts probe score patterns into gated detector-family evidence while reducing self-validation in pseudo-label construction. AMP-OD further combines this evidence with historical reliability through a warm-start prior, a sequential probe/stop policy, and lower-confidence-bound arbitration. Extensive experiments and ablation studies show that detector responses provide useful evidence beyond static meta-features, with the LOO-FPP and conservative arbitration as key contributors.

authors.name: Hong-Phuc Phan, Tuan-Anh Vu, Tung Kieu, Son Ha Xuan, Sean Bin Yang, Bin Yang, Christian S. Jensen

papers.title: DisSparse: Pipelined Top-$p$ Sparse Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
papers.summary: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

authors.name: Nurlan Nazaraliyev, Elaheh Sadredini, Nael Abu-Ghazaleh

papers.title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
papers.summary: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $\mu$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $\mu$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $\mu$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $\mu$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.

authors.name: Mo\"ise Blanchard, Ezra Edelman, Surbhi Goel, Shyam Narayanan, Jialin Yu

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating the Fragility of Self-Rewarding Optimization
papers.summary: Self-rewarding optimization (SRO) promises to improve language models by enabling them to generate their own reward signals. Yet when and how SRO succeeds or fails remains poorly understood. We reveal that SRO is fundamentally fragile: even seemingly benign perturbations to training prompts can corrupt the self-generated preference signal and trigger iterative collapse. We demonstrate this through two prompt-level attacks that serve as controlled stress tests: a Re-Ranking attack that concentrates training on prompts where self-reward diverges from an oracle, and a Preamble attack that learns short prefixes inflating self-reward without any gain in oracle quality. To explain why these attacks succeed, we introduce self-reward fidelity (SRF), a metric quantifying on-policy agreement between self-evaluated and oracle rewards. We show that SRF can serve as a diagnostic signal of self-supervision reliability, and that controlled SRF perturbations induce a phase-transition region: SRO improves when SRF remains sufficiently high, but collapses once SRF drops below a model- and task-dependent threshold. This analysis motivates Projection Decoupling Defense, which suppresses SRO update components along directions to which the reward generator is locally sensitive, improving SRO robustness under adversarial conditions. This work sheds light on the fragility of SRO and charts promising directions toward making it more robust.

authors.name: Rongyi Zhu, Tanqiu Jiang, Fenglong Ma, Ting Wang

papers.title: DRAM: Memory-Efficient Muon via Rank Reallocation in Principal-Random Subspaces
papers.summary: Memory-efficient Muon methods aim to reduce storage overhead while preserving strong performance, yet existing approaches compromise either convergence guarantees or practical efficiency. In this paper, we focus on subspace optimization for Muon, where the choice of subspace determines the gradient information retained for updating. To preserve dominant information while providing the coverage needed for stochastic convergence guarantees, we construct a principal-random subspace that combines leading singular directions of the stochastic gradient with random directions sampled from their orthogonal complement. Under a fixed rank budget, there is a trade-off between principal exploitation and complementary coverage, making rank allocation important for practical optimization. Our key observation is that the preferred balance shifts from principal-heavy early in training to random-heavy later. Motivated by this shift, we propose \dram, a memory-efficient Muon optimizer that reallocates principal and random ranks across stages while maintaining momentum and performing matrix-sign normalization entirely in the subspace. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for general rank-allocation schedules with nondecreasing coverage factors, obtaining rates of $O(T^{-1/4})$ in the stochastic setting and $O(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting, with fixed allocation as a special case. Using a simple linear reallocation schedule, \dram achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings.

authors.name: Haomin Bai, Dingzhi Yu, Xuling Zhao, Sifan Yang, Yibo Wang, Lijun Zhang

papers.title: Interpreting Diffusion Model Activations in Natural Language
papers.summary: Interpreting the intermediate activations of diffusion models (DMs) is key to understanding how they generate images. Existing interpretability methods for DMs provide limited support for open-ended interrogation, making it difficult to extract human-interpretable insights. We extend LatentQA, the task of answering natural-language questions about Large Language Model activations, to DM activations. We introduce the Diffusion-specific Activation Oracle (DAO), which translates DM activations into natural-language answers to open-ended questions about the ongoing generation. Our experiments show that DAO can effectively describe the content of the final image from activations at early denoising steps. Additionally, we demonstrate that DAO captures the structure of the DM's activation space well enough to steer image generation toward target attributes. Furthermore, we show that attribution patching through DAO identifies DM components that contribute to visual attributes specified in natural language. Our code is available \href{https://github.com/yamanoko/dao/tree/main}{here}.

authors.name: Yukinori Yamamoto, Kotaro Yoshida, Ryotaro Shimizu

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound
papers.summary: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $\eta=1/H$ requires $\Omega(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.

authors.name: Asha Barua, Sajad Khodadadian

papers.title: Aegis: A Conversational Prototype for Lung Cancer Risk Information and Follow-up
papers.summary: Collecting self-reported risk information and maintaining continuity between assessment, explanation, and follow-up are practical components of a lung cancer screening workflow. We present Aegis, a browser-based research prototype that combines a conversational questionnaire, rule-based risk categorization, downloadable reports, retrieval-augmented health information, and doctor-user communication. A session-oriented controller manages question progression and clarification, while a language model assists with answer validation. Structured responses are passed to a separate risk-analysis module, and reports are linked to user and session records through Firebase services. The project adopts a multi-agent design that separates information collection, validation, assessment, and report generation. Its documented verification scope comprises 45 functional test specifications covering account management, questionnaire interaction, reporting, doctor-side review, and consultation. The available evaluation describes workflow behavior qualitatively; it provides no per-case execution results, clinical cohort, predictive-performance measurements, or comparative experiments. We therefore present Aegis as an engineering prototype for organizing risk information and follow-up, with clinical validity and the benefits of its agent-based design remaining unestablished. The paper describes the implementation, distinguishes implemented workflows from incomplete extensions, and identifies the evidence required for reproducible and clinically meaningful evaluation.

authors.name: Bowen Han, Chengwei Cao, Runxin Zhang, Yuyang Jiang

papers.title: Stein Guidance without Gradients: Discretization Uniform Diffusion Inference Time Scaling beyond Particle SMC
papers.summary: Reward-guided diffusion requires effective steering and correction of the bias introduced by approximate value functions. A Brownian example shows that SMC with full multinomial resampling at every step can require particle counts to grow linearly with guidance depth to maintain accuracy. We propose Stein Guidance, which combines derivative-free guidance with whole-path independence Metropolis-Hastings correction. Value-weighted selection from centered Gaussian candidates approximates gradient guidance in expectation, using as few as two queries per step. Centering stabilizes the local normalizer estimates, and the same queries yield an explicit path weight for correction. Under uniform value and spatial regularity bounds, we prove superpolynomial decay of finite-grid total variation error in the number of MH updates, with constants that do not grow with guidance depth. The error prefactor tends to zero as the value functions approach exact Doob values and the time grid is refined.

authors.name: Youheng Zhu, Chenyang Wang, Minshuo Chen, Yiping Lu

papers.title: Physical regime changes expose formula misuse in large language models
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for scientific computing across the Earth and environmental sciences, but problems in these fields often involve distinct physical regimes. LLMs may fail to recognize these regime-dependent constraints, applying formulas outside their domains of validity and producing plausible but physically incorrect results. We systematically investigate these failures through controlled experiments and assess whether post-training can improve regime-aware reasoning. Across 72 physical mechanisms, we find frontier LLMs frequently misapply formulas outside their regimes of validity, reducing accuracy by 13-57 percentage points. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards enables Qwen3.5-9B to match DeepSeek V4 Flash (284B) on regime-dependent tasks, but its effectiveness is limited by the formulas available in the base model. Combining supervised fine-tuning on a few worked examples with reinforcement learning improves accuracy by 61 percentage points, while distillation from a teacher supplied with the correct formula raises accuracy from 0% to 71%.

authors.name: Maohao Ran, Yanting Zhang, Chendong Ma, Jun Song

papers.title: Peel, Don't Whack: Partial Coverage, Imperfect Validators, and Intervention Based Shortcut Mitigation
papers.summary: Without group labels, shortcut mitigation increasingly relies on interventions : label-preserving edits, such as background or watermark replacement, that are proposed automatically and accepted by a validator. Invariance to a complete family of valid edits yields robustness, but in practice coverage is partial and validators err. We analyze both in a stylized linear model. For the population logistic solution and the max-margin limit of gradient descent, the decision on every shortcut-flip group follows one additive rule. Hence worst-group accuracy never decreases with coverage, while individual groups can provably degrade, a mechanism for the Whac-a-Mole effect; full coverage is not always needed. In the logistic regime the validator's false-accept rate must stay below a closed-form tolerance that grows with coverage. With noiseless training data, one false accept can make the max-margin solution ignore the core. In this model, sensitivity-based discovery removes shortcuts in decreasing salience. We also give a model-agnostic certificate, valid under content-independent validation, whose validator-error term comes from an audit. Simulations match the theory, and deep networks on synthetic and real images show the predicted Whac-a-Mole signs, monotone worst-group accuracy and validator fragility. The resulting procedure, Peel (Propose-Edit-Evaluate-Learn), can propose candidate edits from the model's own mistakes. Given an oracle library of the benchmarks' intervention operators, it selects the right ones and beats group-label methods on Waterbirds and UrbanCars. With fully generated edits, run end to end from three discovery seeds, it improves on empirical risk minimization (ERM) on five of six benchmarks but trails exact edits.

authors.name: Ali Alavi

papers.title: CLAIR: Consistent LLM Adaptation via Index-free Reprogramming
papers.summary: Time-series forecasting with pretrained large language models (LLMs) uses contextualized patch representations, raising the question of how to align them. Matching patches at the same temporal position is natural, but self-attention allows each patch state to incorporate information from elsewhere in the input window, suggesting that useful correspondences can extend across positions. This flexibility, however, does not necessarily translate into consistent forecasts: similar patch states may play different roles when used in their original temporal order. To address both issues, we propose CLAIR (Consistent LLM Adaptation via Index-free Reprogramming), a teacher-guided framework that combines patch-level transport alignment (PTA) and forecast-level consistency (FC). A clean-view exponential moving average (EMA) teacher guides a mildly perturbed student, with PTA establishing soft, representation-dependent correspondences and FC encouraging agreement at corresponding future steps. The forecasting head retains the original patch order. We test this combination through controlled comparisons: while PTA and index-wise alignment perform similarly without FC, PTA+FC under EMA supervision reduces horizon-averaged mean squared error (MSE) by 2.1% on ETTh1 and 2.6% on ETTm1 relative to Index+FC. The same preference for PTA+FC emerges in comparisons with alternative matching strategies on Weather and ETTh2. Beyond these controls, CLAIR achieves the lowest horizon-averaged MSE on five of six long-term benchmarks and the lowest aggregate overall weighted average (OWA) on M4 among evaluated methods, with competitive few-shot performance. As the teacher and transport are used only during training, inference requires only the student.

authors.name: Dongkuk Kim, Jungkyu Shin, Yoonhyuk Choi, Jong Wook Kim, Beakcheol Jang

papers.title: How many mistakes does it take to learn an interval? Exact Littlestone dimensions of intervals and their unions
papers.summary: The Littlestone dimension of a hypothesis class equals the smallest number of mistakes an online learner can guarantee against an adaptive adversary. For discrete intervals and unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points, only its order of growth was known. We determine it exactly. For every switch budget $k$ (with both end labels fixed when $k$ is odd), the smallest size on which $d$ mistakes can be forced follows a three-regime law: $d+1$ while $d\le k$, then $2d-k+1$, and beyond $d=\lceil 3k/2\rceil+k-1$ doubling the size adds exactly $k$ mistakes. Unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points correspond to $k=2j$ and size $m+1$, and a single interval gives the thresholds $1,2,3,5,7,10,14,20,\dots$. The natural learner that waits for a positive example and binary-searches both endpoints is not optimal: it can be forced into one extra mistake for 50,847 of the domain sizes below $10^5$. Upper bounds come from a gap potential and a block-pairing learner, and lower bounds from adversary strategies and a refinement step. These tools give an explicit optimal learner with $O(\log m)$ time per round, which on random streams makes more mistakes on average than the natural learner. For randomised learners, we compute the randomised Littlestone dimension of thresholds exactly and prove that a greedy adversary forces an explicit closed-form number of expected mistakes on intervals; this bound is within $0.64$ of optimal and, we conjecture, exact (confirmed for $m\le70$). Exact computation tests every result, and the formulas for every switch budget are machine-checked in Lean 4.

authors.name: Miit Daga, Swarna Priya Ramu

papers.title: The Complexity of Oracle-Efficient Realizable Transductive Learning
papers.summary: In realizable transductive online learning, the learner knows the entire sequence of $T$ instances in advance, and the labels are consistent with one of $N$ hypotheses. With explicit access to the hypothesis class, the halving algorithm makes at most $\log_2 N$ mistakes. Can a comparable guarantee be achieved using only polynomially many empirical risk minimization (ERM) queries? We answer this question negatively, even for a weighted-ERM oracle that optimizes arbitrary real-valued linear objectives and returns a complete maximizing hypothesis. For every fixed $\beta\in(0,1)$ and every randomized learner making polynomially many oracle queries, there exists a fixed realizable instance with exactly $N=2^{\lfloor T^\beta\rfloor}$ hypotheses on which the learner makes $\Omega_\beta(\sqrt{T\log N})$ mistakes in expectation. This matches the agnostic-rate upper bound achieved by random playout using $O(T)$ oracle calls. The separation persists for much smaller classes as well: along a sequence with $\log N=\Theta((\log T)^2)$, we establish a mistake lower bound of $\exp(\Omega(\log T/\log\log T))$. Our main technical contribution is a composition lemma that combines two realizable prediction problems such that their mistake lower bounds add, up to a small loss, while their hypothesis class sizes grow only additively. Iterating this lemma yields a family of hard instances spanning the desired parameter regimes, establishing a sharp separation between information-theoretic and oracle-efficient mistake guarantees.

authors.name: Changlong Wu

papers.title: Operating-Condition Normalization in C-MAPSS: Matched Historical Baselines, Multi-Seed Robustness, and Prognostic-Score Trade-offs
papers.summary: Operating-state changes can obscure turbofan degradation signals, but a reduction in remaining-useful-life (RUL) error after condition-wise standardization may reflect weaknesses of the comparison features instead of a unique benefit of normalization. A controlled retrospective audit examines NASA C-MAPSS FD002 and FD004 with engine-disjoint folds, raw condition identifiers, two constructions of causal history, early-life baselines, and continuous operating-setting correction. Ridge regression, random forests and XGBoost are compared under explicit training-engine-only fitting rules. The previously reported XGBoost FD004 terminal RMSE decreased from 30.38 to 29.08 cycles following six-condition standardization; however, raw sensor values accompanied by condition-matched histories and condition identifiers achieved 28.09 cycles, reversing the naive point estimate ranking, although the paired-engine interval spans zero. For FD002, normalized XGBoost reduced terminal RMSE yet increased the asymmetric NASA score (12,616 to 13,289). Additional model-seed, condition count, RUL-cap, grouped-validation and explanation checks test sensitivity rather than postulating a universally optimal representation. The six clusters reproduce known simulator operating regimes; no new condition discovery algorithm, causal diagnostic method, or field ready prognostic system is claimed. Since the official test endpoints were also used in earlier exploratory comparisons, all newly examined alternatives are reported as retrospective benchmark evidence, not as results from a pristine confirmatory holdout.

authors.name: Mohammad Adeel

papers.title: Joint Client Scheduling and Resource Allocation for Optimal Federated Learning over Wireless Networks
papers.summary: Federated learning often relies on partial client participation because full participation is costly in cross-device wireless systems with limited uplink resources, heterogeneous channel conditions, energy constraints, and strict upload deadlines. However, partial participation introduces sampling variance, causing the sampled update to deviate from the full-participation update. Existing optimal client sampling methods reduce this variance but usually rely on simplified client-count budgets, while wireless-aware scheduling methods account for communication constraints but do not directly optimize sampling variance. This paper proposes resource-aware optimal client sampling (RAOCS), a unified variance-minimizing client scheduling framework under uplink resource-block, round deadline, update-information, and energy constraints. The resulting problem admits a capped water-filling solution that balances client update importance, wireless resource cost, and energy feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that RAOCS achieves accuracy comparable to that of OCS while reducing the average upload time per iteration by more than a factor of 252.

authors.name: Ahmad Dabaja, Rachid El-Azouzi

papers.title: ArrythML-II: An Optimized TinyML Framework for ECG Arrhythmia Detection and Multi-Class Beat Classification on Wearable Devices
papers.summary: This paper presents ArrythML-II, an optimized TinyML framework for on-device ECG arrhythmia detection and multi-class beat classification on wearable platforms. A systematic hyperparameter optimization framework is developed to identify compact autoencoder architectures for binary ECG arrhythmia detection. A custom scoring mechanism jointly considers detection performance, reconstruction-error thresholds, and model size to guide architecture selection. The framework is further extended to six-class ECG beat classification using a lightweight classifier derived from the optimized autoencoder architecture. Both models are INT8 quantized and deployed using TensorFlow Lite Micro on a custom-developed, battery-operated, single-lead ECG device based on the PSoC~6 microcontroller. The deployed autoencoder and classifier have model sizes of approximately 44~KB and 22~KB, respectively, with end-to-end processing times of 5.1~ms and 4.7~ms per ECG segment. Model inference accounts for 3.95~ms and 1.38~ms of these processing times, respectively. In the refined arrhythmia detection evaluation using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, the autoencoder achieved an accuracy of 84.76\%, precision of 82.68\%, and recall of 77.99\%. The multi-class classifier achieved 82.29\% accuracy, weighted precision of 90.18\%, and weighted recall of 82.29\%. Beyond offline model evaluation, the wearable platform is validated using preloaded ECG segments, live ECG signals, and an ESP32-S3-based ECG emulator that replays annotated MIT-BIH recordings as analog waveforms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating optimized TinyML models into wearable platforms for real-time ECG analysis.

authors.name: Nagarajan S, Kurian Polachan

papers.title: Synthetic EHR Generators Should Be Audited Like LLMs
papers.summary: Synthetic electronic health record (EHR) generation is increasingly adopting large autoregressive models, yet privacy evaluation has not kept pace, relying heavily on similarity-based heuristics and aggregate metrics that can obscure patient-specific memorisation. We argue that these models should additionally undergo LLM-style memorisation audits at the level of individual patient records. We support this position by comparing membership-inference evaluations across four prominent autoregressive EHR generators, highlighting inconsistent evaluation practices in patient representations and attack procedures. We evaluate trajectory reconstruction from partial context and introduce randomly assigned patient-level canaries to distinguish memorised associations from clinical generalisation. We examine these methods in a GPT-2-style model deliberately overfit to 1,000 MIMIC-IV patient trajectories, creating a controlled setting in which memorisation should be readily detectable. The model systematically recovers training patients' canaries, and their trajectory reconstruction approaches perfect accuracy with increasing context. Held-out patients show no systematic canary recovery, while reconstruction remains low and improves only marginally with additional context. These experiments establish a positive-control baseline for further evaluation of these methods in realistically trained models.

authors.name: Inigo Stibbe, Padmanabhan Ramnarayan, A. Aldo Faisal

papers.title: RadAG: Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment of Diffusion Models
papers.summary: Diffusion and flow-based models have achieved remarkable success in generation, yet their samples often remain suboptimal in fidelity and text alignment. Two lines of inference-time methods address this: extrapolation guidance, such as classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its variants, and reward guidance, which aligns samples with reward models of human preference.
