papers.title: Which Model for Which Role? Cost-Efficient Pareto Recommendation for LLM Agentic Workflows
papers.summary: LLM agentic workflows increasingly employ different models for specialized roles. Users may prefer different trade-offs between task quality and deployment cost, sometimes also considering latency. Finding good assignments incurs a separate search cost from evaluating multiple candidates. We introduce Cost-Coupled Gittins (CC-Gittins), a multi-objective extension of single-objective cost-aware Gittins search for Pareto recommendation. It exploits the coupling between evaluation and deployment costs: assignments that cost more to deploy also cost more to evaluate. The search alternates between seeking higher quality and lower deployment cost, reusing each evaluation to inform both searches. After each batch, CC-Gittins recommends assignments that are nondominated under uncertainty-adjusted estimates of quality and deployment cost. We evaluate CC-Gittins on eight quality--cost matrices from workflows with two to five roles and up to 1,681 candidate assignments. We also evaluate the method with latency as a third objective. Across the eight benchmarks, CC-Gittins recovers a substantial fraction of the true Pareto frontier at roughly 10% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost, and recovers most of the frontier with few false positives by 30%.

authors.name: Qian Xie, Yueli He, Wenyue Hua, Sripad Karne, Armaan Agrawal, Nikos Pagonas, Eugene Wu, Kostis Kaffes, Tianyi Peng, Nairen Cao

papers.title: CaPS: A causal world model for out-of-distribution physical parameter shifts
papers.summary: A world model that serves as a robot's digital twin has to keep working when the robot changes, for example when its links become heavier than anything seen in training. We study this case on the TriFinger robot in CausalWorld, assuming that the link masses and the low-level control law are known. Our model, CaPS (a causal world model for physical parameter shifts), gives each finger a learned energy in which every movable link contributes a term scaled by its measured mass, plus one term that does not depend on mass. Inertia and bias forces both come from this energy, actions pass through the known proportional-derivative controller, and a residual network that never sees the masses accounts for contact. Trained with light links, CaPS forecasts 100 steps open loop on three disjoint test ranges whose mean masses are 1.86, 2.75, and 3.75 times the training mean, with median joint R2 of 0.773, 0.779, and 0.750; an ensemble-residual variant, CaPS-Ens, reaches 0.801, 0.784, and 0.753. Compared with separately trained controls that see only the training-mean mass, the true masses improve both models in all ten runs at every shift. A rigid-body calculation traces the mass-independent term to the fingertips, whose mass is not intervened on, and adding the same term to ModLaNet improves it at every shift.

authors.name: Chu Lin, Yi Sun

papers.title: Variational Optimal Control for Diffusion Guidance
papers.summary: Sampling-time guidance and reward-based post-training act on different variables but share a core geometric objective: realizing an output-space improvement through a generative model. We organize both around a Jacobian pullback evaluated with respect to either the current noisy state or the trainable parameters. Formulating current-state conditional variational optimal control (VOC) yields Variational Optimal Guidance (VOG), which transports a terminal reward proxy into a covariance-weighted sampling correction. Under a linear-subspace denoising model, the exact pullback has no component normal to the data subspace. Distilled Variational Optimal Control (DVOC) realizes the parameter-space counterpart of this local control principle: projected reward ascent constructs a bounded endpoint displacement within a local trust region, and a sparse, forward-pinned Euler surrogate transports it to LoRA parameters. Empirically, VOG reduces DiT-XL/2 FID on ImageNet from 2.27 to 2.04 at 250 sampling steps and from 7.58 to 4.44 at 25 steps. After 20 updates on Z-Image-Turbo, DVOC improves HPSv3++ and four held-out evaluator scores over the untrained model and leads all trained comparators on these five means, while CLIP remains close to the base and DeQA declines across all trained methods. The shared pullback interface cleanly separates the desired output change from the model derivative and the actuation variable.

authors.name: Ruoyu Wang, Xinyi Ye, Yunshuo Shi, Liangyu Yuan, Beier Zhu, Chi Zhang

papers.title: Multi-Token Prediction Done Right
papers.summary: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient-recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found at https://github.com/JaydenTeoh/Soft-MTP.

authors.name: Jayden Teoh

papers.title: Auditing Contextual Knowledge in Multimodal Inference: A Controlled Study with Alpha-TCM
papers.summary: Knowledge-guided multimodal prediction requires measuring how supplied assumptions affect predictions. We present a controlled knowledge-auditing study using Alpha-TCM, with separately represented observations, supplied knowledge and reviewer decisions. Bayesian committee accounting makes the contextual prior replaceable while observation encoders remain fixed. Fully simulated studies use ten paired seeds and four training sizes to compare context representations and intervene on prior assumptions. A compact-head follow-up does not reproduce the original marginal-fusion improvement at 1,200 cases. A further study crosses head depth and training policy on fresh evaluation cohorts. All 16 point estimates in this study favor knowledge, but only one survives Holm correction: at 600 cases, the two-layer extended-policy model reduces MAE by 0.00306 (1.33%) relative to learned-category conditioning. Extended training improves several methods' absolute performance, while relative advantages remain conditional. Wrong priors increase error in every seed across all tested depths, policies and sizes. Separately calibrated conflict thresholds flag 11.3-12.6% of wrong-prior cases in the compact-head follow-up but provide little guidance about individual prediction damage. The study provides a reproducible way to test supplied knowledge and distinguish predictive gains from sensitivity to misspecified assumptions.

authors.name: Yucheng Liu, Everett X. Wang

papers.title: LatentWeave: Test-Time Latent Optimization for Multimodal Reasoning
papers.summary: Recent advances in test-time optimization have shown that the multimodal reasoning performance of large multimodal language models (MLLMs) can be improved during inference without modifying backbone model parameters. However, existing approaches primarily operate at the prompt or output level, leaving the latent reasoning process largely uncontrolled and insufficient to prevent error accumulation during autoregressive generation. To address this limitation, we propose LatentWeave, a test-time framework that treats multimodal reasoning as a controllable latent trajectory. LatentWeave performs structured Latent Weaving, progressively refining intermediate hidden states segment-wise to correct emerging deviations, and further introduces Reasoning Anchors via lightweight WEAVE tokens to stabilize reasoning structure and guide answer-oriented generation. These mechanisms are designed to enable fine-grained, step-aware intervention in the latent reasoning process while keeping the main MLLM backbone parameters fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improvements over the evaluated baselines; the contribution of latent optimization, anchor training, and additional test-time computation is analyzed separately in the ablation and efficiency studies.

authors.name: Fanci Meng, Kun Wang, Guibin Zhang, Xinlei Yu, Jiaming Zhang, Ming Li, Yang Wang

papers.title: Unsupervised Feature Selection Using Local Intrinsic Dimensionality -- Extended Version
papers.summary: High dimensionality degrades both the efficiency and the effectiveness of learning algorithms, and in many applications no class labels are available to guide dimensionality reduction. This paper proposes LIDFS, an unsupervised feature selection method based on Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID). The method builds on the formal equivalence between LID and the indiscriminability of distance measures. The data matrix is transposed so that each feature is treated as a point, and the LID of each feature is estimated by maximum likelihood from the distances to its $k$ nearest neighboring features. Features with lower LID exhibit greater local discriminability and receive higher importance scores. A refinement step then retains one representative per feature neighborhood and demotes locally redundant features. The result is a complete ranking from which any number of features can be selected without rerunning the procedure. LIDFS does not use any information about labels or the number of classes, and runs in $\mathcal{O}(d^2 n)$ time for $n$ instances and $d$ features. LIDFS is compared with classic and state-of-the-art methods and a random baseline on 23 high-dimensional datasets, the classic benchmark collection. The evaluation uses classification accuracy and AUC with five downstream classifiers, as well as clustering accuracy and normalized mutual information, over both full and aggressive selection ranges. LIDFS ranks first in the supervised evaluations and first or tied second in the clustering-based evaluations. It belongs to the top statistical group together with methods that require the number of classes, and it runs faster than its closest competitor. Several recent methods, by contrast, fail to outperform the random baseline. A sensitivity analysis shows that small neighborhood sizes yield the best results.

authors.name: Oussama Chelly, Michael E. Houle, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Muhammad Rajabinasab, Arthur Zimek

papers.title: On the Convergence of Vanilla Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise and Index Sampling
papers.summary: Understanding how stochastic gradient noise affects the convergence of Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) is an important problem in stochastic optimization, particularly when the noise exhibits heavy-tailed behavior. In this paper, we investigate the convergence of vanilla Adam in both the expected risk and the empirical risk minimization, focusing on the effects of heavy-tailed population noise and index-sampling noise. For the empirical risk minimization, we establish convergence guarantees under H\"older smoothness, showing that heavy-tailed population noise can affect the convergence bounds through dataset-dependent constants that may increase with the dataset size. For the expected risk minimization, we firstly establish both asymptotic and non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for vanilla Adam under H\"older smoothness and bounded $\mathfrak{p}$-th moment assumptions, allowing for infinite-variance stochastic gradient noise. In particular, we derive explicit convergence rates in terms of the expected squared gradient norm and show that the convergence rates deteriorate as $\mathfrak{p}$ decreases. Numerical experiments further support these theoretical findings and provide empirical evidence for the relevance of the sufficient conditions underlying our convergence analysis.

authors.name: Kanata Oowada, Hideaki Iiduka

papers.title: Ground-Wing: A Parametric 3D Wing-in-Ground-Effect Dataset for Benchmarking Neural Surrogate Models
papers.summary: This paper presents a CFD dataset of a highly parametrized 3D wing operating in ground effect, designed for benchmarking neural surrogate models for aerodynamic prediction, using a wing shape and flow conditions typically encountered in motorsport applications. The dataset comprises 770 RANS simulations of 194 unique wing configurations, sampled across 27 airfoil profile variants and 4 distances from the ground, spanning variations in wing sweep, chord, taper, angle of attack, and tip twist. Six neural network architectures representing distinct paradigms --- convolutional (DoMINO), graph-based (X-MeshGraphNet), transformer-based (AB-UPT, GeoTransolver, GAOT), and JEPA-based (AeroJEPA) --- are evaluated on their ability to predict surface pressure coefficient and wall shear stress distributions, from which integral drag and lift coefficients are recovered. The dataset is intended to be used as a challenging benchmark for surrogate CFD models, due to the uniqueness of the ground effect being absent from other wing and airfoil datasets. The dataset is available for download at https://huggingface.co/datasets/andreacenzato/Ground-Wing

authors.name: Andrea Cenzato, Lukas Karch, Andre Luckow, Yoran Pichon, Francesco Pasqua, Abouzar Ghasemi, Rishikesh Ranade, Ira Shokar, Julia Kowalski

papers.title: TripletAD: Weakly Supervised Anomaly Detection in Embedding Space with Rare Anomalies and Scarce Labels
papers.summary: As AI and agentic systems automate more processes with less human review, data is increasingly represented, and passed between systems, as embeddings produced by pre-trained models. Detecting rare deviations in these embeddings is becoming a critical guardrail, yet anomaly detection methods were largely developed for hand-built tabular features, where gradient-boosted trees remain the method of choice. We propose TripletAD, a weakly supervised detector for embedding spaces in which anomalies are rare. TripletAD learns a triplet-margin embedding in which every triplet contains an anomaly, so the few anomalies are reused across the entire training set instead of being diluted by it, and calibrates a linear scoring head with a partial cross-entropy on anomalies and a relative-contrast hinge that separates the mean scores of anomalous and normal samples. Across 28 embedding datasets spanning text, images, speech and industrial inspection, TripletAD is consistently among the best-performing methods, matching or exceeding established state-of-the-art weakly supervised detectors (DevNet, PReNet and DeepSAD), supervised contrastive learning and gradient-boosted trees, and it outperforms them when anomalies are rare. On naturally rare speech data it is 43% above the strongest baseline and more than twice the established detectors; at a 1% anomaly rate it has the highest mean AUCPR of seven methods, 20% above DevNet; and pooled over 74 rare-anomaly settings it has the best average rank, with statistically significant gains over every baseline. In a case study on AI-agent traces, it locates the failing step more often than all six baselines, with accuracy on par with or above that reported for frontier LLM judges, at 0.17 ms per step. The method needs no per-dataset tuning and is insensitive to its loss weights and training length.

authors.name: Sumit Wadhwa, Souvik Nath

papers.title: Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation: Evaluating Hierarchical Policies from Non-Hierarchical Data
papers.summary: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the expected return of a target policy from previously collected data without additional environment interaction. While OPE methods for flat Markovian policies are well studied, little work has addressed evaluating hierarchical policies in which a high-level policy selects temporally extended options that generate primitive actions until a termination condition is met. The primary existing approach applies per-decision importance sampling at the option level, but requires option-annotated trajectories and exhibits variance that still grows with the horizon. For non-hierarchical policies, fitted Q-evaluation (FQE) typically achieves lower error than importance sampling by leveraging the classic Bellman equation for policy evaluation; however, a naive extension of FQE to hierarchical policies results in a biased policy value estimate. In this paper, we introduce Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation (IO-FQE), which estimates a value function in the augmented state-option space; this approach enables OPE of hierarchical policies even when we lack annotations of what option was run in the data. We develop two continuous-action instantiations of IO-FQE and show on long-horizon hierarchical continuous control tasks (AntMaze navigation and OGBench Puzzle manipulation) that IO-FQE eliminates the bias incurred by a naive application of FQE to hierarchical policies and substantially lowers mean squared-error compared to option-level importance sampling.

authors.name: Yunfu Deng, Josiah P. Hanna

papers.title: GenISys: Integrated Ship Systems Design Using Subsystem-Conditional Tabular Diffusion
papers.summary: Ship design requires coordinating coupled subsystems to satisfy engineering constraints and balance competing performance and cost objectives. Generative artificial intelligence has supported component design, but integrated ship generation must also account for interactions among hull geometry, structure, propulsion, and operation. This paper presents GenISys, a framework for generating integrated systems, demonstrated through early-stage bulk-carrier design. Its dataset contains 217,999 proposed designs, including 16,247 that satisfy the formulated engineering constraints. The proposed simultaneous conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (SCDDPM) generates subsystems together, allowing each subsystem model to respond to changes elsewhere during generation. Experiments compare this approach with monolithic whole-ship generation and sequential subsystem generation across five independent training runs per architecture. In a study targeting lower cost per tonne of cargo transported, designs were generated for a required voyage range of 5,000 nautical miles. SCDDPM produced designs satisfying the formulated engineering constraints and meeting a common low-cost target in 55.70% of generation requests, compared with 51.10% for the monolithic model and 47.54% for the sequential model. These correspond to 9.0% and 17.2% more qualifying designs, respectively, while maintaining similar estimated transport costs. These results show how generative artificial intelligence can coordinate subsystems to generate feasible, high-performing integrated systems.

authors.name: Noah J. Bagazinski, Faez Ahmed

papers.title: Probabilistic State Space Enumeration in Neural Network Computation
papers.summary: Can we faithfully approximate the output of a dense Transformer multilayer perceptron (MLP) by enumerating only a small set of probable channel configurations? Our primary objective is to characterize and control approximation error under a fixed mask budget. Probabilistic state space enumeration (PSSE) links the selected masks to the residual in the MLP output. For a partition into channel groups, probability weighting makes the expectation over all possible masks equal to the dense output. We derive the exact residual for any retained set by weighting each group's output by the fraction of its inclusion probability outside the set. The omitted probability mass multiplied by the largest masked-output norm therefore bounds the absolute error. To select masks, NORDER-II adapts ORDER-II from network reliability. Under independent group inclusions, it computes an ordering once per layer from frozen weights and finds the $B$ masks with greatest total probability mass without listing all possibilities. With 32 groups, the mean number of masks needed to capture 95% of the mass ranges from 1,020 to 4,725 across models, out of more than four billion possibilities. Across 168 MLP layers in six language models, this approximation yields lower mean relative error than both ordinary and bias-corrected uniform sampling in all 1,008 equal-count comparisons. Our secondary objective is to improve inference efficiency through pruning. We count the distinct channels covered by each layer's retained masks and use those counts to allocate a fixed projection budget offline. The pruned models achieve lower held-out perplexity than both top-$k$ baselines in all 36 settings at matched MLP projection FLOPs. Target projection savings of 10%, 20%, and 30% yield mean decoder MLP speedups of $1.11\times$, $1.23\times$, and $1.36\times$ over dense MLPs, respectively.

authors.name: Victor O. K. Li, Yang Han, Jacqueline C. K. Lam

papers.title: From Shots to Rallies to Sets: Hierarchy-Aligned Multi-Task Learning for Next-Shot Prediction in Racket Sports
papers.summary: Next-shot prediction in racket sports requires learning from event data with different match structures, recorded attributes, and label vocabularies. Table tennis, badminton, and tennis nevertheless share a hierarchy in which shots form rallies and rallies form higher scoring units. We present MT-HTA, a hierarchy-aligned multi-task Transformer that uses this structure to jointly predict the attributes of the next shot. A hierarchical temporal Transformer captures event progression at each level of the hierarchy, a feature-token path models interactions among semantic fields rather than along the time axis, and task-specific attention retrieves information from hierarchical summaries and player context. The architecture supports three- and four-level hierarchies and sport-dependent task sets. Across four datasets from three sports, the final MT-HTA achieves the highest mean task-averaged F1 among the compared main models. Ablations on table tennis support the combination of hierarchical encoding, task attention, and feature-token interaction. Additional modules alter the balance between classification scores and spatial error rather than improving every metric. These results support a reusable architecture for heterogeneous racket-sport event data. We release the code for reproducibility. https://github.com/gndd1221/For-Sports-event-modeling-with-rally-and-score-hierarchical-A-Multi-Task-Hierarchical-Transformer

authors.name: Chao-Wei Cai, Min-Te Sun, Sheng Kuang Wu, Hung-Hsuan Chen

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning for Inventory Control under Regime-Switching Demand: A Controlled Comparison of LSTM, MLP, and (s,S) Policies
papers.summary: Classical inventory policies such as (s,S) are provably optimal under stationary demand but cannot adapt when demand switches between hidden regimes, and memoryless deep reinforcement learning policies, confined to a fixed observation window, cannot maintain a belief over latent demand structure. We ask whether a recurrent policy offers a measurable advantage over both a memoryless policy and a classical baseline under regime-switching demand, and how that advantage scales with supply-chain lead time. We build a custom Gymnasium environment in which daily demand is generated by a two-state hidden Markov process with Poisson emissions, so that the regime is known at evaluation time but hidden from the agent. An optimised (s,S) heuristic, an MLP PPO agent, and an LSTM Recurrent PPO agent are trained under matched compute and evaluated at lead times of 0, 3, 6, and 10 days over 30 deterministic episodes each. The recurrent policy outperforms both alternatives at every lead time, and its margin over the MLP widens monotonically with lead time, from parity at lead time 0 to 2.17$\times$ at lead time 10. Principal component analysis of the LSTM hidden state explains the widening gap: the representation shifts from encoding a binary regime indicator at short lead times to encoding multi-step pipeline state at long lead times. Recurrent memory becomes the decisive architectural factor as the credit-assignment horizon lengthens.

authors.name: Alex Haines, Nathanael L. Baisa

papers.title: Asymmetric Multimodal Learning: The Alignment Redundancy Bound and Decomposed JEPAs
papers.summary: Cross-modal alignment is the default objective for multimodal representation learning, but it rests on an implicit assumption: that the two modalities are roughly symmetric views of the same underlying state. We show that this assumption fails on real multimodal data, and that alignment as a sole objective is provably lossy under informational asymmetry. We formalize the failure through Partial Information Decomposition, proving that cross-modal alignment retains at most the redundant information atom and annihilates the modality-unique and synergistic structure on which asymmetric tasks depend. We give the exact PID decomposition of the alignment information bottleneck, characterize its failure regime, and derive a sufficiency condition that any encoder objective must satisfy to preserve all four informational atoms. We then introduce Decomposed JEPA (D-JEPA), which realizes this condition by factorizing each modality's latent space into an aligned shared core and a private fiber anchored by contextual masked prediction. On compositional reasoning benchmarks, alignment-only training undergoes catastrophic semantic collapse on relational queries; D-JEPA prevents this collapse, recovering the referent structure alignment discards, restoring most of the mutual information available from a frozen backbone, and producing positive multimodal synergy where alignment inverts it. Information-theoretic and causal audits confirm that the recovered information is causally localized in the private fibers.

authors.name: Yusuf Shihata

papers.title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
papers.summary: Symmetry is a foundational principle of physics: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the coordinate frame, unit system, or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet today's leading neural surrogates lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation), rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs. Because the boundary determines the interior solution, ISLA encodes the posed boundary once into learned slices and evaluates arbitrary interior points independently through a tree-accelerated learned boundary kernel. Inputs are nondimensionalized in scales computed from the boundary, sums over boundary cells are area-weighted quadratures that converge under mesh refinement, and geometry enters only as distances and relative angles to equivariant slice anchors, making the model equivariant to rigid motions and reflections up to optional token subsampling and tree clustering. On AeroZoo, 2,816 3D flows spanning diverse geometries, poses, physical scales, and boundary conditions, ISLA's mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are 1.9 and 2.2 times lower than the best baseline's. On full AirfRANS, ISLA is second only to an explicit boundary-integral network (GLOBE), with errors 1.6 to 2.6 times lower than the better of Transolver's and GeoTransolver's in every field.

authors.name: Peter Sharpe

papers.title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics
papers.summary: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on single-family, fixed-domain datasets that cannot test the minimum bar for an aerodynamic foundation model: predicting CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (URANS) solutions with a transition model across seven geometry families, eight enclosures, and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem as a solver receives it: boundary meshes grouped by condition type, prescribed values, and fluid properties. The 2,816 time-mean-stable samples form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, mean engineering metrics with an overall flow score $S_{\mathrm{flow}}$ (1.000 for uniform inlet flow), and 22 frozen geometry-disjoint splits holding out shapes, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts, and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's mean velocity error from 89.8% to 15.2% of inlet speed (uniform flow: 44.0%; $S_{\mathrm{flow}} = 0.290$). ISLA, a boundary-driven transformer, reaches 8.2% ($S_{\mathrm{flow}} = 0.153$; 0.123 with boundary targets), about 6 times mesh-refinement sensitivity. On shared test samples, holding out a geometry family barely changes ISLA's mean velocity error, whereas holding out enclosures or boundary-condition layouts raises it 3.8 to 8.4 times. The dataset is public; the scoring code will be released.

authors.name: Peter Sharpe, Carmelo Gonzales, Corey Adams, Mohammadmehdi Ataei, Sanjay Choudhry

papers.title: On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions
papers.summary: Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), as well as Monte Carlo KL estimates and entropy. When the distributions are nearly equal, rounding and cancellation issues affect the forward and gradient computations. These issues can affect settings using divergences in optimization objectives, such as knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. We propose numerically stable reformulations and provide example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests.

authors.name: Brandon Amos

papers.title: Multi-Objective Causal Bandits: Minimal Intervention Space and Policy-Level Learning
papers.summary: Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. We study multi-objective causal bandits with multiple reward nodes, where actions correspond to interventions on subsets of variables in a causal graph and performance is evaluated through Pareto optimality. Existing approaches to multi-objective bandits often rely on pairwise Pareto dominance or optimize a fixed scalarization. However, pairwise comparisons alone can fail to identify actions dominated by randomized policies, whose expected reward vectors lie in the convex hull of action-level rewards. Thus, an intervention may be suboptimal even if no single intervention dominates it, because it can be dominated by a randomized policy over other interventions. We formalize this policy-level phenomenon and show that it has consequences for both causal action-space reduction and online learning. First, we provide a necessary-and-sufficient graphical characterization of possibly Pareto- optimal minimal intervention sets. Our characterization yields a minimal, sound, and complete candidate intervention family from the graph alone, correcting prior formulations that may include intervention sets that are never Pareto-optimal under any compatible structural causal model. Second, over this reduced intervention space, we design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions using dominance tests against convex combinations of other actions, and prove logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret. Finally, we study constrained multi-objective causal bandits, where feasibility and optimality may be realized only with randomized policies, and develop an online UCB-style constrained bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.

authors.name: Muhammad Qasim Elahi, Mahsa Ghasemi, Murat Kocaoglu

papers.title: UrbanROI: Causal Modeling for Regional ROI Forecasting under POI Entry
papers.summary: As urban commercial environments continue to evolve rapidly, accurately modeling the economic impact of point of interest (POI) entry is essential for supporting data-driven advertising allocation, merchant onboarding, and regional business decision-making. Existing return on investment (ROI) prediction methods mainly focus on individual ads or merchants, overlooking the interaction effects among POIs and failing to capture the causal influence of structural changes in urban commercial ecosystems. In this paper, we introduce a novel research problem -- regional ROI forecasting under POI entry, which aims to predict the future ROI trajectory of a commercial region after the introduction of a new POI by modeling temporal ROI evolution and competition-driven interactions among surrounding POIs. To address these challenges, we propose UrbanROI, an intervention-aware causal forecasting framework for region-level economic outcome prediction. UrbanROI leverages an Interaction-aware Regional Graph Module to explicitly model competitive relationships among POIs based on user request contexts, spatial proximity, and request-level commercial signals, and constructs structurally aligned treatment and control graphs to simulate factual and counterfactual regional states. Extensive experiments on large-scale real-world POI and advertising datasets demonstrate that UrbanROI consistently outperforms strong baselines in post-entry regional ROI forecasting. The results demonstrate its effectiveness in temporal economic modeling, inter-POI interaction representation, and intervention-aware forecasting, providing support for regional economic analysis in dynamic urban commercial systems. Source code is available at GitHub.

authors.name: Zhaoqi Zhang, Miao Xie, Linyou Cai, Qianlong Xie, Xingxing Wang, Siqiang Luo, Gao Cong

papers.title: Find, Count and Fix Wrong Labels from a Trained Model, without Clean Labels or Shared Data
papers.summary: How many labels in a training set are wrong, and which ones? The question arises when labels are accepted from annotators and when a trained model is taken over with its training data. Readings from a model's outputs fail once it fits its wrong labels, because a fitted wrong label has a small loss and the prediction agrees with it. We read it from the per-example gradients of a single trained model. We normalise the magnitudes of an example's gradient into a gradient allocation, which records where the example asks the network to change, and compare it with the mean allocation of every class. An example is flagged when relabelling it as its nearest other class makes its allocation fit better than under its own label, and the share of flagged examples is the reading of the noise rate. The rule has no threshold, needs no clean data, held-out set or further training, and the data owner can compute the few numbers per example it needs, so the data need not be shared: a decoder trained to invert these numbers recovers images no closer to the originals than the mean image of their class. After the model has fitted 99-100% of its wrong labels, the allocation still separates wrong from right labels with an AUC of 0.94-0.96 on the noisiest human labels of CIFAR-10N, where the loss, gradient norm and self-influence fall to 0.73-0.76. Over 22 image and 9 text settings it is the highest of the scores that read only the final model in every setting. On a fitted model it reads 54-96% of the true noise rate on CIFAR-10, where readings from predictions or feature margins fall to 0-6%. Retraining without the flagged examples raises the test accuracy by up to 47 points, while removing as many random examples does not. Confident learning, given four further trainings on all the data, is not significantly better and flags less precisely. Auditing 5,000 images takes 14 to 27 seconds on one GPU.

authors.name: Yuchen Li, Zongqi Fan, Xintong Li, Nguyen H. Tran, Ken-Tye Yong

papers.title: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?
papers.summary: Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.

authors.name: Hanlin Wu, Yifei Wang, Zhicheng Cai, Wenxuan Tan, Jiahao Li, Huan-ang Gao, Wei-Ying Ma, Ya-Qin Zhang, Jingjing Liu, Hao Zhou

papers.title: Probing Physics in Motion Diffusion Models Against Their Own Estimate
papers.summary: Recent studies report that video diffusion models "know more than they show": physical properties decode better from their activations than from their inputs or outputs. But a diffusion model computes its clean-sample estimate from those same activations, so such a comparison measures how easily a readout extracts the information. Whether the model hides anything is a separate question. We set out to find hidden physical knowledge in kinematic text-to-motion diffusion models, where the physics of every intermediate estimate can be computed exactly, and recorded every layer along the sampling trajectories of MDM (two checkpoints) and MotionDiffuse. Against the usual baselines the layers do look ahead of the model's own estimate on balance and flight. With every readout tuned the same way, the estimate closes the gap: for balance and flight, adding a layer gains at most 0.01, a size that a positive control shows we would detect. The fall rate of jumps is the one clear exception. Early in denoising, MDM's layers add about 0.08 in $R^2$ (up to 0.11 in a refit) that the estimate does not yet show, and the gain fades as sampling proceeds; on MotionDiffuse it is small and not robust. The estimate also flags floating samples without training, but aborting them saves under a tenth of the compute. In a video model, plausibility that linear probes miss in Wan 2.1's clean latent becomes readable after one fixed nonlinearity.

authors.name: Saeed Ghorbani

papers.title: Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.summary: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are effective tools for mechanistic interpretability by decomposing neural representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, a single sparse representation in traditional SAEs is responsible for both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, which are not guaranteed to align. To separate these objectives, we propose DualSAE, a modular framework that augments standard SAEs with a plug-in Residual Branch. A standard SAE serves as the Sparse Branch, learning a sparse code that contains the dominant semantics of the input. The added Residual Branch models the non-semantic information omitted by the Sparse Branch. We ensure that the contributions of the two branches towards the overall reconstruction have minimal overlap through a decorrelation loss. We also adopt a two-stage training strategy that first stabilizes sparse representation learning before coupling with the Residual Branch. Across diverse encoder-SAE configurations on two vision datasets and two language corpora, DualSAE achieves mean relative improvements of approximately 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability (measured by monosemanticity score). Moreover, with more interpretable representations, DualSAE yields consistent performance gains in the downstream applications of topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and LLM steering. Qualitative analysis further suggests that the Sparse Branch indeed preserves dominant semantic content, whereas the Residual Branch captures non-semantic information to improve reconstruction fidelity.

authors.name: Anh Tien Nguyen, Dimitris Samaras, Mahdi S. Hosseini

papers.title: Hierarchical Hybrid-Coordinate Flow Matching for Accurate and Physically Plausible Apo-to-Holo Protein Generation
papers.summary: Predicting holo-like protein conformations from apo structures is essential in structure-based drug design. Most existing apo-to-holo models operate in Cartesian space and achieve strong global accuracy. However, high global accuracy does not ensure physically valid local backbone geometry. Internal-coordinate models offer local control and validity, but regressive generation can amplify angular errors, known as the lever-arm effect. We introduce CrypticFlow, a hierarchical flow-matching model that combines these two complementary representations. An ESM-3-conditioned E(3)-equivariant graph network first generates sparse C$\alpha$ anchors in Cartesian space. A conditional midpoint Transformer then recursively fills the gaps in local internal coordinates. During recursive generation, the decoder constrains the distance between each midpoint and any sequence-adjacent parent anchor to the corresponding apo C$\alpha$-C$\alpha$ distance. On the D3PM test split, CrypticFlow achieves the lowest median and mean C$\alpha$ RMSD at published baseline capacities. Across five independent training models, the median and mean direct RMSD are 1.333 $\pm$ 0.056 angstroms and 2.766 $\pm$ 0.041 angstroms, respectively. The quality of local geometry also improves substantially. Our model achieves 99.58 $\pm$ 0.02% adjacent-distance fidelity and 95.87 $\pm$ 0.25% pseudo-angle fidelity, measured within 0.2 angstroms and 20{\deg} of the holo reference. Then, we reconstruct the predicted C$\alpha$-only traces into all-atom structures using the cg2all coarse-to-all-atom backmapping method and evaluate their physical and geometric quality with MolProbity. Our model achieves a MolProbity score of 3.034 $\pm$ 0.054, outperforming the evaluated baselines. These results show that a hierarchical flow-matching model with hybrid coordinates can recover global accuracy while retaining local fidelity.

authors.name: Minjong Kim, Jaemin Sim, Dongwoo Kim, Myunghyun Jang, Eun-Sol Kim, Juyong Lee

papers.title: Lift Out, Kick In: Decoupling Event Effects for Time Series Forecasting
papers.summary: Real-world time series are often shaped by exogenous events whose effects are superimposed on the system's underlying temporal dynamics. Historical observations therefore entangle persistent dynamics with event-induced deviations, making it difficult to determine which patterns should be extrapolated and which should be attributed to specific event contexts. Existing event-aware forecasting methods can incorporate event information or model event-related variation, but typically treat historical event attribution and future event generation separately. We propose Loki (Lift Out, Kick In), a general event-aware forecasting framework built on a shared Event Response Function (ERF). The ERF models event effects according to event type and relative temporal position and is shared across the historical and forecast windows. Loki lifts out estimated event-induced deviations from historical observations before forecasting, then uses the same ERF to kick in responses to known future events. This formulation separates event-response modeling from temporal forecasting while coupling historical attribution and future generation through a shared mechanism. Across five forecasting benchmarks, Loki achieves the best standardized MAE on all five datasets, reducing error by approximately 2.2%-11.7% over the strongest non-Loki baseline. Ablations and controlled analyses further support the roles of Lift Out, Kick In, shared response modeling, and compatibility across forecasting backbones.

authors.name: Yunying Zhu, Zichun Cao, Siwei Sun, Xiaocen Guo, Shengsheng Lin, Jing Hu, Enyun Yu, Zhichao Zou

papers.title: Quantum-Informed Regularized Poisson Learning for Graph-Based Semi-Supervised Classification
papers.summary: We introduce IPQSSL, a quantum-informed regularized Poisson framework for graph-based semi-supervised classification under scarce labels. Local graph feature contexts are QR factorized, lifted to unitary encodings, and processed by a shared variational circuit whose measurements yield node wise diagonal weights that stabilize a symmetrized Poisson system. We establish positive definiteness of the symmetrized, regularized operator under explicit spectral conditions and derive a Hermitian, block encoding compatible formulation that separates the classical NISQ oriented implementation from a future fault-tolerant pathway. Across seven benchmarks spanning tabular data and a citation network, the effect of regularization is dataset- and budget-dependent: IPQSSL improves over the Poisson baselines on Iris and Wine at all but the single-label budget, reaching 0.946 accuracy on Iris at ten labels per class and at every budget on German Credit, where, however, all methods remain below the majority class rate. Original Poisson remains preferable on Breast Cancer, Heart Disease, Optdigits, and Cora, with the deficit narrowing as the label budget grows on the two largest graphs. Ablations attribute the gains to diagonal stabilization rather than variational training. The result is a resource transparent bridge between Poisson graph learning and quantum linear algebra, with an explicit empirical delineation of when diagonal regularization helps.

authors.name: Hamed Gholipour, Farid Bozorgnia, Hamzeh Mohammadigheymasi, Joao Neves, Moharram Challenger

papers.title: Optimal Rate of Kernel Regression in Large Dimensions
papers.summary: We perform a study on kernel regression for large-dimensional data (where the sample size $n$ is polynomially depending on the dimension $d$ of the samples, i.e., $n\asymp d^{\gamma}$ for some $\gamma >0$ ). We first build a general tool to characterize the upper bound and the minimax lower bound of kernel regression for large dimensional data through the Mendelson complexity $\varepsilon_{n}^{2}$ and the metric entropy $\bar{\varepsilon}_{n}^{2}$ respectively. When the target function falls into the RKHS associated with a (general) inner product model defined on $\mathbb{S}^{d}$, we utilize the new tool to show that the minimax rate of the excess risk of kernel regression is $n^{-1/2}$ when $n\asymp d^{\gamma}$ for $\gamma =2, 4, 6, 8, \cdots$. We then further determine the optimal rate of the excess risk of kernel regression for all the $\gamma>0$ and find that the curve of optimal rate varying along $\gamma$ exhibits several new phenomena including the multiple descent behavior and the periodic plateau behavior. As an application, For the neural tangent kernel (NTK), we also provide a similar explicit description of the curve of optimal rate. As a direct corollary, we know these claims hold for wide neural networks as well.

authors.name: Weihao Lu, Haobo Zhang, Yicheng Li, Manyun Xu, Qian Lin

papers.title: Inferring behind-the-meter demand components from net load via inverse optimization
papers.summary: Understanding and forecasting electricity demand responses to price signals is essential to support the operational decisions of system operators, retailers, and regulators. Traditional time series and machine learning approaches have performed well under stable consumption patterns. However, the rise of active consumers with flexible assets, such as solar-plus-storage systems and electric vehicles, introduces new complexities. These consumers exhibit behind-the-meter behavior that is generally unobservable to system operators and retailers, who can typically only measure net demand at the boundary meters which are located at the connection points to the grid. Net demand reflects the aggregate of baseload consumption, flexible load shifting, and self-generation, all of which may respond nonlinearly to market prices. As these unobservable components grow, existing forecasting models may fail to capture the true dynamics of consumer behavior. This work develops and implements a data-driven inverse optimization framework to reveal behind-the-meter consumption patterns using only net demand data. By analyzing net demand as revealed at the grid connection point, we estimate parameters for a latent optimization model, enabling predictions that infer the unobservable components. This enables more accurate point and probabilistic forecasting of electricity demand under varying price signals. Thus, it provides actionable insights for system operators to improve local congestion management and flexibility extraction, as well as for retailers and aggregators, who could thereby optimize operations and tariffs to leverage consumer flexibility. We validate the methodology using real-world data, demonstrating improved forecasting accuracy over leading machine learning and time-series benchmarks.

authors.name: Adrian Esteban-Perez, Derek Bunn, Yashar Ghiassi-Farrokhfal

papers.title: Enhancing Diabetic Retinopathy Detection with CNN-Based Models: A Comparative Study of UNET and Stacked UNET Architectures
papers.summary: Diabetic Retinopathy DR is a severe complication of diabetes. Damaged or abnormal blood vessels can cause loss of vision. The need for massive screening of a large population of diabetic patients has generated an interest in a computer-aided fully automatic diagnosis of DR. In the realm of Deep learning frameworks, particularly convolutional neural networks CNNs, have shown great interest and promise in detecting DR by analyzing retinal images. However, several challenges have been faced in the application of deep learning in this domain. High-quality, annotated datasets are scarce, and the variations in image quality and class imbalances pose significant hurdles in developing a dependable model. In this paper, we demonstrate the proficiency of two Convolutional Neural Networks CNNs based models, UNET and Stacked UNET utilizing the APTOS Asia Pacific Tele-Ophthalmology Society Dataset. This system achieves an accuracy of 92.81% for the UNET and 93.32% for the stacked UNET architecture. The architecture classifies the images into five categories ranging from 0 to 4, where 0 is no DR and 4 is proliferative DR.

authors.name: Ameya Uppina, S Navaneetha Krishnan, Talluri Krishna Sai Teja, Nikhil N Iyer, Joe Dhanith P R

papers.title: Lightweight Detection and Model Attribution of Synthetic Speech via Residual Statistical Fingerprints
papers.summary: As speech generation technologies advance, so do risks of impersonation, misinformation, and spoofing. We present a lightweight, training-free method for synthetic speech detection and source model attribution. Our method builds on model-specific fingerprints that are computed as the average of the differences between audio signals and their filtered versions, referred to as residuals. Leveraging the Mahalanobis distance of the residual for a given audio signal to these model-specific fingerprints allows to identify the source model as well as to distinguish real from fake audio. A broad set of experiments across multiple synthesis systems and languages demonstrate a supreme performance of the proposed approach on four tasks: open-world single-model attribution, closed-world multi-model attribution, real vs. synthetic speech classification, and out-of-domain detection.

authors.name: Mat\'ias Pizarro, Mike Laszkiewicz, Dorothea Kolossa, Asja Fischer

papers.title: Scaling Structure-Aware Virtual Screening to Billions of Molecules with SPRINT
papers.summary: Virtual screening of small molecules against protein targets can accelerate drug discovery and development by predicting drug-target interactions (DTIs). However, structure-based methods like molecular docking are too slow to allow for broad proteome-scale screens, limiting their application in screening for off-target effects or new molecular mechanisms. Recently, vector-based methods using protein language models (PLMs) have emerged as a complementary approach that bypasses explicit 3D structure modeling. Here, we develop SPRINT, a vector-based approach for screening entire chemical libraries against whole proteomes for DTIs and novel mechanisms of action. SPRINT improves on prior work by using a self-attention based architecture and structure-aware PLMs to learn a co-embedding space for drugs and targets, enabling efficient binder prediction, search, and retrieval. SPRINT achieves competitive enrichment factors in virtual screening on LIT-PCBA, DTI classification benchmarks, and binding affinity prediction benchmarks, while providing interpretability in the form of residue-level attention maps. In addition to being both accurate and interpretable, SPRINT is ultra-fast: querying the whole human proteome against the ENAMINE Real Database (6.7B drugs) for the 100 most likely binders per protein takes 16 minutes. SPRINT promises to enable virtual screening at an unprecedented scale, opening up new opportunities for in silico drug repurposing and development.

authors.name: Andrew T. McNutt, Abhinav K. Adduri, Caleb N. Ellington, Nonso N. Duaka, Tyler J. Katz, Monica T. Dayao, Eric P. Xing, Hosein Mohimani, David R. Koes

papers.title: Financial Volatility and Risk Forecasting Incorporating a Larger Number of Realized Measures
papers.summary: High-frequency data have led to the development of numerous realized volatility measures, while standard Realized GARCH models typically rely on a single measure. This paper proposes three approaches to incorporate information from multiple realized measures within the Realized GARCH framework. First, we develop an autoencoder-enhanced Realized GARCH model that constructs a synthetic realized measure through nonlinear dimensionality reduction. Second, we propose a linear weighted Realized GARCH model that jointly estimates convex aggregation weights and model parameters. Third, we introduce a functional weighted Realized GARCH model based on parsimonious Beta weighting functions. Using approximately 22 years of data for 29 international equity indices, we evaluate the proposed methods in volatility, Value-at-Risk, and Expected Shortfall forecasting. Compared with benchmark models based on single realized measures, equal weighting, and linear dimension reduction, the proposed methods consistently deliver more accurate volatility and risk forecasts.

authors.name: Qianli Zhao, Chao Wang, Richard Gerlach, Giuseppe Storti, Lingxiang Zhang

papers.title: A characteristic-graph reduction for deterministic L-system inference with classical and quantum-heuristic solvers
papers.summary: L-systems are widely used to model and simulate biological growth processes, including plant development. Motivated by the broader goal of automating L-system construction, this paper studies the formal deterministic context-free L-system (D0L-system) inference problem in which the input is a finite, noise-free sequence of strings. We introduce the characteristic graph of a string sequence and prove that the existence of a compatible D0L-system is equivalent to the existence of an independent set of a prescribed size in this graph. This gives polynomial reductions from D0L inference to maximum independent set (MIS) and SAT, and hence an exact classical decision route when combined with an exact MIS or SAT solver. We also describe a Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)-based quantum heuristic for generating candidate independent sets. This heuristic is not a decision procedure for D0L inference, and failure of the heuristic is inconclusive rather than a certificate of nonexistence. We include computational validation on $22$ generated D0L traces and $8$ negative controls, explicitly incorporate known fixed-identity symbols, and report small statevector QAOA simulations. The quantum component is presented as a proof-of-concept candidate generator, not as a claimed quantum speedup; the immediately useful contribution is the characteristic-graph reduction and the exact classical/SAT decision framework it enables.

authors.name: Ali Lotfi, Ian McQuillan, Steven Rayan

papers.title: A Unified Comparative Study with Generalized Conformity Scores for Multi-Output Conformal Regression
papers.summary: Conformal prediction provides a powerful framework for constructing distribution-free prediction regions with finite-sample coverage guarantees. While extensively studied in univariate settings, its extension to multi-output problems presents additional challenges, including complex output dependencies and high computational costs, and remains relatively underexplored. In this work, we present a unified comparative study of nine conformal methods with different multivariate base models for constructing multivariate prediction regions within the same framework. This study highlights their key properties while also exploring the connections between them. Additionally, we introduce two novel classes of conformity scores for multi-output regression that generalize their univariate counterparts. These scores ensure asymptotic conditional coverage while maintaining exact finite-sample marginal coverage. One class is compatible with any generative model, offering broad applicability, while the other is computationally efficient, leveraging the properties of invertible generative models. Finally, we conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across 13 tabular datasets, comparing all the multi-output conformal methods explored in this work. To ensure a fair and consistent comparison, all methods are implemented within a unified code base.

authors.name: Victor Dheur, Matteo Fontana, Yorick Estievenart, Naomi Desobry, Souhaib Ben Taieb

papers.title: Coresets for Density-Based Clustering via Bayesian Predictive Partition Matching
papers.summary: Density-based clustering identifies groups as connected high-density regions, accommodating irregular shapes and reflecting their geometry, but this reliance on density estimation introduces uncertainty into the resulting partitions, which is often costly to quantify. To represent this uncertainty efficiently, we construct a compact representation of the data, or coreset, designed to preserve the distribution of predictive density-based partitions. We sample observations from a Dirichlet process surrogate, smooth them to estimate densities, and use the resulting level sets to partition a common reference set. Starting from a uniform subsample, we learn an affine transformation that improves agreement with full-data partitions by minimizing a tractable approximation to paired expected variation of information. Fresh, independent predictive simulations then guide the selection of the final transformation. Our analysis provides approximation and selection guarantees and establishes consistency for ideal fixed-resolution partitions under geometric conditions. Simulations and an application to mass cytometry show improved partition agreement over uniform subsampling, often matching substantially larger supports.

authors.name: Bernardo Flores

papers.title: New Lower Bounds for Stochastic Non-Convex Optimization through Divergence Decomposition
papers.summary: We study fundamental limits of first-order stochastic optimization in a range of nonconvex settings, including L-smooth functions satisfying Quasar-Convexity (QC), Quadratic Growth (QG), and Restricted Secant Inequalities (RSI). While the convergence properties of standard algorithms are well-understood in deterministic regimes, significantly fewer results address the stochastic case, where only unbiased and noisy gradients are available. We establish new lower bounds on the number of noisy gradient queries to minimize these classes of functions, also showing that they are tight (up to a logarithmic factor) in all the relevant quantities characterizing each class. Our approach reformulates the optimization task as a function identification problem, leveraging divergence decomposition arguments to construct a challenging subclass that leads to sharp lower bounds. Furthermore, we present a specialized algorithm in the one-dimensional setting that achieves faster rates, suggesting that certain dimensional thresholds are intrinsic to the complexity of non-convex stochastic optimization.

authors.name: El Mehdi Saad, Wei-Cheng Lee, Francesco Orabona

papers.title: Learning mechanical systems from real-world data using discrete forced Lagrangian dynamics
papers.summary: We introduce a data-driven method for learning the equations of motion of mechanical systems directly from position measurements. This is particularly relevant in system identification tasks where only positional information is available, such as motion capture, pixel data or low-resolution tracking. Our approach takes advantage of the discrete Lagrange-d'Alembert principle and the forced discrete Euler-Lagrange equations to construct a physically grounded model of the system's dynamics. We decompose the dynamics into conservative and non-conservative components, which are learned separately using feed-forward neural networks. In the absence of external forces, our method reduces to a variational discretization of the action principle naturally preserving the symplectic structure of the underlying Hamiltonian system. We validate our approach on a variety of synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness compared to baseline methods. In particular, we apply our model to (1) measured human motion data and (2) latent embeddings obtained via an autoencoder trained on image sequences. We demonstrate that we can faithfully reconstruct and separate both the conservative and forced dynamics, yielding interpretable and physically consistent predictions

authors.name: Martine Dyring Hansen, Elena Celledoni, Benjamin Kwanen Tapley

papers.title: Scheduling in Queueing Systems with Uncertain and Evolving Holding Costs
papers.summary: In queueing systems, the holding costs of jobs may evolve in uncertain ways. For example, in content moderation for social media platforms, the cost of delaying the review of a content piece is proportional to its view trajectory, which fluctuates and is a priori unknown. To capture such uncertain and evolving holding cost patterns, we consider a queueing model where job states evolve based on a Markov chain with state-dependent instantaneous holding costs. We demonstrate that in the presence of such uncertain and evolving holding costs, the two canonical algorithmic principles, instantaneous-cost ($c\mu$-rule) and expected-remaining-cost ($c\mu/\theta$-rule), are suboptimal. By viewing each job as a Markovian ski-rental problem, we develop a new index-based algorithm, Opportunity-adjusted Remaining Cost (OaRC), that adjusts to the opportunity of serving jobs in the future when uncertainty partly resolves. We show that the suboptimality gap of OaRC scales as $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$, where $N$ is the system size. This bound shows that OaRC achieves asymptotic optimality for overloaded systems when the system size $N$ scales to infinity. Moreover, the bound is independent of the state-space size, which is a desirable property when job states contain contextual information. We corroborate our results with an extensive simulation study based on two holding cost patterns (online ads and user-generated content) that arise in content moderation for social media platforms. Our simulations based on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that OaRC consistently outperforms existing practice, which is based on the two canonical algorithmic principles.

authors.name: Caner Gocmen, Thodoris Lykouris, Deeksha Sinha, Wentao Weng

papers.title: Distribution free M-estimation
papers.summary: The basic question of delineating those statistical problems that are solvable without making any assumptions on the underlying data distribution has long animated statistics and learning theory. This paper characterizes when a convex M-estimation or stochastic optimization problem is solvable in such an assumption-free setting, providing a precise dividing line between solvable and unsolvable problems. The conditions we identify show, perhaps surprisingly, that Lipschitz continuity of the loss being minimized is not necessary for distribution free minimization, and they are also distinct from classical characterizations of learnability in machine learning.

authors.name: Felipe Areces, John C. Duchi

papers.title: Resource-Efficient Quantum Reinforcement Learning on NISQ Devices with Dynamic-Circuit Qubit Reuse and Grover-Based Trajectory Search
papers.summary: A resource-efficient quantum reinforcement learning framework for finite-horizon quantum Markov decision processes is presented, employing dynamic-circuit qubit reuse to reduce the interaction-workspace requirements of multi-step execution. The framework integrates quantum state-transition and reward encoding, dynamic-circuit execution, quantum return evaluation, and Grover-based trajectory search. Its central contribution is a dynamic execution model in which a fixed interaction workspace is reused across sequential agent-environment interactions through mid-circuit measurement, qubit reset, and next-state propagation. For the considered benchmark, this approach reduces the interaction-workspace requirement from 7T qubits under a static circuit to a constant seven qubits, independent of the interaction horizon T. This corresponds to a 66% reduction for the three-step benchmark and transforms the interaction-workspace complexity from O(T) to O(1). Trajectory returns are evaluated using reversible quantum arithmetic, and Grover's algorithm identifies the optimal trajectories, so that return evaluation and trajectory search are performed within a unified quantum-native pipeline. Ideal simulations demonstrate that the dynamic implementation preserves the valid trajectory structure of the static formulation, with quantitative comparisons assessing the agreement between their trajectory distributions. Finally, execution on an IBM Heron-class processor demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed dynamic-circuit architecture on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware.

authors.name: Thet Htar Su, Shaswot Shresthamali, Masaaki Kondo

papers.title: Two Heads Are Better Than One: Audio-Visual Speech Error Correction with Dual Hypotheses
papers.summary: This paper introduces a new paradigm for generative error correction (GER) framework in audio-visual speech recognition (AVSR) that reasons over modality-specific evidences directly in the language space. Our framework, DualHyp, empowers a large language model (LLM) to compose independent N-best hypotheses from separate automatic speech recognition (ASR) and visual speech recognition (VSR) models. To maximize the effectiveness of DualHyp, we further introduce RelPrompt, a noise-aware guidance mechanism that provides modality-grounded prompts to the LLM. RelPrompt offers the temporal reliability of each modality stream, guiding the model to dynamically switch its focus between ASR and VSR hypotheses for an accurate correction. Under various corruption scenarios, our framework attains up to 57.7% error rate gain on the LRS2 benchmark over standard ASR baseline, contrary to single-stream GER approaches that achieve only 10% gain. To facilitate research within our DualHyp framework, we release the code and the dataset comprising ASR and VSR hypotheses at https://github.com/sungnyun/dualhyp.

authors.name: Sungnyun Kim, Kangwook Jang, Sungwoo Cho, Joon Son Chung, Hoirin Kim, Se-Young Yun

papers.title: Fault Detection in Solar Thermal Systems using Probabilistic Reconstructions
papers.summary: Solar thermal systems (STS) present a promising avenue for low-carbon heat generation, with a well-running system providing heat at minimal cost and carbon emissions. However, STS can exhibit faults due to improper installation, maintenance, or operation, often resulting in a substantial reduction in efficiency or even damage to the system. As monitoring at the individual level is economically prohibitive for small-scale systems, automated monitoring and fault detection should be used to address such issues. Recent advances in data-driven anomaly detection, particularly in time series analysis, offer a cost-effective solution by leveraging existing sensors to identify abnormal system states. Here, we apply probabilistic reconstruction-based anomaly detection to the publicly available PaSTS dataset of operational domestic STS, which features real-world complexities and diverse fault types. We combine an LSTM-based Variational Autoencoder with heteroscedastic uncertainty estimation and evaluate it exclusively on systems unseen during training. Our experiments show that reconstruction-based methods detect faults in domestic STS both qualitatively and quantitatively. Our model achieves the best generalisation to unseen systems among all evaluated methods, while a rescaled PCA reconstruction baseline remains competitive on pooled threshold-free metrics. An ablation shows that heteroscedastic uncertainty estimation drives the gain in cross-system generalisation. Finally, we discuss the engineering overhead required to unlock these improvements and make a case for simple deep learning models.

authors.name: Florian Ebmeier, Nicole Ludwig, Jannik Thuemmel, Georg Martius, Volker H. Franz

papers.title: Understanding temperature tuning in energy-based models
papers.summary: Generative models of complex systems often require post hoc parameter adjustments to produce useful outputs. For example, energy-based models for protein design are sampled at an artificially low "temperature" to generate novel, functional sequences. This temperature tuning is a common yet poorly understood heuristic used across machine learning contexts to control the trade-off between generative fidelity and diversity. Here, we develop an interpretable, physically motivated framework to explain this phenomenon. We demonstrate that in systems with a large "energy gap" separating a small fraction of meaningful states from a vast space of unrealistic states, learning from sparse data causes models to systematically overestimate high-energy state probabilities, a bias that lowering the sampling temperature corrects. More generally, we characterize how the optimal sampling temperature depends on the interplay between data size and the system's underlying energy landscape, and that this interplay is sufficient to elicit the tuning phenomenon; regularizing while training can contribute, but is not necessary. Crucially, our results show that lowering the sampling temperature is not always desirable. We identify the conditions under which raising it results in better generative performance. Our framework reveals that post hoc temperature tuning is indicative of both specific properties of the true data distribution and the limits of the learned model due to insufficient data availability.

authors.name: Peter W Fields, Vudtiwat Ngampruetikorn, David J Schwab, Stephanie E Palmer

papers.title: Graph-based Nearest Neighbors with Dynamic Updates via Random Walks
papers.summary: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANN) is a common way to retrieve relevant search results, especially now in the context of large language models and retrieval augmented generation. One of the most widely used algorithms for ANN is based on constructing a multi-layer graph over the dataset, called the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). While this algorithm supports insertion of new data, it does not support deletion of existing data. Moreover, deletion algorithms described by prior work come at the cost of increased query latency, decreased recall, or prolonged deletion time. In this paper, we propose a new theoretical framework for graph-based ANN based on random walks. We then utilize this framework to analyze a randomized deletion approach that approximately preserves hitting time statistics compared to the graph before deleting the point. However, this guarantee needs at least as many edge samples as there are edges in the clique over the neighbors of the deleted point. We then turn this theoretical framework into a deterministic deletion algorithm, and show that it provides a better tradeoff between query latency, recall, deletion time, and memory usage through an extensive collection of experiments.

authors.name: Nina Mishra, Yonatan Naamad, Tal Wagner, Lichen Zhang

papers.title: Stochastic Deep Learning: A Probabilistic Framework for Modeling Uncertainty in Structured Temporal Data
papers.summary: I propose a novel framework that integrates stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with deep generative models to improve uncertainty quantification in machine learning applications involving structured and temporal data. This approach, termed Stochastic Latent Differential Inference (SLDI), embeds an It\^o SDE in the latent space of a variational autoencoder, allowing for flexible, continuous-time modeling of uncertainty while preserving a principled mathematical foundation. The drift and diffusion terms of the SDE are parameterized by neural networks, enabling data-driven inference and generalizing classical time series models to handle irregular sampling and complex dynamic structure. A central theoretical contribution is the co-parameterization of the adjoint state with a dedicated neural network, forming a coupled forward-backward system that captures not only latent evolution but also gradient dynamics. I introduce a pathwise-regularized adjoint loss and analyze variance-reduced gradient flows through the lens of stochastic calculus, offering new tools for improving training stability in deep latent SDEs. My paper unifies and extends variational inference, continuous-time generative modeling, and control-theoretic optimization, providing a rigorous foundation for future developments in stochastic probabilistic machine learning.

authors.name: James Rice

papers.title: Sublinear Time Quantum Algorithm for Attention Approximation
papers.summary: Given the query, key and value matrices $Q, K, V\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, the attention module is defined as $\mathrm{Att}(Q, K, V)=D^{-1}AV$ where $A=\exp(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})$ with $\exp(\cdot)$ applied entrywise, $D=\mathrm{diag}(A\mathbf{1}_n)$. The attention module is the backbone of modern transformers and large language models, but explicitly forming the softmax matrix $D^{-1}A$ incurs $\Omega(n^2)$ time, motivating numerous approximation schemes that reduce runtime to $\widetilde O(nd)$ via sparsity or low-rank factorization. We propose a quantum data structure that approximates any row of $\mathrm{Att}(Q, K, V)$ using only row queries to $Q, K, V$. Our algorithm preprocesses these matrices in $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1} n^{0.5} (s_\lambda^{3} + s_\lambda^{2} d + d) + \epsilon^{-2} s_\lambda d)$ time, where $\epsilon$ is the target accuracy and $s_\lambda$ is the $\lambda$-statistical dimension of the exponential kernel defined by $Q$ and $K$. Each row query can be answered in $\widetilde{O}(s_\lambda^2 + s_\lambda d)$ time. If every row sum of $A$ exceeds $\epsilon\|A\|+\lambda\sqrt n$, then with probability $1-1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ the answers have Frobenius-norm error $O(\beta\|D^{-1}\|(\epsilon\|A\|_F+\lambda\sqrt n)\|V\|_F)$. Here $\beta=(1-(\epsilon\|A\|+\lambda\sqrt n)\|D^{-1}\|)^{-1}\geq 1$ is close to $1$ when every row sum is much larger than $\epsilon\|A\|+\lambda\sqrt n$. To our knowledge, this is the first quantum data structure that approximates rows of the attention matrix in sublinear time with respect to $n$. Our approach relies on a quantum Nystr\"om approximation of the exponential kernel, quantum multivariate mean estimation for computing $D$, and quantum sampling of the rows of $V$ by their squared norms, with a median over independent samples, for the multiplication with $V$.

authors.name: Zhao Song, Jianfei Xue, Jiahao Zhang, Lichen Zhang

papers.title: How much perceived-stress signal is in the maternal ECG? An exclusion bound across deep-learning and heart-rate-variability representations in pregnancy
papers.summary: Deep learning can read physiological states from the electrocardiogram (ECG), prompting attempts to detect psychological stress. We asked how much information about perceived stress the maternal ECG carries. In 144 pregnant women, with every cross-validation split taken over participants, across 94 arms spanning 21 self-supervised, foundation-model, and heart-rate-variability architectures, the best discrimination of moderate-to-high stress (PSS-10 >= 19) was AUC 0.604 (95% CI 0.511-0.696), and AUC >= 0.70 was rejected in all eleven arms tested. Three pre-registered tests in a second cohort from the same center, recorded on different hardware, were null, at 30% power. Which of the three simultaneously recorded ECG channels was analyzed accounted for 96% of the predicted score's variance, against 4% between women; across 20 combinations of channel rule, label variant, and visit, the external correlation with perceived stress ranged from r = -0.095 to r = +0.307, a spread no larger than such a search produces by chance (raw one-sided p of the maximum 0.011; calibrated max-statistic p = 0.583). Hair cortisol was not predicted either.
