In the second cohort, PSS-10 scores were not stable across administrations spanning pregnancy and the postpartum period (ICC 0.06-0.16), so one administration is a weak measure of a woman's stress level at another visit. A single-recording ECG screener for perceived stress is excluded in this population, and multi-channel studies must pre-register their channel rule.

authors.name: Martin G. Frasch, Marlene J. E. Mayer, Clara Becker, Peter Zimmermann, Camilla Zelgert, Nicolas B. Garnier, Marta C. Antonelli, Silvia M. Lobmaier

papers.title: Variance Reduction Based Experience Replay for Policy Optimization
papers.summary: Effective reinforcement learning (RL) for complex stochastic systems requires leveraging historical data to improve sample efficiency and accelerate policy optimization. However, classical experience replay treats all past observations uniformly and fails to account for their varying contributions to learning. To address this limitation, we propose Variance Reduction Experience Replay (VRER), a principled framework that selectively reuses informative samples to reduce the variance of policy gradient estimates. VRER is algorithm-agnostic and can be integrated with existing policy optimization methods, yielding the sample-efficient off-policy algorithm, Policy Gradient with VRER (PG-VRER). To provide rigorous theoretical guarantees, we develop a novel analysis framework for experience replay that explicitly accounts for dependencies induced by Markovian dynamics and behavior-policy interactions. Using this framework, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees for PG-VRER and characterize a fundamental bias-variance trade-off: reusing older samples reduces gradient variance but may introduce greater estimation bias. Extensive experiments show that VRER consistently accelerates learning and outperforms state-of-the-art policy optimization algorithms

authors.name: Hua Zheng, Wei Xie, M. Ben Feng, Keilung Choy

papers.title: On the Meta-Design of Allocation Problems
papers.summary: There is an extensive literature that studies how to find optimal policies in resource allocation problems, taking the underlying design parameters that define the allocation, such as what data is collected, how many people can be served, and quality of service as fixed constraints. Yet, from a planner's perspective, these design parameters are themselves optimization variables that are just as important in determining overall welfare as selecting the optimal targeting rule for a given set of constraints. This realization motivates a rich set of meta-design questions exploring how planners should make principled decisions about investments in prediction, capacity constraints, and treatment quality, all of which lie upstream of classical policy optimization. Building on initial theoretical work in this space, our paper has three main contributions. First, we formally define the broad meta-design space of resource allocation problems. Second, we develop empirical tools that enable practitioners to reliably navigate it. Third, we demonstrate the framework in two real-world case studies on German employment services and targeted cash transfer programs in Ethiopia.

authors.name: Unai Fischer-Abaigar, Emily Aiken, Christoph Kern, Juan Carlos Perdomo

papers.title: Neural Learning of Fast Matrix Multiplication Algorithms: a Geometric Perspective
papers.summary: We combine neural learning and geometric diagnostics to investigate the rank and border rank of the \(3\times3\) matrix-multiplication tensor \(M_3\). Using the Bhattacharya--Mesner product, we derive \textsc{MatMulNet}, a differentiable architecture encoding bilinear maps. Constrained refinement yields a length-\(23\) numerical solution with machine-precision full-tensor residual and bounded decomposition weight. Along the explored length-\(22\) branch, the residual instead decreases as the gauge-invariant weight grows. This contrast supports \(R_{\mathbb R}(M_3)=23\) as a working hypothesis. A Laurent-parametrised extension probes border rank, giving a tentative, protocol-dependent motivation to investigate \(r=19\) and the adjacent \(r=18\) case. For \(M_4\), the same diagnostics distinguish bounded numerical solutions recovered from perturbed known schemes, structured residual plateaus, and weight-growing approximations, revealing the dependence of the search on initialisation. Together, the experiments connect approximation accuracy with decomposition growth and identify concrete targets for exact or certified investigation.

authors.name: Paolo Andreini, Alessandra Bernardi, Monica Bianchini, Barbara Toniella Corradini, Sara Marziali, Giacomo Nunziati, Franco Scarselli

papers.title: A Trust-Region Interior-Point Stochastic Sequential Quadratic Programming Method
papers.summary: In this paper, we propose a trust-region interior-point stochastic sequential quadratic programming (TR-IP-SSQP) method for solving optimization problems with a stochastic objective and deterministic nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. In this setting, exact evaluations of the objective function and its gradient are unavailable, but their stochastic estimates can be constructed. In particular, at each iteration our method builds stochastic oracles whose estimates of the objective value and gradient satisfy proper adaptive accuracy conditions with a fixed probability. To handle inequality constraints, we adopt an interior-point method (IPM), in which the barrier parameter is taken from a prescribed decreasing sequence and is reduced once a stochastic stationarity test is passed. Under standard assumptions, we show that, almost surely, the KKT residual vanishes along the iterations at which the barrier parameter is reduced, and every limit point of these iterates is a KKT point. We implement the method on a subset of problems from the CUTEst test set, as well as on constrained logistic regression problems, to demonstrate its practical performance.

authors.name: Yuchen Fang, Jihun Kim, Sen Na, James Demmel, Javad Lavaei

papers.title: CT-VDETR: Semi-supervised 3D Trauma Detection in Computed Tomography (CT) scans using Dense Vertex Relative Position Encoding
papers.summary: Accurate detection and localization of traumatic injuries in abdominal CT remain challenging because voxel-level annotations are limited and expensive to obtain. We present a label-efficient framework for 3D abdominal trauma detection that combines self-supervised pretraining with semi-supervised transformer-based detection. First, we use Masked Image Modeling (MIM) on 1,098 CT volumes to pretrain a 3D U-Net encoder for anatomical representation learning. Next, we adapt V-DETR to dense volumetric CT through a feature adapter that converts the encoder feature grid into a compact token sequence for transformer decoding. The pretrained encoder is then integrated with V-DETR and 3D Vertex Relative Position Encoding (3DV-RPE) to improve the localization of irregularly shaped injuries. Finally, semi-supervised teacher-student consistency regularization leverages 2,000 additional unlabeled volumes during detector training. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of a 3D DETR-style detector to the RSNA abdominal trauma detection task. On this benchmark, the proposed method achieves 31.33% test mAP@0.50 using only 78 labeled training volumes, corresponding to a 1.53x improvement over supervised-only training. These results show that combining medical-domain pretraining with semi-supervised learning is an effective strategy for label-scarce 3D medical detection.

authors.name: Shivam Chaudhary, Sheethal Bhat, Andreas Maier

papers.title: How to find expressible and trainable parameterized quantum circuits?
papers.summary: Whether parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) can be systematically constructed to be both trainable and expressive remains an open question. Highly expressive PQCs often exhibit barren plateaus, while several trainable alternatives admit efficient classical simulation. We prove that deciding whether a PQC family exhibits a barren plateau is undecidable in general. However, we derive a practical finite-sample, dimension-independent concentration bound for estimating the variance of a PQC cost function, yielding explicit trainability guarantees. Across commonly used ans\"atze, we observe an anticorrelation between trainability and expressibility, consistent with theoretical insights. Building on this observation, we propose a property-based ansatz-search framework for identifying circuits that combine trainability and expressibility. We demonstrate its practical viability on a real quantum computer and apply it to variational quantum algorithms. We identify quantum neural network ans\"atze with improved effective dimension using over six times fewer parameters, and for VQE on $\mathrm{H}_2$ we achieve UCCSD-like accuracy at substantially reduced circuit complexity.

authors.name: Peter R\"oseler, Dennis Willsch, Kristel Michielsen

papers.title: Communication-Aware Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Decentralized Cooperative UAV Deployment
papers.summary: Autonomous Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) swarms are increasingly used as rapidly deployable aerial relays and sensing platforms, yet practical deployments must operate under partial observability and intermittent peer-to-peer connectivity. We present a graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework trained under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE): a centralized critic and global state are available only during training, while each UAV executes a shared policy using local observations and messages from nearby neighbors. Under restricted communication, neighbor relations are induced by an SNR-threshold connectivity graph. Our architecture encodes local agent state and nearby entities with an agent-entity attention module and aggregates inter-UAV messages with neighbor self-attention over a signal-quality-limited communication graph defined by a channel model. We evaluate the framework on a cooperative relay-deployment task, DroneConnect. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves an approximately 12% increase in target coverage over MAPPO under restricted communication and partial observability, while remaining competitive with a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP)-based offline upper bound with full node observability.

authors.name: Enguang Fan, Zihan Shan, Yifan Chen, Klara Nahrstedt, Matthew Caesar, Jae Kim

papers.title: Amortized Inference for Correlated Discrete Choice Models via Equivariant Neural Networks
papers.summary: Discrete choice models are fundamental tools in management science, economics, and marketing. Logit models dominate applied work because they yield closed-form choice probabilities, but IID Gumbel errors impose restrictive substitution patterns. We propose an amortized inference approach based on a neural network emulator that approximates choice probabilities under general, potentially correlated, error distributions. We develop a specialized neural network architecture respecting the invariance properties of discrete choice models and provide group-theoretic foundations for universal approximation from a minimal set of invariant features. Using Sobolev training, the emulator learns choice probabilities and their derivatives, enabling rapid likelihood and gradient evaluation. We show that emulator-based maximum likelihood estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal under mild approximation conditions. Simulations show substantial gains over the GHK simulator in accuracy and speed. Using NielsenIQ data on household laundry-detergent purchases, we estimate correlated-probit and correlated-Gumbel models with rich household-level random effects. The IID period-error restriction---and hence the conditional-IIA restriction underlying conventional mixed logit---is strongly rejected. The Bayesian information criterion (BIC) selects a correlated-Gumbel model with a three-factor period-error covariance structure. We find that allowing correlated period errors materially changes predicted product substitution patterns.

authors.name: Easton Huch, Michael Keane

papers.title: One-sided certification of surrogate near-minimizers: exact worst-case envelopes under strong convexity and smoothness
papers.summary: We study target suboptimality for points that approximately minimize a surrogate objective. Unlike standard uniform perturbation estimates, the available comparison is one-sided, thresholded at a certified lower target level, and restricted to the entire surrogate-selected sublevel set. We first show that selected comparison alone cannot yield a finite worst-case guarantee, even for strongly convex quadratics with identical Hessians. A single scalar upper bound on the surrogate minimum closes this information gap and leads to a sharp general estimate. For pairs of $\mu$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth objectives, we then solve the associated worst-case information problem exactly. We obtain a sharp feasibility barrier and a dimension-free envelope; in its nontrivial regime, the value reduces to a scalar maximization over a compact interval. Explicit one-dimensional piecewise-quadratic objectives attain the bound while satisfying the one-sided constraint on the full selected set. We characterize when curvature strictly improves the general certificate and provide a threshold-preserving finite-net validation procedure. The results identify the best guarantee permitted by the prescribed partial information, independently of any particular optimization algorithm or additive perturbation model.

authors.name: Karim Bounja, Boujema\^a Achchab, Abdeljalil Sakat

papers.title: On Higher-Order Geometric Refinements of Classical Covariance Asymptotics: An Approach via Intrinsic and Extrinsic Information Geometry
papers.summary: Classical Fisher-information asymptotics describe the covariance of regular efficient estimators through the local quadratic approximation of the log-likelihood, and thus capture first-order geometry only. In curved models, including mixtures, curved exponential families, latent-variable models, and manifold-constrained parameter spaces, finite-sample behavior can deviate systematically from these predictions. We develop a coordinate-invariant, curvature-aware refinement by viewing a regular parametric family as a Riemannian manifold \((\Theta,g)\) with Fisher--Rao metric, immersed in \(L^2(\mu)\) through the square-root density map. Under suitable regularity and moment assumptions, we derive an \(n^{-2}\) correction to the leading \(n^{-1}I(\theta)^{-1}\) covariance term for score-root, first-order efficient estimators. The correction is governed by a tensor \(P_{ij}\) that decomposes canonically into three parts, an intrinsic Ricci-type contraction of the Fisher--Rao curvature tensor, an extrinsic Gram-type contraction of the second fundamental form, and a Hellinger discrepancy tensor encoding higher-order probabilistic information not determined by immersion geometry alone. The extrinsic term is positive semidefinite, the full correction is invariant under smooth reparameterization, and it vanishes identically for full exponential families. We then extend the picture to singular models, where Fisher information degenerates. Using resolution of singularities under an additive normal crossing assumption, we describe the resolved metric, the role of the real log canonical threshold in learning rates and posterior mean-squared error, and a curvature-based covariance expansion on the resolved space that recovers the regular theory as a special case. This framework also suggests geometric diagnostics of weak identifiability and curvature-aware principles for regularization and optimization.

authors.name: Malik Amir, Sourangshu Ghosh

papers.title: Rare Event Analysis via Stochastic Optimal Control
papers.summary: Rare events, from biomolecular conformational changes and phase transitions to chemical reactions, are central to many physical systems, yet extremely difficult to study computationally because unbiased simulations seldom produce them. Transition Path Theory provides a rigorous statistical framework for analyzing such events: it characterizes the ensemble of reactive trajectories between two metastable states (reactant and product), and its central object, the committor function (the probability that the system next reaches the product rather than the reactant), encodes essential kinetic and thermodynamic information. We introduce a framework for committor estimation that builds on stochastic optimal control, with a principled formulation that grounds committor learning on capped hitting-time trajectories. In this framework the committor defines a feedback control, proportional to the gradient of its logarithm, that steers trajectories toward the reactive region, enabling sampling of reactive paths. As practical algorithms, we develop two training losses: a heuristic on-policy direct backpropagation loss and a principled off-policy Value Matching loss, for which we establish first-order optimality guarantees. Being off-policy, Value Matching can leverage simulated trajectories from alternative sampling processes and reuse them from a replay buffer, which enables efficient learning. In particular, we derive a reactive current-preserving sampling process that can accelerate exploration. On reversible and non-reversible dynamics, the framework yields more accurate committor estimates, reaction rates, and transition path samples than existing methods.

authors.name: Yuanqi Du, Jiajun He, Dinghuai Zhang, Eric Vanden-Eijnden, Carles Domingo-Enrich

papers.title: Well-Conditioned Oblivious Perturbations in Linear Space
papers.summary: Perturbing a deterministic $n$-dimensional matrix with small Gaussian noise is a cornerstone of smoothed analysis of algorithms [Spielman and Teng, JACM 2004], as it reduces the condition number of the input to $O(n)$, and with it the complexity of many matrix algorithms. However, when deployed algorithmically, these perturbations are expensive due to the cost of generating and storing $n^2$ Gaussian random variables. We propose a perturbation that requires generating and storing $O(n)$ random numbers in $O(\log n)$ bits of precision, and reduces the condition number of any deterministic matrix to $O(n)$, matching Gaussian perturbations. Our result takes a step towards derandomizing matrix perturbations in numerical linear algebra, and in particular, implies that we can solve an $n\times n$ linear system to within $\varepsilon$ backward error in $O(n^2\log(n)/\varepsilon)$ time using only $O(n\log n)$ random bits. In our construction, we introduce the concept of a pattern matrix, which is a dense deterministic matrix that maps all sparse vectors into dense vectors in a way that goes beyond the classical uncertainty principle of the Fourier transform. We combine this with a sparse perturbation whose entries are dependent and located in a non-uniform fashion. In order to analyze this construction, we develop new techniques for lower bounding the smallest singular value of a random matrix with dependent entries.

authors.name: Shabarish Chenakkod, Micha{\l} Derezi\'nski, Xiaoyu Dong, Mark Rudelson

papers.title: Deep Learning of Solver-Aware Turbulence Closures from Nudged LES Dynamics
papers.summary: The differentiable physics paradigm may be leveraged as an a-posteriori approach for discovering turbulence closure models by embedding a neural network parameterization directly inside the solver and optimizing it given potentially sparse target data. This addresses a key limitation of a-priori learning where direct numerical simulation (DNS) data is used to approximate the subgrid stress with the assumption of a low-pass filter. Closures trained in this a-priori manner frequently lead to unstable deployments due to the mismatch between the assumed filter and the effect of numerical discretizations and coarse-graining. In comparison, while typically stable during deployment, a-posteriori learning incurs high computational costs due to the need to backpropagate through a large eddy simulation (LES) solver. Furthermore, a-posteriori methods are challenging to apply broadly since they require significant modification of existing solvers. Finally, both approaches are limited when generalization is desired across different numerical schemes with their implicit filtering characteristics. In this work, we present a deep-learning approach for turbulence closure modeling built on the continuous data assimilation framework. Our approach enables the a-priori training of closures using DNS data observed only at coarse-grid points without modifying or differentiating through the LES solver, while preserving stability during deployment for the recovery of long-term statistics. We focus on the model's ability to adapt to different discretizations by explicitly conditioning it on the numerical scheme. We use two- and three-dimensional canonical cases to test our framework and show that the learned correction systematically tracks the discretization error of the coarse solver.

authors.name: Ashwin Suriyanarayanan, Dibyajyoti Chakraborty, Romit Maulik

papers.title: Sliced-Regularized Optimal Transport
papers.summary: We propose a new regularized optimal transport (OT) formulation, termed sliced-regularized optimal transport (SROT). Unlike entropic OT (EOT), which regularizes the transport plan toward an independent coupling, SROT regularizes it toward a sliced OT (SOT) plan. To the best of our knowledge, SROT is the first approach to leverage a version of SOT plan as a reference to improve classical OT. We provide a formal definition of SROT, derive its dual formulation, and provide a post-Bayesian interpretation of SROT. We then develop a Sinkhorn-style algorithm for efficient computation. It retains the scalability of EOT and, when the SOT plan is sparse, achieves even lower per-iteration complexity. By incorporating a scalable SOT plan as a prior, SROT yields more accurate approximations of the exact OT plan than EOT under the same level of regularization. Moreover, the resulting transport plan improves upon the reference SOT plan itself. We further introduce the corresponding OT divergence induced by SROT, named SROT divergence, and analyze its topological and computational properties. Finally, we validate our approach through experiments on synthetic datasets and color transfer tasks, demonstrating that SROT is better than both EOT and SOT in approximating exact OT. Additional experiments on gradient flows further highlight the advantages of SROT divergence

authors.name: Khai Nguyen

papers.title: MARGIN: Margin-Aware Regularized Geometry for Imbalanced Vulnerability Detection
papers.summary: Software vulnerability detection is critical for ensuring software security and reliability. Despite recent advances in deep learning, real-world vulnerability datasets suffer from two severe challenges: frequency imbalance and difficulty imbalance. We reinterpret these challenges from an embedding geometry perspective, observing that such imbalances induce geometric distortions in hyperspherical representation space. To address this issue, we propose MARGIN, a metric-based framework that learns discriminative vulnerability representations through adaptive margin metric learning and hyperspherical prototype modeling. MARGIN dynamically adjusts geometric regularization according to the distribution structure estimated by the von Mises-Fisher concentration, aligning the probability mass of embedding distributions with their corresponding Voronoi cells, thereby reducing geometric distortion and yielding more stable decision boundaries. Extensive experiments on public vulnerability datasets show that MARGIN consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving notable improvements in classification and detection, especially on challenging, imbalanced datasets. Further analysis demonstrates that MARGIN produces more structured embedding geometries, improving robustness, interpretability, and generalization.

authors.name: Yuteng Zhang, Huifang Ma, Jiahui Wei, Qingqing Li, Yafei Yang, Xin Ji

papers.title: On the global convergence of gradient flow for wide shallow models beyond homogeneous nonlinearities
papers.summary: A surprising phenomenon in the training of neural networks is the ability of gradient descent to find global minimizers of the training loss despite its non-convexity. Following earlier work, we investigate this behavior for wide shallow models. Existing global convergence results primarily concern models with positively one-homogeneous nonlinearities, such as ReLU activations, and models with scalar output weights and bounded nonlinearities, such as sigmoid activations. We study a broader class of models, including multi-head attention layers and two-layer fully connected networks with bounded or asymptotically positively one-homogeneous activations and vector output weights. Building upon (Chizat and Bach, 2018), we prove that, in the limit of infinitely many hidden neurons or attention heads, non-minimizers of the training loss are unstable under the mean-field gradient flow dynamics by constructing "escape regions" in the parameter space. Our global convergence statements are conditional in the following sense: if the mean-field gradient flow converges for the Wasserstein 2-distance, then its limit must be a global minimizer. We revisit the bounded nonlinearity, scalar-output setting of (Chizat and Bach, 2018), giving an escape region construction adapted to unbounded nonlinear parameter domains. We also propose new constructions for nonlinearities with at most linear growth under a non-degeneracy assumption and for asymptotically positively one-homogeneous nonlinearities. Finally, we show the well-posedness and stability estimates for the mean-field training dynamics under sub-Gaussian initializations.

authors.name: Romain Petit, Clarice Poon, Gabriel Peyr\'e

papers.title: Calibrating LLMs with Semantic-level Reward
papers.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed in consequential settings such as medical question answering and legal reasoning, the ability to estimate when their outputs are likely to be correct is essential for safe and reliable use, requiring well-calibrated uncertainty. Standard reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains models with a binary correctness reward that is indifferent to confidence, providing no penalty for confident but wrong predictions and thereby degrading calibration. Recent work addresses this by training models to produce verbalized confidence scores alongside answers and rewarding agreement with correctness. However, verbalized confidence is calibrated at the token level and thus exhibits inconsistency across textual variations with same semantic meaning. We propose \textbf{Calibration with Semantic Reward (CSR)}, a framework that calibrates language models directly in semantic space without a verbalized confidence interface. CSR combines the correctness reward with a novel semantic calibration reward that encourages exploitation among correct rollouts by promoting semantic agreement, and exploration among incorrect ones by discouraging spurious consistency. Experiments across three model families on HotpotQA (in-distribution) and TriviaQA, MSMARCO, and NQ-Open (out-of-distribution) show that CSR consistently achieves lower ECE and higher AUROC than verbalized-confidence baselines across nearly all settings, reducing ECE by up to $40\%$ and improving AUROC by up to $31\%$ over verbalized-confidence baselines, with calibration behavior generalizing robustly across all four evaluation settings.

authors.name: Fengfei Yu, Ruijia Niu, Dongxia Wu, Yian Ma, Rose Yu

papers.title: GRTO: Group Relative Tool Optimization for Referring Segmentation
papers.summary: Referring segmentation requires reasoning to connect language with visual evidence and identify the intended target in challenging scenarios. This makes GRPO a natural choice for training VLMs together with a segmentation tool. However, existing approaches optimize only the VLM, assuming that the tool is perfect and leaving it untouched. This assumption is particularly limiting when the tool faces domain shift, as segmentation errors can undermine even correct reasoning. We therefore argue that the segmentation tool should be optimized together with the reasoning policy. However, this is challenging because policy optimization and differentiable tool learning rely on fundamentally different objectives. In this work, we introduce group relative tool optimization (GRTO), a mathematically grounded two-stage framework for jointly optimizing a policy and its differentiable tool. The key idea is to first align the tool with the policy expected after joint training, rather than the initial policy. The prealigned tool then leads to a more robust reward signal and superior policy convergence in subsequent policy training. In the first stage, GRTO bootstraps the tool toward the theoretically optimal policy, capturing readily attainable gains without costly on-policy rollouts. This alignment bootstraps the second stage, where GRTO extends GRPO to jointly refine the policy and tool. Across three challenging referring segmentation benchmarks, GRTO achieves substantial improvements over plain GRPO and alternative tool training procedures, matching or surpassing domain-specific state-of-the-art methods. This demonstrates the value of unifying reinforcement learning with differentiable auxiliary objectives for reasoning-intensive segmentation.

authors.name: Mario Markov (INSAIT, Sofia University "St. Kliment Ohridski"), Stefan Maria Ailuro (INSAIT, Sofia University "St. Kliment Ohridski"), Mohammad Mahdi (INSAIT, Sofia University "St. Kliment Ohridski"), Luc Van Gool (INSAIT, Sofia University "St. Kliment Ohridski"), Danda Pani Paudel (INSAIT, Sofia University "St. Kliment Ohridski")

papers.title: FlatVPR: Plug-and-play Geo-linear Residual Adapter for Geometric Rectification of Foundation Model Feature Manifolds
papers.summary: This paper proposes ``FlatVPR,'' a novel geometric rectification paradigm that effectively bridges the trade-off between map lightweightness and localization accuracy in visual place recognition (VPR) by enforcing a feature manifold structure where any descriptor between two adjacent anchors $\mathbf{z}_A$ and $\mathbf{z}_B$ can be accurately reconstructed via linear interpolation $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{pseudo} = (1-t)\mathbf{z}_A + t\mathbf{z}_B$, where $t \in [0,1]$ denotes the relative position. While state-of-the-art foundation models such as DINOv2-ViT-S/14 provide robust semantic features, their latent manifolds exhibit prominent curvature, projecting uniform linear motion in physical space onto highly non-linear trajectories in the feature space, which hinders reliable reconstruction under sparse anchor conditions. To enable the aforementioned interpolation-based reconstruction, we introduce a residual transformation $\hat{\mathbf{z}} = \mathbf{z} + \text{Res}(\mathbf{z})$ to the raw foundation features $\mathbf{z}$, where $\text{Res}(\cdot)$ represents a learnable adapter. Our method explicitly suppresses manifold curvature using a mathematically grounded Pullback Flatness Loss that minimizes the deviation of intermediate features from the linear segment connecting adjacent anchors, thereby minimizing the intrinsic curvature of the manifold. Through this spatial flattening, map construction is formulated within an Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework, decoupled into a continuous M-step for manifold adaptation and a conceptual E-step for optimal anchor selection guidelines. Experiments on the NCLT dataset demonstrate that the application of our adapter leads to significant performance improvements even under extremely sparse anchor conditions with 100m intervals and extreme seasonal changes.

authors.name: Rai Hisada, Kanji Tanaka

papers.title: Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filtering for Data-Efficient Joint Tracking and Classification
papers.summary: Kalman filtering performance is highly sensitive to model mismatch and noise covariance tuning. Classical adaptive filtering methods address these issues by estimating model parameters or noise covariances from measurement data but rely on a predefined model structure. Learning-based methods provide greater flexibility but typically require large supervised datasets and often lack well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. This article proposes a self-supervised Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filter (HAKF) that learns time-varying corrections to the system dynamics and process-noise covariance directly from measurements while jointly estimating the measurement-noise covariance. Because these corrections are learned from measurements alone, we analyze the structural identifiability of the corresponding time-invariant parameterizations. For a constant-velocity model with position-only measurements, an unrestricted process-noise covariance is not identifiable even when the dynamics are known, whereas a physically structured parameterization that couples the dynamics and process covariance is jointly identifiable with the measurement-noise covariance. This analysis motivates a structured HAKF variant, compared with a flexible variant that adapts the dynamics and process covariance independently. The innovation likelihood of HAKF also enables model classification through generalized Bayesian inference. In Isaac Lab simulations, the structured HAKF improves tracking accuracy over a fitted Kalman filter across all training-set sizes. When training data are limited, its advantage over the flexible variant is largest, and it outperforms a supervised recurrent neural network in both tracking and classification. On recorded DPJAIT flight trajectories, it achieves the best tracking and classification performance with near-consistent state covariance, whereas the flexible variant becomes overconfident.

authors.name: Jiho Lee, Nisar R. Ahmed, Rebecca Russell

papers.title: Learning-Augmented Online Minimization with Dual Predictions
papers.summary: We present learning-augmented algorithms for two general classes of online minimization problems: metrical task systems and laminar set cover. Both algorithms achieve improved theoretical guarantees using machine-learned predictions of an optimal solution to the dual linear program. Unlike optimal primal solutions, which can change drastically under tiny instance perturbations, these dual solutions are much more stable, which ensures the existence of good (and learnable) predictions for families of similar instances. While previous work has used dual predictions in offline settings and for online maximization problems, our algorithms are, to the best of our knowledge, the first demonstration that such dual predictions can be effective for online minimization. Our theoretical results are complemented by experiments on the $k$-server problem and the parking permit problem.

authors.name: Christian Coester, Alexa Tudose, Alexander Turoczy

papers.title: Scalable Deep Unfolding of Conic Optimizers
papers.summary: Deep unfolding (DU) accelerates iterative optimizers by training learnable components through unrolled iterations, but extending DU to the large-scale semidefinite programs (SDPs) common in robotics has remained limited. Unrolling a full-update conic solver such as COSMO exposes two obstacles: backpropagating through the per-iteration linear-system solve incurs memory quadratic in the problem size when the coefficient matrix is formed explicitly, and backpropagating through the positive semidefinite (PSD) cone projection is numerically unstable under repeated eigenvalues. We address the first with a matrix-free implicit differentiation rule that reduces memory from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n + \mathrm{nnz}(A))$, and the second with a stable backward rule based on the Dale\v{c}kii--Krein representation of the Fr\'echet derivative. Together, these enable learning lightweight hyperparameter policies and warm starts for COSMO. On standalone SDPs and second-order cone programs, ranging from max-cut and Lov\'asz $\vartheta$ to robust estimation and control, the learned policies outperform tuned COSMO on every problem class, reducing iterations to tolerance by up to 60$\times$, and transfer without retraining to instances up to 10$\times$ larger in the size parameter while retaining 2--5$\times$ speedups. Our matrix-free solver implementation also batches naturally on the GPU, solving 64 Lov\'asz $\vartheta$ SDPs 14$\times$ faster than sequential COSMO. When embedded in sequential convex programming for nonlinear covariance steering, our learned optimizers outperform the interior-point solver Clarabel in terms of both success rate and solve time.

authors.name: Alex Oshin, Rahul Vodeb Ghosh, Evangelos A. Theodorou

papers.title: Conformal Selection under Prevalence Shift: FDR Bounds and Finite Calibration
papers.summary: Conformalized Benjamini--Hochberg (cfBH) uses labeled calibration data to select candidates while controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) under suitable assumptions. We examine how differences between source and test populations affect FDR and power. When non-target scores have the same distribution in both populations, existing results guarantee FDR control for clipped cfBH if non-targets are at least as common in the source population as in the test population. When this prevalence condition fails, FDR can exceed the nominal level. We determine the worst-case FDR in large samples. For example, a nominal level of 10\% can yield FDR approaching 40\% when the source population has 20\% non-targets and the test population has 80\%. Calibrating only against labeled non-targets avoids this restriction on their proportions, provided their score distributions still agree. However, every nonempty selection must contain a minimum number of candidates. This requirement can limit power when few true targets are present. More calibration non-targets can lower the minimum. We use the same minimum to bound FDR inflation when non-target score distributions differ. In worst-case examples, a contamination fraction inversely proportional to the number of calibration non-targets can drive FDR close to 100\% in large test pools. A random labeled sample from the test population provides a representative calibration reference. Pooling its non-targets with source non-targets can improve power when their score distributions agree. Without this agreement, we give a correction for pooling that controls FDR but selects only a subset of the candidates selected using the random sample alone. Simulations and molecular-screening experiments on AqSolDB, with no shared molecular identities across data splits, illustrate these findings.

authors.name: Seungjin Choi

papers.title: Complete virtual unwrapping and reading of a rolled Herculaneum papyrus
papers.summary: The carbonized papyrus scrolls from Herculaneum preserve the only large-scale library to survive from classical antiquity. Many scrolls have remained unread because physical unrolling risks irreversible damage. Non-invasive imaging offers a route to their texts, yet previous work on sealed Herculaneum scrolls has recovered only localized readings. Here, by combining high-resolution X-ray computed microtomography ($\mu$CT) data acquired on the BM18 beamline at the ESRF with machine-learning-assisted virtual unwrapping, we study three still-closed scrolls. For PHerc. 1667, a remnant of earlier attempts at physical unrolling, we achieve the complete unwrapping and reading of the preserved writing surface, making it the first Herculaneum papyrus read completely by virtual unwrapping. The text was transcribed and cross-verified by nine papyrologists. In PHerc. Paris. 4, the source of the Vesuvius Challenge 2023 Grand Prize text, the high-resolution scan makes ink directly visible in the tomographic volume, allowing 3D ink segmentation and comparison of recovered text with visible deposits. In PHerc. 139, we recover title and author-attribution evidence identifying the scroll as Philodemus, On Gods, Book 8. These results establish a basis for the ongoing, systematic recovery and scholarly study of texts preserved within the still-closed Herculaneum library.

authors.name: Giorgio Angelotti, Stephen Parsons, Federica Nicolardi, Youssef Nader, Sean Johnson, David Josey, Paul Henderson, Hendrik Schilling, Johannes Rudolph, Forrest McDonald, Elian Rafael Dal Pr\'a, Paul Tafforeau, Alessandro Mirone, Clifford Seth Parker, Jan Paul Posma, Benjamin Kyles, Claudio Vergara, Alessia Lavorante, Rossella Villa, Maria Chiara Robustelli, Marzia D'Angelo, Gianluca Del Mastro, Michael McOsker, Kilian Fleischer, Christy Chapman, Nat Friedman, William Brent Seales

papers.title: Convergence of Large-Stepsize SGD for the Cross-entropy Loss via Stochastic Lyapunov Stability
papers.summary: Modern deep learning has been shown to operate using learning rates far larger than those justified by classical optimization theory. Most prior analyses of this phenomenon focus on deterministic gradient descent, leaving the stochastic setting largely unexplored. In this work, we provide sharp convergence guarantees for Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) applied to the multiclass cross-entropy loss, for both linear classifiers and two-layer neural networks. We show that the stochasticity of SGD may cause the dynamics to alternate between an edge-of-stability regime that is dominated by curvature-driven oscillations, and a stable regime in which the expected loss decreases at a controlled rate. Despite that, we prove that SGD stabilizes the dynamics, ensuring that the iterates return to stability in a fixed number of iterations and allowing convergence in the best-iterate sense even with large learning rates. Experiments validate our theoretical findings and illustrate the benefits of SGD in the large-stepsize regime.

authors.name: Konstantinos Emmanouilidis, Lachlan MacDonald, Salma Tarmoun, Rene Vidal

papers.title: MILES: Modular Instruction Memory with Learnable Selection for Self-Improving LLM Reasoning
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly improve their reasoning at test time via additional computation, yet most existing works treat each problem in isolation. When problems arrive sequentially, accumulating reusable experience across them can further improve performance. Existing memory-based methods either store whole-solution templates that generalize poorly to novel problems or use heuristic step-level selection that is not optimized for final-answer correctness. Learning selection policies requires large-scale training data and fixed action spaces, making such approaches unsuitable for test-time settings where memory expands incrementally and only limited supervision is available. We propose MILES (Modular Instruction Memory with LEarnable Selection), a framework that dynamically expands step-wise memory and applies correctness-optimized memory composition under realistic test-time constraints. MILES maintains modular memory units consisting of asymmetric pairs of sub-goal embeddings and sub-instructions, each associated with a learnable selection head. This memory structure enables a coarse-to-fine retrieval mechanism: The coarse level enables memory expansion and collects supervision for training selection heads from confident samples, while the fine stage applies learned selection heads to rerank coarse-level candidates and guide reasoning for uncertain samples. MILES achieves self-improvement by using its own confidence as the learning signal at test time, or given feedback such as labeled data in an offline setting. MILES consistently matches or outperforms prior methods while achieving superior accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness, robustness, and transferability.

authors.name: Ruilin Tong, Dong Gong

papers.title: Analyzing Image Encoder Choices and Graph Homophily in GCN Frameworks for Breast Ultrasound Classification
papers.summary: Breast ultrasound is widely used for screening, yet automated analysis remains challenging due to speckle noise, acquisition variability, and weak separation of benign and malignant cases in standard ultrasound imaging. Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have recently emerged as a promising approach by leveraging relationships among similar patient samples. However, it remains unclear how the choice of image encoder influences graph construction and downstream classification performance. In this work, we systematically evaluate five image encoders spanning convolutional and transformer-based architectures for GCN-based breast ultrasound classification. Image embeddings are used to construct cosine similarity k-nearest-neighbor graphs, which are classified using a single-layer GCN with a linear classification head. Across three patient-wise cross-validation folds, higher-capacity encoders consistently improve graph homophily and downstream classification performance, yielding gains in accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score. Moreover, test-set graph homophily exhibits a strong linear correlation with classification accuracy (R-squared = 0.875), with higher-capacity encoders consistently occupying the high-homophily, high-accuracy region, suggesting that encoder-driven improvements in graph structure are a key mechanism underlying the observed performance gains. On 798 images from two external sources, the encoder ordering was preserved, but accuracy was 0.13-0.21 lower than in cross-validation and the homophily-accuracy association was weaker (R-squared = 0.759). These findings establish encoder selection as a critical factor in graph-based breast ultrasound classification and identify graph homophily as a key indicator linking representation quality to downstream classification performance.

authors.name: Sabahattin Mert Daloglu, Ceren Coskun, Harvey Castro, Soner Hacihaliloglu, Ilker Hacihaliloglu

papers.title: Handling Missing Data in Probabilistic Regression Trees
papers.summary: Probabilistic regression trees are a smooth alternative to classical regression trees, consistent in the complete-data case, producing continuous predictions through probabilistic split assignments. This paper extends this framework by proposing three approaches to accommodate missing predictor values directly during tree construction, without a separate imputation step. These modifications are defined to preserve the fundamental probabilistic properties of the original methodology, including probability conservation and marginal compatibility, under arbitrary patterns of missing covariate values. The proposed methods are evaluated on several real-world datasets exhibiting different levels of missingness and are compared with classical regression trees. In addition, a semi-synthetic study, in which missing values are injected completely at random, at random and not at random, compares the proposed strategies with impute-then-fit pipelines based on commonly applied imputation methods.

authors.name: Taiane Schaedler Prass, Alisson Silva Neimaier, Guilherme Pumi

papers.title: Cascade: Exploiting SLO-Aware latency budget for fair and high goodput LLM inference serving
papers.summary: The reasoning and agentic capabilities of LLMs have expanded the range of applications they support, from short interactive exchanges to long, prefix-heavy requests. LLM serving platforms today define response-latency service-level objectives (SLOs), yet requests under the same SLO differ by orders of magnitude in input length, generation length, execution cost, and reusable KV-cache availability, leaving each request with a different amount of latency headroom. This headroom must cover not only execution, but also scheduling and preemption delays and the cost of retrieving KV state from deeper memory tiers. Existing systems manage these decisions independently, despite their combined impact on latency. We present Cascade, an LLM serving system that coordinates these decisions using a per-request latency budget: the difference between a request's SLO and its predicted remaining service time, continuously updated from request characteristics, KV-cache state, and system load. Cascade uses this budget to prioritize requests and to decide how much non-resident KV state to prefetch from deeper tiers, with the remainder fetched on demand or recomputed given the serving system. On production traces across three LLMs, Cascade improves goodput by 10.4x over vLLM and 1.8x over a SLO-aware scheduler, and reduces SLO violations by 76% and 31%, respectively, while remaining fair across heterogeneous requests.

authors.name: Muhammad Adnan, Rohan Mahapatra, Prashant J. Nair, Daniel Berger, Pantea Zardoshti, Rodrigo Fonseca, Esha Choukse

papers.title: Online Inference for Quantile Distributional Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: In this work, we initiate a systematic study of online statistical inference for quantile-based distributional policy evaluation, which aims to characterize the distribution of discounted cumulative rewards under a given policy. To obtain a finite-dimensional representation of the return distribution, we consider the fixed point $\bm\eta_m$ of the quantile-projected distributional Bellman equation, parameterized by the quantile vector $\bm\theta_m$. We develop two online inference procedures for $\bm\theta_m$, covering synchronous and asynchronous sampling from a generative model as well as Markovian data. The first method uses the trajectory of quantile temporal-difference learning (QTD). We establish functional central limit theorems for the partial sums of QTD iterates and construct a recursively computable random-scaling statistic. The resulting confidence intervals have asymptotically exact coverage at deterministic times, with length of order $T^{-1/2}$ in probability. The second method constructs anytime-valid confidence intervals directly from samples. We invert multiscale tests of the Bellman estimating equation and use dyadic reward histograms to evaluate conservative evidence bounds online. The resulting intervals have finite-sample simultaneous coverage, and the histogram contribution to their length bound is of order $T^{-\zeta}$ for $\zeta\in[1/2,1)$. Under positive limiting state-visit frequencies, the resulting confidence intervals have lengths of order $\sqrt{\log\log T/T}$, which we establish as classwise optimal through a matching lower bound. Together, these results provide complementary guarantees for online inference in quantile distributional reinforcement learning, combining asymptotically exact fixed-time inference with finite-sample anytime validity.

authors.name: Zijie Cheng, Zhihua Zhang

papers.title: Equivariant learning of a transferable three-dimensional classical density functional
papers.summary: Liquids exhibit collective behavior that depends sensitively on thermodynamic conditions, interfaces and confinement, yet predicting each new state commonly requires a separate atomistic simulation. Classical density functional theory offers a reusable variational description, but its central excess free-energy functional is generally unknown, and learned approximations for fluids have largely been developed in reduced-dimensional geometries. Here we show that this functional can be learned directly from fully three-dimensional canonical equilibrium density fields while preserving spatial symmetry and variational consistency, without free-energy or chemical-potential training labels. A functional learned from coarse three-dimensional density fields remains predictive at finer resolution, separating the sampling demands of training from the spatial resolution of subsequent predictions. A single learned functional transfers across temperatures, system sizes and statistical ensembles, and recovers the equation of state, liquid--vapor coexistence and interfacial broadening, none of which are used as training targets. Applied to complex three-dimensional geometries, it predicts the potential of mean force between colloids due to solvent mediation, and adsorption isotherms in an interconnected gyroid pore. These results demonstrate that molecular dynamics equilibrium density data can be converted into a transferable thermodynamic generator connecting microscopic liquid structure to response, phase behavior and collective phenomena.

authors.name: Bingqing Cheng

papers.title: A Controlled, Internally Audited Negative Result: Training Recipe, H.264 Compression Levels and a Frequency-Stream Deepfake Detector
papers.summary: We test CAFRL, which adds block-DCT and FFT-phase streams with compression-conditioned band attention, and an adversarial compression-invariance loss, to an EfficientNet-B0 face backbone for deepfake detection. Decision rules were frozen before the comparisons they govern were run; controls were matched on data, augmentation and, after an internal audit, training recipe; contrasts are paired on test videos. (1) Configuration result (registered STOP-gate, one seed): CAFRL as specified scored 3.66 AUC points below a backbone-matched EfficientNet-B0 at CRF 40 -- as configured, not an architectural effect. (2) Recipe sensitivity: the control's recipe recovered 3.96 points for CAFRL's own components (post-audit pre-specified); of changes reverted singly (one seed, descriptive), only the backbone learning rate's interval excluded zero, which replicated on two further seeds (exploratory; a sensitivity, not a causal decomposition). (3) Neutral result: at that baseline-derived recipe, the frequency-stream variants, not separately tuned, showed no detectable difference at the resolution of this experiment from the spatial control, under the evaluated configurations (post-audit pre-specified); a standalone frequency head scored 85.27 points at CRF 40 (exploratory). (4) One-configuration neutral result: the adversarial loss, restored at one strength, made no detectable difference (registered; 0.87 points, Holm-adjusted p = 0.084). (5) Registered three-seed results: real H.264 outperforms JPEG at matched mean PSNR, by 7.48 points at CRF 40 (averaged over CRF-40 exposure), and CRF-40-level data added 1.88 points averaged over codec. These findings, and the advice to train on real compression levels, cover FaceForensics++-family, GAN-era, single-pass H.264 data; diffusion content, transcoding chains and unknown codecs are untested.

authors.name: Abbas Aliyev, Samir Rustamov

papers.title: Physiological Information Reliability: Contextual-Bandit Allocation of Coding Redundancy and Computation in Multimodal Cardiovascular Sensing
papers.summary: A packet can arrive intact and still be nearly worthless. On a body-worn node the radio and processor share one small battery, yet ECG and photoplethysmography (PPG) windows differ widely in how much an estimator can recover from them. We propose Physiological Information Reliability (PIR): a hand-designed window-value proxy, PIV, built from signal quality and cross-modal heart-rate agreement, joins channel, energy and compute telemetry in one state vector, and a LinUCB bandit chooses coding redundancy and processing site. Over 25 paired seeds on a synthetic burst-erasure testbed, PIR-LinUCB used 4.3% less energy than a hand-written rule, with lower error and higher delivery. A rule that also reads PIV matches it on error and delivery but spends 3.7 mJ more per window. On five real fetal ECG recordings, PIV tracked heart-rate error better than signal quality alone (mean within-record Spearman $\rho = -0.50$ against $-0.40$). The evidence is simulated, small and non-clinical.

authors.name: Navaneetha Krishnan Kamalakannan, Janakiraman Kamalakannan, Harinisri Velmurugan

papers.title: Relational Task Generation Language: A Declarative Specification Framework for Relational Deep Learning
papers.summary: Relational Deep Learning (RDL) has become a powerful paradigm for learning from multi-tabular data. However, manually defining RDL prediction tasks is a laborious process that frequently results in data leakage. To address this issue, we introduce the Relational Task Generation Language (RTGL), an open-source declarative language that streamlines RDL task formulation by abstracting away low-level SQL details. We showcase RTGL by reconstructing existing RDL benchmark tasks and uncovering their inconsistencies stemming from hand-written SQL definitions of RDL prediction targets, thereby underscoring the value of a dedicated declarative language. In addition, we demonstrate the practical utility of RTGL by designing various new tasks with diverse forms and target types. Our experiments confirm the robustness and usability of RTGL, as well as its integration with existing RDL frameworks, making it widely accessible to the community.

authors.name: Oleksii Kolesnichenko, Jakub Pele\v{s}ka, Gustav \v{S}\'{\i}r

papers.title: Maverick: Private and Verifiable LLM Inference Made Practical via Matrix-Vector Multiplication Delegation
papers.summary: Open-source large language models (LLMs) are increasingly competitive with closed-source models while offering transparency and the ability to run inference without exposing user inputs to a service provider. However, running large-scale models locally requires substantial computational resources. In practice, users may still resort to a third-party provider, giving rise to privacy and correctness concerns. Existing solutions that address these problems often impose substantial server overhead or introduce additional trust assumptions. In this paper, we present Maverick, a novel approach to private and verifiable LLM inference based on a protocol for delegating matrix-vector multiplication, a dominant operation in LLMs. At its core, Maverick provides, to our knowledge, the first information-theoretically sound verification protocol for matrix-vector multiplication delegation with transparent preprocessing, efficient (batch) verification, and virtually no server overhead. We combine this verification primitive with LPN-based pseudorandom masking to provide input privacy. We implement Maverick and evaluate both of its modes on large open-source models. When only verification is required, Maverick lets commodity clients use models far beyond their own capacity: a laptop and a desktop with a 16 GB GPU generate tokens 81-270$\times$ faster on Qwen3-32B than with local inference, and reach 7-33 tokens per second on Llama 4, a 400B-parameter model that neither can run at all. When input privacy is also required, Maverick generates tokens 10-12$\times$ faster on Qwen2.5-72B than the concurrent system MOSAIC, using precomputed masks.

authors.name: Ben Merbaum, Mohammad Amin Raeisi, Wenhao Wang, Charalampos Papamanthou, Katerina Sotiraki, Fan Zhang

papers.title: A Station-Based Evaluation of Machine Learning-based Weather Forecasting Models in Northern Norway
papers.summary: Recent machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models have demonstrated remarkable forecasting skill on global reanalysis-based benchmarks. However, their performance remains unclear in challenging environments such as Northern Norway, where narrow fjords and rapidly changing weather result in highly variable local wind conditions. In this case study, we evaluate FourCastNet3 (FCN3), GraphCast, and ECMWF High Resolution Forecast (HRES) for wind speed forecasting using multi-year station observations from Northern Norway, focusing on their relative performance, generalization beyond the training period, and performance under high-wind conditions. Our results show that HRES slightly outperforms FCN3 and GraphCast, with an overall RMSE of 2.89 $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, compared to 2.96 $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for FCN3 and 2.94 $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for GraphCast. Notably, the MLWP models maintain comparable performance beyond their respective training periods, with no clear evidence of noticeable degradation. FCN3 performs best under high-wind conditions, although all models substantially underestimate strong winds. Our findings suggest that MLWP has become competitive with NWP for local wind, but further refinements are still needed to capture complex terrain better.

authors.name: Siyan Chen, Lars Uebbing, Eirik Mikal Samuelsen, Georgios Leontidis, Arnt-B{\o}rre Salberg, S\'ebastien Lef\`evre, Robert Jenssen, Kristoffer Wickstr{\o}m

papers.title: Coherent Floquet quantum reservoirs for molecular property prediction
papers.summary: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) uses observables of a driven quantum system to make predictions from a sequence of inputs. The robust subharmonic response of discrete time crystals (DTCs) has motivated their use as quantum reservoirs. Here we develop a DTC-QRC architecture for molecular property prediction in which successive graph events or surface-hopping frames drive a fixed Floquet reservoir. An adjustable reset probability controls how long earlier inputs influence the state, and measurements of the final polarizations and pair correlations yield a feature vector of fixed dimension. Weak reset favors classification of inhibitor activity and blood-brain barrier penetration from long graph prefixes, whereas forecasting electronic gaps in ethene favors greater weight on recent nuclear motion. With nonlinear decoding, DTC-QRC outperforms an echo-state network on these tasks at matched input lengths and readout widths. For gap forecasting with this decoder and final-state readout, the dissipative reservoirs share a low-error drive window near the DTC transition reported for related spin chains. Dephasing lowers prediction performance in both molecular applications. In six-qubit classification without programmed reset on the Quafu superconducting quantum cloud platform, pair correlations retain more of their noise-free predictive power toward the DTC side, and the full readout performs best near the transition among the drives tested. The architecture provides a common framework for molecular screening and time-resolved property prediction using quantum reservoir computing.

authors.name: Luofei Wang, Da Zhang, Congren Wang, Yiming Li, Yuxiao Yang, Xuan Zhang, Xuefeng Cui, Zhang-Qi Yin

papers.title: A Single-Loop Method with Optimal Leading-Order Oracle Complexity for Optimization and Game Stationarity in Nonconvex--Concave Minimax Optimization
papers.summary: We develop a single-loop first-order framework for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax optimization, with matching leading-order upper and lower bounds for optimization and game stationarity in a projected zero-respecting oracle model. We propose a single-loop projected damped extragradient method coupling projected extragradient updates with dual momentum and a moving proximal center. Each iteration uses at most three gradient evaluations, without nested subproblems. For game stationarity, a deterministic best iterate has first-order residual below $\varepsilon$ with leading oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(L^{3/2}D_Y^{1/2}\Delta_\phi\varepsilon^{-5/2})$, where $L$ is the gradient Lipschitz constant, $D_Y$ bounds the dual feasible-set diameter, and $\Delta_\phi$ is the initial-point-dependent value-function gap. For optimization stationarity, a uniformly selected iterate has expected squared Moreau-envelope gradient norm at most $\varepsilon^2$ with leading oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(L^2D_Y\Delta_\phi\varepsilon^{-3})$. Matching lower bounds are $\Omega(L^{3/2}D_Y^{1/2}\Delta_\phi\varepsilon^{-5/2})$ for game stationarity and $\Omega(L^2D_Y\Delta_\phi\varepsilon^{-3})$ for optimization stationarity over projected zero-respecting first-order methods. Under dual strong concavity, the same framework achieves leading first-order oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_\phi\varepsilon^{-2})$ under both criteria, where $\kappa$ is the dual condition number. Matching lower bounds hold for both criteria in the same oracle model. To our knowledge, this is the first work to close the oracle complexity gap for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax optimization under both stationarity criteria by simultaneously improving upper and lower bounds in the projected zero-respecting oracle model.

authors.name: Minghao Zhang, Zi Xu, Anthony Man-Cho So

papers.title: Connectivity-Aware Exploration of Robotic Grasp Spaces
papers.summary: Robotic grasping is typically formulated as the problem of identifying successful actions from a space of candidate grasp poses. However, the organization of successful actions within this space has received less attention. We study the multiscale structure of viable robotic grasps in SE(3) and investigate whether this structure can be exploited for more efficient exploration. Using a large-scale grasp dataset, we show that successful grasp sets exhibit heterogeneous and reproducible connectivity structure across objects. We then introduce a connectivity-aware sampling strategy that incrementally explores the currently observed grasp space by prioritizing potential bridges between components, structural frontiers, boundary extensions, and geometric novelty. In controlled reconstruction experiments, the method recovers the connectivity structure of successful grasp sets substantially more efficiently than random sampling and farthest-point sampling. We further evaluate whether connectivity acquired under hidden grasp viability can improve subsequent grasp discovery, and whether structural experience from previously explored objects can be retrieved and transferred to unseen objects. These results suggest that the spatial organization of viable actions provides information relevant to grasp-space exploration beyond the viability of individual candidate actions. More broadly, they motivate structure-aware exploration as a means of exploiting the geometry of viable action spaces in robotic manipulation.

authors.name: Maksim A Kazanskii

papers.title: Leveraging Industrial Foundation Models at the Edge of Particle Physics Detectors via Distillation Learning and Hardware Co-design
papers.summary: Data acquisition (DAQ) systems at future particle physics experiments stand to benefit from the extremes of AI/ML development: large-scale foundation models can enhance the performance of feature extraction algorithms, and small-scale on-detector deployments can enable real-time intelligent data handling. This work provides the first tokenizer fine-tuning of an industrial foundation model for particle physics DAQ. Starting from the backbone of Google Research's TimesFM (Time Series Foundation Model), we address real-time regression tasks for drift chamber trackers and dual-readout calorimeters by jointly training the pretrained tokenizer and a newly initialized residual adapter, then fitting task-specific linear heads while keeping the transformer backbone frozen. Furthermore, the resulting TimesFM teachers can be distilled into students and co-designed with FPGA implementation to support real-time operation at future colliders. The distilled and compressed models achieve competitive performance, while distillation reduces reliance on labeled training data. Further, the pipeline of distillation and model compression from TimesFM is generic and can be easily adapted to a variety of 1D waveform tasks across domains.

authors.name: Gia Ancone, Qibin Liu, Liangyu Wu, Julia Gonski

papers.title: Scaling Density Functional Theory with Gaussian Splatting
papers.summary: Density functional theory (DFT) strikes a practical balance between accuracy and computational cost in many problems of computational chemistry and materials science. However, many DFT calculations are limited by fixed atom-centered basis sets, which dictate how accuracy and cost scale with system size. We propose Gaussian Splatting for Density Functional Theory (GS-DFT), which represents molecular orbitals as a cloud of Gaussians whose positions, shapes, and mixing coefficients are optimized jointly by gradient descent to minimize the energy without training data. Conceptually, GS-DFT is 3D Gaussian splatting with the renderer replaced by quantum mechanics. We introduce two key solver components: adaptive density fitting with screening for efficient evaluation of two-electron integrals, and a regularized differentiable orthogonalization of the molecular orbitals. Empirically, the optimized basis reaches the accuracy of the largest conventional basis sets with a fraction of the parameters, converging systematically in energy, density, and nuclear forces. At equal parameter count, it captures the stretched-bond and anion physics that fixed bases only recover with specialized basis augmentation. The resulting solver exhibits quadratic peak memory scaling in the cloud size, allowing us to simulate systems of up to 2,742 atoms (10,406 electrons) without any modifications at triple-zeta scale using a single four-GPU node.

authors.name: Andr\'es Guzm\'an-Cordero, Cindy Zhang, Majdi Hassan, Marta Skreta, Kirill Neklyudov, Matija Medvidovi\'c

papers.title: A Single-Loop, Constant-Batch First-Order Penalty Method for Stochastic Bilevel Optimization
papers.summary: Recent advances in penalty-based methods for stochastic bilevel optimization (SBO) have eliminated the need for second-order derivative oracles. However, for stochastic nonconvex-strongly convex bilevel problems, existing first-order methods typically rely on nested loops and/or large batch sizes for attaining $O(\epsilon^{-6})$ or $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ sample complexity under standard bounded-variance assumption or mean-square smoothness assumption. Achieving these rates with a single-loop penalty method and a constant batch size remains challenging due to a large penalty value needed for an accurate approximation. To address this challenge, we develop a stochastic SIngle-loop COnstant-Batch first-order penalty method (SICO) that combines two complementary ingredients. First, it performs one stochastic-gradient update per-iteration for both the original lower-level and penalized problems, with a projection that controls the separation between their iterates. Second, it applies an exponential moving average to stabilize the upper-level gradient estimator. We show that this combination achieves $ O(\epsilon^{-6}) $ sample complexity using only $O(1)$ stochastic-gradient samples per iteration under unbiased, bounded-variance stochastic gradients. Under the additional mean-square smoothness assumption on the lower-level stochastic gradients, the same algorithm improves the complexity to $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ also with $O(1)$ batch size. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to match the best-known convergence rate for fully first-order SBO methods using a single loop and a constant batch size. This result addresses an open problem posed in the literature.

authors.name: Xingyu Chen, Ming Yang, Quanqi Hu, Tianbao Yang

papers.title: A Wasserstein Trust-Region Method for Smooth Potential-Interaction Energies
papers.summary: Finding low-energy particle configurations and approximating probability distributions both lead to minimizing potential-interaction energies in Wasserstein space. Second-order information can speed up minimizing these possibly nonconvex energies, but a quadratic model is accurate only near the current measure. We introduce a Wasserstein trust-region (WTR) method for smooth, possibly nonconvex energies of this type. Each iteration transports the current measure $\rho$ along a displacement field $s$, producing $(\mathrm{Id}+s)_\#\rho$. The field approximately minimizes a quadratic model built from the second variation of the energy, subject to $\|s\|_{L^2(\rho)}\le\Delta$, using a truncated conjugate-gradient method. The ratio of actual to predicted decrease determines step acceptance and updates the trust-region radius. Under a lower energy bound and globally bounded Hessians of the potential and interaction kernel, we prove that the objective is nonincreasing, the Wasserstein-gradient norms converge to zero, and an $\varepsilon$-stationary iterate is reached within $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ iterations, rejected ones included. If the potential is quadratically coercive, every weak accumulation point is stationary. For empirical measures, WTR is an ordinary trust-region method in the particle positions, and its complexity bound does not depend on the number of particles provided the initial energy exceeds its infimum by a bounded amount. For $2048$ and $4096$ particles with Gaussian pair repulsion in a two-dimensional harmonic trap, WTR reaches the gradient tolerance $2\times10^{-4}$ a median $1.40$ times faster than L-BFGS. For equal-weight integration rules on two non-Gaussian targets, WTR reaches an integration error of $10^{-4}$ about $1.8$ times faster than L-BFGS and $1.3$ times faster than a Krylov trust-region solver.

authors.name: You Wan, Ting Gao, Jinqiao Duan, Jie Sun

papers.title: FLoRa: Flight-Assisted Data Collection from Duty Cycling LoRa Nodes under Energy Constraints
papers.summary: Data collection using Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) is challenging when LoRa IoT Devices (IoTDs) duty-cycle to conserve battery. Under energy constraints, a UAV must decide which IoTDs to visit, in what order, where to hover, and how many times to probe each node, while time-based data freshness decays. Tractably solving this problem requires a multi-level optimization architecture: discrete combinatorial optimization for routing, continuous global optimization for spatial positioning, and sequential decision-making under uncertainty. We propose FLoRa, a Flight-assisted LoRa data collection architecture using Simulated Annealing (SA) for path planning, Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) for hover positioning, and Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) for probing IoTDs. To quantify collection utility from duty-cycling nodes, we introduce the Value of Information for Pull-based systems (VIP), a metric that rewards fresh data and penalizes failed probes, imposing well-posedness and preventing indefinite probing when an IoTD is off. Tracking hard battery constraints on every POMDP sample path requires state augmentation, worsening the curse of dimensionality. For tractability, SA and CMA-ES work on the hard battery constraints, while at the POMDP layer we relax them into soft average constraints via Lagrangian relaxation. Since solving the network-wide POMDP is computationally complex, we decompose it into node-level POMDPs by approximating inter-node time dependency using a forward-decomposition technique. Evaluation shows that FLoRa outperforms greedy, metaheuristic, and deep reinforcement learning baselines, as well as recent UAV data collection methods, by 27.8-76.1% in total expected VIP, 23.5-45.7% in node coverage, and 23.3-54.4% in successful collections.

authors.name: Naresh Babu Kakarla, V. Mahendran

papers.title: Gluing Local Contexts into Global Meaning: A Sheaf-Theoretic Decomposition of Transformer Representations
papers.summary: Prior research into interpretability does not test whether a representation stays consistent under paraphrasing. Each pair of paraphrases can be thought of as a local witness that two activations should be the same. From these local witnesses we can build a cellular sheaf on the paraphrase graph. The question of what is consistent under paraphrasing can be answered by the Laplacian $L_\mathcal{F}$ given a frozen model. No training required. Our kernel $H^0$ gives us a content subspace. We show that with only 20 dims the kernel outperforms the subspace that LEACE retains with all dims on held-out CounterFact fact retrieval by $+17.1$\,pp on average across 8 models. By constraining all paraphrases of a fact together we see an additional increase of $+6.5$\,pp. Our spectral complement shows us where the causal influence is concentrated. Ablating the coordinates that vary the most when paraphrased (which approximates ablating the spectral complement at the coordinate level) leads to $5.6$ to $26.5\times$ larger changes in model outputs compared to ablating coordinates with matched per-coordinate variability. We find this across 9 models from 124M to 13B params. By stacking layers we can create a grid which has $b_1 = N(L-1)$ algebraic 1-cycles. The harmonic mass derived from the model varies by nearly 3 orders of magnitude between the 6 architectures. It also tracks the order of steering fragility (Spearman's $\rho = 0.90$, exact one-sided permutation $p = 0.014$). The kernel, its spectral complement and the harmonic mass all come from the same paraphrase graph. Project page: https://cwru-aism.github.io/gluing-lc-page/.

authors.name: Bryce Grant, Peng Wang

papers.title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
papers.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens. Yet most drafters are trained on short sequences and degrade on long inputs, while long-context training is costly. Existing training-free approaches restrict the context window, rescale positions, or augment recent context with retrieved distant entries. Drafters, however, read target hidden states that already encode contextual and positional information, and their lightweight architecture makes full-history attention affordable. We propose FOLD, a training-free method that preserves exact local positions and treats all distant entries as far memory at a shared position. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, we sharpen attention within it to emphasize relevant entries while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window. Across six target-drafter pairs and diverse benchmarks of up to 256K tokens, FOLD predominantly delivers the highest speedup, with the best case more than doubling the speedup over autoregressive decoding, from 2.08$\times$ to 4.22$\times$.

authors.name: Shuxuan Li, Jialiang Kang, Yanghao Zhou, Ziye Zhu, Zhilin Zhao, Xiao Yang

papers.title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
papers.summary: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so the probability that a loop survives $m$ more repetitions is, under any sampler, a product of per-step continuation probabilities computable from one forward pass. A lock, where this probability stays exactly one, is its limiting case. Pure sampling never locks; top-$p$ with threshold $\pi>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $\pi$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis shows a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $\lambda b^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 61% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 0.2% with $g=8$. In free generation with llama.cpp, all 199 loops that survive DRY, on six models, have $g\le 7$. We propose a count term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window, and closes this blind spot.
