We show that multimodal fusion improves ambiguity-aware metrics but remains visually dominated under strict evaluation, exposing limitations of current VLMs for older-adult affect recognition. Robustness and label agreement experiments show how age-related facial morphology introduces misclassifications, and how cross-modal label disagreement (e.g., happy text / sad image) influences fusion results.

authors.name: Rita Frieske, Bertram E. Shi

papers.title: UniAIDet: A Unified and Universal Benchmark for AI-Generated Image Content Detection and Localization
papers.summary: With the rapid proliferation of image generative models, the authenticity of digital images has become a significant concern. While existing studies have proposed various methods for detecting AI-generated content, current benchmarks are limited in their coverage of diverse generative models and image categories, often overlooking end-to-end image editing and artistic images. To address these limitations, we introduce UniAIDet, a unified and comprehensive benchmark that includes both photographic and artistic images. UniAIDet covers a wide range of generative models, including text-to-image, image-to-image, image inpainting, image editing, and deepfake models. Using UniAIDet, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of various detection methods and answer three key research questions regarding generalization capability and the relation between detection and localization. Our benchmark and analysis provide a robust foundation for future research.

authors.name: Huixuan Zhang, Xiaojun Wan

papers.title: Evaluating Small Open LLMs for Medical Question Answering: A Practical Framework
papers.summary: Incorporating large language models (LLMs) in medical question answering demands more than high average accuracy: a model that returns substantively different answers each time it is queried is not a reliable medical tool. Online health communities such as Reddit have become a primary source of medical information for millions of users, yet they remain highly susceptible to misinformation; deploying LLMs as assistants in these settings amplifies the need for output consistency alongside correctness. We present a practical, open-source evaluation framework for assessing small, locally-deployable open-weight LLMs on medical question answering, treating reproducibility as a first-class metric alongside lexical and semantic accuracy. Our pipeline computes eight quality metrics, including BERTScore, ROUGE-L, and an LLM-as-judge rubric, together with two within-model reproducibility metrics derived from repeated inference (N=10 runs per question). Evaluating three models (Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 12B, MedGemma 1.5 4B) on 50 MedQuAD questions (N=1,500 total responses) reveals that despite low-temperature generation (T=0.2), self-agreement across runs reaches at most 0.20, while 87-97% of all outputs per model are unique -- a safety gap that single-pass benchmarks entirely miss. The clinically fine-tuned MedGemma 1.5 4B underperforms the larger general-purpose models on both quality and reproducibility; however, because MedGemma is also the smallest model, this comparison confounds domain fine-tuning with model scale. We describe the methodology in sufficient detail for practitioners to replicate or extend the evaluation for their own model-selection workflows. All code and data pipelines are available at https://github.com/aviad-buskila/llm_medical_reproducibility.

authors.name: Avi-ad Avraam Buskila

papers.title: Pop-Up Distractions Reveal Bag-of-Events Behavior in Video Large Language Models
papers.summary: A key capability for video understanding is reliably linking subjects to events across time, yet whether Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) actually achieve this remains unclear. In this work, we introduce DistractionBench to evaluate whether VideoLLMs can robustly link subjects and events in the presence of unrelated video segments. Through controlled interventions, such as inserting short advertisement clips into longer videos, we show that VideoLLMs frequently hallucinate interactions between entities from different segments, incorrectly attributing actions from injected advertisements to subjects in the main video. We characterize this systematic hallucination as bag-of-events (BoE) behavior, where models process videos as collections of events rather than temporally structured sequences. Evaluating 11 popular VideoLLMs, we find that all models exhibit substantial BoE behavior. Our findings suggest that VideoLLMs lack reliable mechanisms for temporal grounding and motivate the development of models with more robust subject-event association.

authors.name: Oscar Chew, Serhii Honcharenko, Qian-Hui Chen, Patricia Lu, Dishant Zaveri, Khoa D. Doan, Kuan-Hao Huang

papers.title: NAMESAKES: Probing Identity Memorization in Text-to-Image Models
papers.summary: Text-to-image (T2I) models generate realistic likenesses of some individuals when prompted with their names, raising privacy concerns. However, distinguishing whether a generated face is memorized or fabricated currently requires ground-truth photos, access to training data, or white-box access to model internals, limiting applicability. We introduce a fully black-box behavioral probe that distinguishes between memorized and unrecognized names, while requiring no reference photos or prior knowledge of training data. To benchmark this task, we present the NAMESAKES dataset of over one thousand names and faces of public figures spanning a wide range of fame levels, along with perturbed, less famous names. Experiments on state-of-the-art T2I models show that our probe substantially predicts identity memorization and separates memorized from unrecognized names, with further insights into differences across model families.

authors.name: Morris Alper, Vasudha Varadarajan, Moran Yanuka, Angelina Wang, Hadar Averbuch-Elor

papers.title: Invisible to humans, visible to machines: a preregistered audit of Unicode fidelity across four biomedical bibliographic APIs
papers.summary: To develop a reusable, preregistered method for auditing the character-level fidelity of bibliographic application programming interfaces (APIs), and to apply it to four public APIs used to build biomedical text corpora. Preregistered audit (OSF osf.io/zjevr). From the 2024 PubMed Central (PMC) Open Access subset, a simple random sample of 4,000 English-language research articles was drawn. Abstracts returned by the PubMed E-utilities, Crossref, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were compared with the PMC Journal Article Tag Suite (JATS) XML abstract for 51 registered code points, 34 of them in four primary classes: typographic punctuation, mathematical/scientific symbols, Greek letters and special whitespace. A cell (API x class) was classified as systematic loss when the upper 95% Wilson bound of conditional preservation was below 5%, and as faithful when the lower bound exceeded 90%. The mechanism of each loss was examined in the aligned text and the raw API responses. Two of 16 cells met the loss criterion. PubMed preserved typographic punctuation in 0.6% of eligible abstracts (12/2,113; 95% CI 0.3-1.0%), replacing it with ASCII equivalents. OpenAlex preserved special whitespace in 0.0% (0/1,085; 95% CI 0.0-0.4%), which its inverted-index format cannot store. Mathematical symbols and Greek letters were preserved by all four APIs (95.2-99.7%). Crossref returned an abstract for 75.4% of papers (95% CI 74.1-76.7%) and for none published by Elsevier (0/360) or the American Chemical Society (0/105). The same published abstract reaches text-mining pipelines with different characters depending on the API that serves it. Studies that analyze characters, including character-level markers of writing assisted by large language models, should take text from a source shown to preserve those characters, or normalize all sources identically, and report the API and retrieval date.

authors.name: Przemys{\l}aw Czuma

papers.title: GameEngineBench: Full-Session Verification of Coding Agents in a Networked Game Engine
papers.summary: Coding agents face new challenges in game development, where they must produce code that is not only syntactically correct but also consistent with engine-managed lifecycle, state, and networking behavior. Existing game-development benchmarks, however, do not combine assertions over engine-based runtime states with cross-client consistency, failing to evaluate how well generated code adheres to the desired behavioral specifications. To address these limitations, we present GameEngineBench, a benchmark of 110 C++ implementation tasks derived from 9 existing Unreal Engine 5 projects. Each task requires an agent to implement missing behavior within an established gameplay architecture. We also introduce Full-Session Verification, a testing framework that injects hidden tests after the agent finishes and evaluates the resulting implementation inside Play-in-Editor (PIE) sessions, with networked client worlds in 71 tasks. The tests evaluate Unreal's game loop, actor lifecycle, subsystems, and replication stack while directly inspecting runtime state. In 53 tasks, 119 tests additionally inspect a distinct client world to determine whether the authoritative server state is correctly replicated. To our knowledge, this is the first coding benchmark to evaluate cross-client replication. Across 11 model-harness configurations, the best-scoring configuration achieves 46.4% pass@1, while 43 tasks remain unsolved by every evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate that compilation and shallow verification overestimate agents' ability to implement behavior that remains correct during full engine execution.

authors.name: Brian La, Sungbin Jo, Sejoon Chang, Ben Kim, Junyoung Bae, Aamish Ahmad Beg, Sei Chang, Gonzalo Gonzalez-Pumariega

papers.title: Vision-Language Truck Driving Advisories Grounded in Provincial Rules and Forecast Risks
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can generate context-aware driving advisories, but their outputs may conflict with road conditions or traffic rules, and they typically address a hazard only once it is visible. This matters for long-haul trucking, where heavy trucks need long stopping distances and a single trip may cross several jurisdictions with different traffic regulations. This paper proposes a data generation and distillation framework that integrates structured scene understanding, risk forecasting, and traffic-rule retrieval to generate truck driving decisions and natural-language advisories, with a consistency check on every record. The records, written by an 8B teacher, are then used to distill a 3B-parameter student model for onboard deployment. We also introduce a dashcam dataset covering four Canadian provinces, comprising 11,142 annotated lane-marking frames and 9,494 driving segments. On held-out driving data across all four provinces, the student passes the consistency check in 94.6% of the segments, against 20.2% for the untuned 8B teacher, and announces 26.2% of the risks in the next 10 to 30 seconds before they appear. Of the generated advisories, 97.7% conform to the provincial traffic rules and guidance. These findings suggest that the framework can produce rule-conforming training data for compact driving advisory models.

authors.name: Xintong Jiang, Shucheng Huang, Qiaoxuan Zhang, Jincheng Xu, Yukun Lu

papers.title: BehaviorICL: Task-Conditioned Decoder States for Visual In-Context Learning
papers.summary: The usefulness of an in-context demonstration for a vision-language model (VLM) depends on both the query image and the task posed about it. We study whether the frozen target VLM's own decoder states, read before answer generation, can select such demonstrations. BehaviorICL represents each image and task by a task-conditioned processing signature, the hidden states at the final input position across all decoder layers. Its training-free variant, BehaviorICL-Raw, averages cosine similarities between corresponding layer states and passes the retrieved examples with their reference answers to the same VLM. When the same NICO++ images are asked about their object or their context, Raw retrieves largely different demonstrations for the two questions and outperforms an image retriever given task-matched demonstrations on both VLMs. Across two VLMs and eight classification and visual question answering datasets, Raw gives the highest average accuracy among training-free retrievers on both VLMs and exceeds RICES with a CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder by 3.83 points on Qwen and 1.85 on InternVL. A lightweight shared projection, BehaviorICL-Proj, brings further gains on classification. Analyses of extraction text, decoder depth and bank answers help explain these gains, and attention analysis describes how the task text shifts attention at the extraction position toward the classified object. These results support the target VLM's internal states as a practical basis for visual in-context learning.

authors.name: Chenyang Wang, Jiamo Hu, Chengrui Wu, Lingyue Chen, Jianguo Chen, Xun Xu, Xulei Yang

papers.title: OSLA: Observation-Aware Local Alignment and Cross-Scene Relation Learning for Any-Scenario Person Re-Identification
papers.summary: Any-Scenario Person Re-Identification (AS-ReID) aims to retrieve identities across spectral modalities and aerial-ground viewpoints using a unified model. However, changes in viewpoint and spectrum can make local correspondences unreliable, while conventional sampling may omit cross-camera positive relations needed for training. To address these challenges, we propose OSLA, an observation-aware framework built on supervised CLIP-ReID that combines Local Identity Alignment (LIA) and Cross-Scene Relation Learning (CSR). Specifically, LIA uses historical identity observations and competing-identity information to select reliable cross-scene local correspondences while allowing unmatched regions. Local-to-global distillation transfers identity knowledge from correctly classified historical local features into the global representation. CSR couples observed-cell sampling with spectrum-grouped ranking to jointly organize and optimize cross-camera relations. Sampling across two cameras and two spectra provides same- and cross-spectrum positives, while ranking constrains positive-negative scores separately by gallery spectrum on the final retrieval descriptor. Both modules operate only during training, preserving the original visual encoder and retrieval descriptor at inference. Experiments on WHU-MARS-1000 and WHU-MARS-2337 demonstrate that OSLA achieves absolute Rank-1 gains of 5.0% and 4.8% over UAD, respectively, under the AS-ReID protocol. The code will be available.

authors.name: Xinyang Zhang, Feiyu Han, Chenhao Wu, Yang Liu, Shang Luo, Yingguang Yang, Feng Zhang, Chongyang Zhang, Hao Zheng, Kefu Xu, Congjing Ran, Bin Chong

papers.title: Teacher-Guided Multimodal Dual Representation Reconstruction for Egocentric Human Activity Recognition
papers.summary: Multimodal Egocentric Human Activity Recognition (Ego-HAR) leverages complementary cues from first-person vision (V) and inertial sensor data (S) to recognize daily activities, where video mainly captures appearance and object-related context while inertial signals capture motion cues that video may miss. However, existing pre-training methods typically supervise the fused representation with a single joint objective, which may underemphasize the complementarity between the two modalities and limit the model's ability to learn from distinct modality-oriented signals. To address this issue, we propose Multimodal Dual Representation Reconstruction (MDR2), a teacher-guided pre-training framework in which frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers each provide dense, modality-specific targets to a multimodal student trained on temporally sparse inputs. On the EvIs-Kitchen dataset, MDR2 improves noun/verb F1-macro over the supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at K=4 video key frames and by 1.21/1.82 points at K=32. These results show that MDR2 consistently achieves higher mean recognition performance across the evaluated video-observation settings under the unified backbone setting, with more pronounced gains under sparse inputs.

authors.name: Yuzhe Hao, Ikuro Sato, Rei Kawakami, Koichi Shinoda

papers.title: When Recognition Meets Discovery: Learning Need Not Be Entangled in One Representation Space
papers.summary: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to recognize known classes while discovering novel categories from unlabeled data containing both old and novel samples. Existing methods typically optimize recognition and discovery within a shared representation space, implicitly assuming that the same representation geometry can serve both objectives. Through controlled spectral analysis, we uncover a striking asymmetry: old-class discrimination is increasingly concentrated in the dominant singular directions, while novel-class structure is better preserved in the complementary residual space. More importantly, strengthening the former can even degrade the latter, revealing that recognition and discovery compete for representation capacity rather than merely for optimization weight. Motivated by this observation, we propose Dual-Space Spectral Routing, which dynamically decomposes the representation via online SVD and routes supervised recognition and unsupervised discovery to complementary discriminative and general subspaces. We further exploit their distinct responses to old and novel samples to construct a dual-space novelty signal, which guides Subspace Relation Aggregation (SRA) for organizing candidate novel categories. Extensive experiments across multiple GCD baselines, backbones, and benchmarks demonstrate a consistently improved recognition-discovery balance without introducing additional inference parameters. Code will be open source.

authors.name: Chenglin Liu, An Tian, Mingxuan Du, Shang Rui Yang

papers.title: LightOnOCR for AMNLT: Reading Chant Notation and Lyrics in One Pass, from Single Staves to Whole Pages
papers.summary: Aligned music notation and lyrics transcription (AMNLT) asks for the notes of a chant, its sung text and the assignment of syllables to notes in one output. Fuentes-Mart\'inez et al., who defined the task, found that the one vision-language model they tested fell far behind specialised recognisers. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B, a page OCR model with one billion parameters, end to end, vision encoder included, to write a staff as a GABC string whose letters denote staff positions. Trained on the published AMNLT training split alone, it more than halves the best published aligned music and lyrics error rate (AMLER) on Solesmes, the one directly comparable dataset (9.9 against 21.0 %); on Einsiedeln and Salzinnes, measured in a different encoding, its figures are also lower. The benchmark does not measure generalisation to unseen manuscripts: while the pitch error on AMNLT validation stays between 1.7 and 1.9 %, on 200 staves from five unseen manuscripts it falls from 24.9 to 1.3 % as we add chant aligned through CantusDB, Transkribus ground truth and silver staves kept only where two readers agree. Trained also on multi-staff images, it reads whole pages without staff detection (pitch error 3.3 to 3.8 % on validation and test pages, 1.9 % on pages of unseen manuscripts). Remaining errors include Gothic F clefs read as C clefs, notes dropped with abbreviated or illegible text and lower accuracy on pages with small notation. Controlled ablations are needed to explain the gains.

authors.name: Robert Klugseder (Austrian Centre for Digital Humanities)

papers.title: ORDO: Fine-Grained Motion Understanding in Video LLMs via Order-Dependent Supervision
papers.summary: Video large language models (video LLMs) answer a wide range of questions about real videos, yet they remain weak at fine-grained motion such as whether an object speeds up or slows down. Existing methods train these models on synthetic motion clips, on order pretext tasks such as reordering shuffled clips, or with rewards that compare ordered and perturbed frames. None of them requires that the label be unrecoverable from the frames once their order is discarded, so a model can fit such data from static cues without learning to use frame order. We propose ORDO, a framework that builds this requirement into the training data. We define order-necessary supervision as data in which the unordered set of frames has the same distribution under competing labels, and we realise it for motion attributes with three constructions, time-reversal pairing, matched spatial extent and uniform interval coverage. A procedural curriculum of six motion primitives instantiates these constructions, and low-rank adapters of the language model are trained on it with an answer-level objective and self-distillation replay on real videos. With 4,000 synthetic clips, ORDO raises the mean accuracy over four motion benchmarks by +7.6, +4.9 and +5.1 points on Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-VL-8B and Molmo2-8B, while the same training with shuffled frames changes it by less than one point. Code and generator will be made publicly available.

authors.name: Jiaye Luan, Chaoning Zhang, Pengcheng Zheng, Dongshen Han, Sheng Zheng, Ping Guo, Caiyan Qin, Yang Du, Yang Yang

papers.title: Scale-Aware Reference Attention for Mannequin-to-Model Gown Generation
papers.summary: Formal gowns are sold online with photos of models wearing them, and buyers zoom in to inspect sequins, lace and beading. Image editors can turn a photo of a gown on a mannequin into a convincing photo of a person wearing it, but they receive every reference photo without any notion of its magnification, and the fine detail of the gown is lost when the output is viewed up close. We propose scale-aware reference attention (SARA), which tells an open diffusion transformer the zoom level of the output and of every reference photo, biases the attention of the output toward references of a similar zoom level, uses macro photos of the fabric as references, and is trained on a mix of whole-garment and zoomed targets. To train and evaluate it, we introduce Kiss3000, a dataset of 915 high-resolution mannequin photos and 2274 on-model photos of formal gowns with cross-domain pairs and splits by style, and zoom-crop evaluation, which compares garment crops at full, half and local scale without pixel alignment and judges local fidelity with two vision-language models gated on control crops. With this protocol, Nano Banana Pro at 4K, the highest-resolution commercial editor we test, loses or redraws local detail on 14 of 20 test gowns. At 1536x2048 pixels, both judges prefer SARA over a LoRA fine-tuning baseline on 18 test items and the baseline on 6 (p=0.023), and over the base model on 26 against 4 (p=5.9e-5), while SARA keeps the gown design as often as the baseline.

authors.name: Guang Yang, Fengchen Liu

papers.title: Gradient-Free Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision Models via Agentic Coding
papers.summary: Adapting a vision model to new classes from a few labeled images usually relies on gradient fine-tuning, which is unstable with so few images. We ask whether a coding agent can replace gradient descent for this task. We propose the Agent edit, a method in which a coding agent writes a program that sets the new class weights in the class head of a frozen COCO-trained detector, with no gradient step. The agent runs the detector on the labeled images a limited number of times and sees how much its edit lowers COCO mAP; the program rebuilds the weights without the agent. In the same head and with the same labels, the Agent edit outperforms full-decoder fine-tuning at five shots on 2 of four fine-grained sets, by 11.2 and 12.3 F1 points, and ties on the rest. At ten shots, fine-tuning ties with or outperforms it. Moreover, when the new classes are scored jointly with the COCO classes, the AP of the COCO class to which they belong falls by up to 33.3 points, and limiting that loss lowers F1 on the new classes. Most of the agent's programs share three parts, which we write as a formula that needs no agent. A classifier on frozen backbone features reaches a higher F1 than every method inside the head on every set. Hence a coding agent can replace gradient descent only in part: inside the head and at five shots.

authors.name: Khayrul Islam

papers.title: Cyclic Discrete Diffusion: A Novel Multi-Class Segmentation Refinement Technique
papers.summary: We cast image segmentation refinement as a discrete diffusion process. To solve this task we introduce Cyclic Discrete Diffusion (CDD), a novel forward-reverse formulation with a cyclic label topology that maps a discrete label set to the uniform distribution and back. Instead of injecting Gaussian noise as is done for continuous diffusion, CDD evolves segmentation masks through label jumps: at each step, every pixel either remains in its current class or jumps to the next label with a fixed rate. This jump-or-stay mechanism defines a finite-state Markov process with bounded forward and reverse steps, featuring analytically consistent and tractable reverse dynamics. CDD operates natively in a multi-class label space, enabling joint refinement of all classes in a single pass without requiring class-wise decomposition, as commonly needed in prior binary refinement approaches. The proposed formulation admits a finite and controllable number of refinement steps, for which we analyze the convergence properties through spectral gap analysis. We evaluate CDD across diverse segmentation tasks, including multi-class semantic, instance-level, and binary segmentation refinement. Our method consistently improves both region accuracy and boundary quality across multiple backbones and datasets.

authors.name: Libo Chen, Souvik Ghosh, Vinay P. Namboodiri

papers.title: GC-GS: Optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting with Gradient Conflict as a Geometry Signal
papers.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is commonly optimized with multiple reconstruction losses, which naturally forms a multi-objective optimization problem. This issue becomes more pronounced when perceptual losses are introduced to improve visual quality, as different objectives may impose competing update directions on Gaussian primitives and make it difficult to simultaneously improve fidelity, perceptual quality, and representation efficiency. Based on this view, we reformulate 3DGS training as a multi-objective optimization problem and derive selective conflict-aware position updates that reduce interference between competing objectives while preserving the contribution of each loss. We further observe that gradient conflicts persist throughout training and are most severe in Gaussian position parameters, indicating that objective conflict is closely tied to geometry optimization. We therefore treat position-gradient conflict as a geometry-aware signal to guide densification and pruning. Experiments show that our method achieves better rendering performance while improving representation compactness and rendering efficiency over existing 3DGS variants.

authors.name: Chenhao Zhang, Fengze Zhang, Fengqing Zhu

papers.title: ROSE-SAM3: Response-Oriented Prompt Selection for Open-Vocabulary Remote Sensing Segmentation
papers.summary: In open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) of remote-sensing imagery, class-name prompts can miss objects with varied appearances, while richer descriptions can activate competing classes. We propose Response-Oriented Prompt Selection for SAM 3 (ROSE-SAM3), a training-free framework that selects descriptions using frozen SAM 3 responses on unlabeled target-domain images. We screen candidate descriptions for coverage beyond the native prompts while protecting reliable native class responses, retaining candidates that pass these checks on at least four of five image folds. An offline directed acyclic graph (DAG) search then evaluates candidate combinations and builds a compact PromptBank for each class. Each bank retains the native prompts and adds selected descriptions, which we call residual prompts. At inference, the bank is fixed, and Semantic-Instance Cooperative Head (SICH) uses instance evidence to refine semantic responses before assigning pixel labels. We also introduce RS-OVSS-C to evaluate robustness under six image corruption families across eight remote-sensing datasets, preserving their class vocabularies and reference labels. ROSE-SAM3 achieves 57.3% mean mIoU across eight clean benchmarks and 54.7% on RS-OVSS-C, achieving state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/YanghuiSong/ROSE-SAM3.

authors.name: Yanghui Song, Chengfu Yang, Yongpeng Wen, Zhanxuan Hu, Wei Lu, Qi Ming, Nanqing Liu, Heng-Chao Li

papers.title: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Bone Scaffold Pore Detection: A Comparative Analysis of Few-Shot Performance
papers.summary: Evaluating the mechanical properties of bone scaffolds conventionally requires destructive testing or costly Finite Element Analysis, while deep learning alternatives are constrained by the scarcity of labeled biomaterial imaging data. This study introduces the first expert-annotated, pixel-dense dataset of biopolymer bone-scaffold SEM images, spanning five magnification series, and uses it to benchmark two state-of-the-art pre-trained foundation models under a 12-shot fine-tuning regime. SAM3, an instance segmenter, and YOLOv26, a bounding-box detector, feed the predicted pore geometry to regression heads that estimate Young's modulus and compressive yield strength. Our central finding is that both models fail by pore density rather than magnification: YOLOv26's predicted pore counts saturate and porosity estimation collapses on the most crowded frames, whereas SAM3 over-fragments sparse pore fields and merges adjacent pores in dense ones, producing eight catastrophic failures against three for YOLOv26. Averaged across the 44-image evaluation set, YOLOv26 achieves lower porosity error (19.9% vs. 23.1% MAE), higher precision, and a higher F1 score, whereas SAM3 offers pixel-level instance segmentation that YOLOv26's bounding boxes cannot reproduce. We conclude that model selection should be driven by pore density rather than SEM magnification alone.

authors.name: Tri Tin Vo, Vu Thien An Ngo, Nhi Kieu, Cuong Hung Luu, Giang V. H. Phan, Kien Nguyen, Clinton Fookes

papers.title: NOVA: Normalization-Aware Output-Guided Attention Acceleration for Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.summary: Video diffusion transformers (vDiTs) have become the main backbone for video generation. The quadratic cost of self-attention limits their efficiency at high resolutions and long durations. Existing sparse attention methods often rely on preserving high attention weights. However, these criteria do not fully capture the fidelity of the final value-weighted output, whose error depends jointly on changes to the attention numerator and the softmax denominator. We propose NOVA, a coarse-to-fine sparse attention framework that first approximates the full normalized output using size-weighted key/value centroids. Building on this estimate, we construct a residual proxy that accounts for coupled numerator-denominator errors by centering value contributions around the estimated output. This proxy guides the selection of query-key blocks for refinement under a predefined block budget for each query cluster. Selected blocks are evaluated through exact token-level computation, while the remaining blocks contribute through their centroids under a shared softmax normalization. On five vDiTs, NOVA achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among sparse attention methods, improving PSNR by up to 1.55\,dB over the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 1.82$\times$ end-to-end speedup on an H100 GPU.

authors.name: Wenxuan Miao, Haosong Liu, Aiyue Chen, Yiwu Yao, Zihan Liu, Anbang Wu, Yiming Gan, Jingwen Leng, Minyi Guo, Yu Feng

papers.title: Is It the Agent or the Retry? Separating Selection from Agency in Text-to-Image Generation
papers.summary: Agentic text-to-image systems wrap generators in loops of planning, routing, verification and refinement, and report large gains on compositional benchmarks, almost always relative to a single sample. We ask how much of the gain survives against Single-tool Rejection Retry (\ours): the strongest generator already in the system's pool, an off-the-shelf verifier, and retries that stop at the first accepted image under the system's own budget. Auditing four recent systems with official evaluators, we find that on GenEval SRR matches the accuracy of OctoT2I (0.962 vs.\ 0.96), recovers 63 to 90% of the gain of GEMS depending on the verifier, and exceeds GenPilot by 12 points with 2.3 generations per image; the effect persists with generators not tuned to the benchmark and on T2I-CompBench++. A closed-form analysis predicts the accuracy of SRR at every budget and shows that its gain is capped by the verifier's likelihood ratio. The same analysis also exposes genuine agentic gains: on GenEval 2, even the best of five samples chosen by the evaluator stays 15 points below the score GEMS reports (12 at the upper end of its 95% interval). We prove a ceiling on the accuracy that routing across generators can add, bracket it between one and three points on OctoT2I's own pool, and show that what OctoT2I's routing buys is compute (about 2.5 less than SRR at equal accuracy), not accuracy. In our offline distillation experiments selected samples teach the generator no more than random ones, which a short information argument explains. We end with a reporting checklist for agentic generation papers.

authors.name: Jian Xu, Delu Zeng, Qibin Zhao

papers.title: PhoneQC: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Order-Level Smartphone Trade-in Inspection
papers.summary: As vision-language models enter remote smartphone trade-in, sellers already upload six views and a diagnostic screen, which makes it easy to treat the human quote as a step a model can take over. A model may mark a crack or read the screen, yet the quote is a staff form: appearance fill stays near 0.25, and the closed models that score a little higher do so only on the orders they answer, so human appraisal remains necessary. Two obstacles stand in the way. (1) Single-view defect sets and attribute benchmarks do not score an order-level form under a fixed input contract, so a box or a leaked field can be mistaken for a finished quote. (2) The unread half of the form is the staff fields, and a model left to emit boxes or captions does not learn them. We present PhoneQC, a 335-order iPhone-heavy cut that ranks systems by a 0 to 100 form score (Score100) only inside matched protocols (images alone; images plus a detector sidecar), with a declared upper bound that is not ranked as a peer. As a case study on that board, field-only LoRA freezes the backbone, adapts attention projections, and supervises staff fields while leaving the defect list empty; the adapter sees the same images as the zero-shot model. On image-only T1 the 3B model rises from 26.6 to 33.3 at coverage 0.928; without the empty-blocker item the open ranking still favors the adapter, while the remaining gap to a person stays large on this cut.

authors.name: Zihan Deng, Xinpei Lin, Du Tiantian, Lequan Yu

papers.title: StateBind: Exposing the Symbol-to-State Binding Gap in Visual Measurement
papers.summary: Reliable vision systems should connect numerical claims to visible evidence. In visual measurement, this requires mapping candidate values to image-specific physical states. StateBind-200 augments 200 real images with human-refined local geometry and matched Numeric, Calibrated, and Physicalized interfaces. Across a 128-image held-out evaluation and 6,696 controlled calls, physicalizing identical candidates raises three-model majority accuracy from 75.54% to 91.13%, a source-image-balanced gain of +15.30 points. Calibration and additional reasoning leave most of the gap intact; target localization can succeed despite incorrect value-lattice binding, with a larger burden for two-endpoint ruler spans. An independent 40-image geometry audit yields a 0.08-tick median target discrepancy and preserves the main effect under disagreement sensitivity. We further propose Factorial StateBind, a training-free selective verifier. Two VLMs propose target and lattice components, an independent VLM validates their evidence, and valid combinations are resolved deterministically. A precision mode selected on 69 development images combines component validity, four-way agreement, and state separation. Applied unchanged to held-out evaluation, this high-precision evidence gate reaches 91.67% candidate precision across 36/128 images (28.12%) and 9.68% of ordered cells. The results identify instance-specific symbol-to-state binding as a distinct reliability bottleneck and provide an interpretable evidence gate for numerical visual claims.

authors.name: Qing Mu, Jiani Zheng

papers.title: Separating Module Gain From Transport Plan Contribution in Audio-Visual Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition
papers.summary: A cross-modal routing module can improve over its backbone while its transport plan accounts for no demonstrable part of that improvement. In ABVnet with DFEW, Sinkhorn cross-modal routing (SCR) exceeds the retrained baseline by 0.87 unweighted average recall (UAR) points, a resolved difference, yet sits 0.17 points above an individually trained, parameter-matched pooled variant, an unresolved difference that establishes no equivalence; under the development protocol the comparison with the baseline reverses. Separating the two needs comparisons a module-against-backbone test cannot supply: parameter-matched variants changing only the plan rule, and interventions replacing the plan without retraining. The evaluation covers MMA-DFER and ABVnet on DFEW and MAFW, and MMA-DFER on CREMA-D, with a single training run per configuration and paired fold intervals. ABVnet with DFEW motivated the follow-up after the broader results were available. Replacing the plan everywhere with a uniform one reduces UAR by 0.72, whereas permuting its rows gives an unresolved difference of -0.20 UAR points; permutation is less damaging by 0.51 UAR points, a resolved contrast. Replacing the plan with the product of its own marginals, preserving both marginals and removing only frame-specific mixtures, reduces UAR by 0.70. These reductions concern reliance at inference; attribution of the module gain to the transport plan remains unestablished. Under the 1.5 fold-dependence widening, the baseline gain remains resolved, whereas the replacement reductions and the paired contrast are unresolved.

authors.name: Vu Nhat Minh Pham, Cong Khanh Nguyen, Minh Tuan Le, Van Thong Huynh

papers.title: RALC: Risk-Controlled Local Adoption of Segmentation Updates with Few Calibration Images
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a road-scene segmenter for rain and nighttime driving can introduce errors on normal daytime images. With few labeled normal images for calibration, a whole-image risk check may reject changes that would pass if adopted locally. Risk-Controlled Adoption of Label Changes (RALC) selects local changes from a fixed model update, using confidence differences and an image score to form nested candidates. On each normal calibration image, RALC measures how many more errors each candidate makes than the original model, assigning zero loss when errors stay the same or fall. At test time, each replacement can add at most one error, so the replacement count bounds the net increase without test labels. RALC combines this candidate-dependent bound with recorded calibration losses to select the largest set that passes the risk check. If the models and adoption rules are fixed before calibration and normal calibration and test images are exchangeable, the expected per-image loss stays within budget. On held-out BDD100K, we evaluated three weight-interpolated updates with 10 additional normal images per calibration draw. At a common fixed budget, adverse-scene mIoU was 1.89--3.19 percentage points higher with RALC than with whole-image adoption, while measured mean normal loss was also higher. After matching this loss post hoc at 1,000 pixels per image, RALC still led by 1.135--2.428 points. Selecting changes in $8\times8$-pixel cells recovered 93--98% of this advantage. With 250 calibration images at the original budget, both rules adopted all three updates in full.

authors.name: Shize Yin

papers.title: ReMiC: Representation-Driven Token Pruning for 3D VLMs via Minimax Hierarchical Clustering
papers.summary: 3D vision-language models (3D VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. However, their reliance on multi-view inputs produces long visual token sequences, imposing substantial computational overhead during inference. Existing pruning methods often rely on token salience or feature diversity as proxies for representativeness, without explicitly modeling the representation gap between the original token set and the retained subset, thereby leading to suboptimal representation of the original scene. In this paper, we propose ReMiC, a training-free, representation-driven token pruning framework based on minimax hierarchical clustering. ReMiC treats retained tokens as prototypes for the original observations, formulating pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget. Local prototype initialization allocates tokens according to regional representation needs, while global prototype refinement updates the selected prototypes using cross-region information to further reduce the maximum representation error. Extensive experiments conducted on three representative 3D VLMs across five 3D scene understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method. Notably, by retaining only 10% of visual tokens, ReMiC preserves 93.2% of the performance of Video-3D LLM and achieves a $2.04\times$ faster inference speed.

authors.name: Bangfeng Yan, Chaoning Zhang, Yuanhao Liu, Pengcheng Zheng, Mengyuan Li, Wei Dong, Sheng Zheng, Yang Yang

papers.title: DINO-KNN: Training-Free Multiclass In-Context Segmentation via Nearest Neighbors
papers.summary: In-context segmentation (ICS) segments a target image given a few annotated reference images. Recent training-free methods built on frozen foundation models segment one class at a time and gain little from additional references. We study the multiclass, multi-reference setting and ask how far a simple joint decision rule can go. We introduce DINO-KNN, which stores every labeled reference patch of a frozen DINOv3 encoder in a single memory and labels each target patch by a distance-weighted vote of its k nearest neighbors. All classes are predicted in a single pass, with one label per pixel, without training or a mask decoder. We evaluate on eight datasets, four natural and four medical, with R=1 to 15 reference images and three reference seeds. DINO-KNN achieves the best average mIoU at every R; it is the best method on six of the eight datasets from R=3 and on seven of the eight from R=7. Its accuracy continues to grow with the number of references, from 37.8 mIoU at R=1 to 56.2 at R=15, while the strongest baseline, INSID3, rises from 36.1 to 42.9. DINO-KNN is also 2.1x faster than INSID3. The code will be made public.

authors.name: Hussain Alasmawi, Numan Saeed, Mohammad Yaqub

papers.title: Robust Trajectory Prediction Under Sensing and V2X Noise: Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies
papers.summary: Anticipating the future behavior of surrounding objects is key for the safe and efficient navigation of autonomous vehicles. State-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models are typically trained and evaluated on large-scale, highly curated datasets obtained by filtering any object detection and tracking noise through extensive offline post-processing. However, in real-world deployments, the detected objects' state (position, heading, and speed) estimates are inherently affected by sensing and localization uncertainties. These uncertainties can be even higher for connected and automated vehicles receiving information from other road users through Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications. In this paper, we first investigate the sensitivity of five state-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models to realistic noisy object state estimates. Numerical results show that prediction accuracy degrades by up to a 6x factor as the noise level increases, highlighting the models' sensitivity to the mismatch between the noise conditions encountered during training and those experienced at deployment. We then show that retraining models on a more realistic noise-augmented dataset is a more effective strategy to mitigate the impact of noisy object state estimates on trajectory prediction accuracy than using denoising modules at the input. Retrained models limit the prediction accuracy degradation below a 1.5x factor. The noise-augmented dataset is openly released to support further research.

authors.name: Shahab Salehi, Luca Lusvarghi, Miguel Sepulcre, Javier Gozalvez

papers.title: ENGRAM: Reliability-Weighted Latent Fusion and Occlusion-Aware Layered Readout for Video World Models
papers.summary: Camera-conditioned video world models aim to generate 3D-consistent videos from a single image along specified camera trajectories. However, set-union updates in latent spatial memory leave repeated observations unconsolidated, while frontmost-only readout limits simultaneous access to stored evidence at different depths. To address these limitations, we present ENGRAM, a latent spatial memory framework combining reliability-weighted latent fusion and occlusion-aware layered readout. Specifically, recursive fusion integrates geometrically and visually compatible observations in a channel-normalized latent space, consolidating repeated evidence into a shared scene representation. Layered readout exposes multiple depth-ordered latent candidates with their reliability and availability at each target cell. This gives the generator access to information from multiple surfaces as visibility changes. Explicit camera rays provide viewpoint information independently of memory coverage, while geometric consistency constraints guide memory updates. Memory retrieval uses a single projection at latent resolution, avoiding intermediate RGB rendering and VAE re-encoding. We adapt a pretrained video generator using only 256 training scenes. On 100 RealEstate10K test scenes, ENGRAM improves novel-view-synthesis and closed-loop PSNRs over Spatia by 0.82 and 4.48 dB, respectively. On a 200-case WorldScore evaluation subset, it achieves an average score of 67.78, exceeding Spatia by 3.31 points. Project page: https://wchkoutian.github.io/engram-website/.

authors.name: Chenhao Wu, Zhaolong Su, Yang Liu, Tianrui Su, Yingguang Yang, Shang Luo, Yancheng Chen, Chongyang Zhang, Hao Zheng, Kefu Xu, Congjing Ran, Bin Chong

papers.title: Dynamics-Guided Conditional MeanFlow from Regional Interaction to Internal Revision and Its Application to CT Imaging
papers.summary: Conditional image enhancement requires spatially varying corrections, yet fixed-depth models allocate similar computational budgets regardless of where additional refinement is needed. Although one-step flow models reduce inference costs and iterative restoration methods introduce subsequent corrections, how predicted transformation dynamics can guide internal feature refinement remains underexplored. We introduce IRCMF, a dynamics-guided Conditional MeanFlow framework that combines regional interaction with recurrent internal revision. The decoder predicts signed interval velocity and a learned velocity-change cue. A soft-region graph aggregates contextual information for velocity estimation, while a dynamics-conditioned graph establishes regional relationships to guide recurrent bottleneck updates. The revised features are processed by the shared decoder to recompute velocity, establishing feedback between transformation dynamics and internal representations. An actor-critic policy controls regional updates and further revisions to balance enhancement quality and computational cost. We evaluate IRCMF on two computed tomography (CT) datasets, NLST for STANDARD-to-LUNG kernel enhancement and LDCT-and-Projection-data for simulated low-to-routine-dose enhancement. With nine decoder evaluations, IRCMF achieves slice-level PSNR of $36.24 \pm 3.49$ dB and SSIM of $0.97 \pm 0.01$ on NLST, and PSNR of $32.45 \pm 1.97$ dB and SSIM of $0.84 \pm 0.05$ on LDCT-and-Projection-data. The learned policy reduces average decoder evaluations to 4.42 and 3.45, respectively, lowering per-slice latency from 97.00 to 51.82 ms and from 97.12 to 41.95 ms, with PSNR reductions of only 0.20 and 0.06 dB.

authors.name: Md Shifatul Ahsan Apurba, Md Selim, Jin Chen

papers.title: VideoJSON: A Minimal Harness Beats Purpose-Built Memory for Ultra-Long Video Understanding
papers.summary: Answering questions over days or weeks of video requires searching for scattered clues across long timelines. Existing video agents rely on complex memory graphs and fixed retrieval pipelines, which restrict how the agent can search. We propose VideoJSON, a minimal harness for ultra-long video understanding that keeps the memory simple and lets a coding agent write its own search programs. During indexing, a vision-language model turns each minute of video into a single JSON record containing a dense caption and structured fields such as events, entities, places, and speech transcripts. At query time, the agent writes Python or Bash programs in a sandboxed container to filter, link, and read these records over multiple steps, without task-specific training or raw video access. On four ultra-long video benchmarks, VideoJSON with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash outperforms MAGIC-Video by 7.0, 20.0, and 24.75 points on EgoLifeQA, Ego-R1-Bench, and MM-Lifelong Week, and beats the best prior EgoMemReason score by 12.6 points. Across four policy models of increasing capability, VideoJSON's average score rises by up to 11.58 points over the weakest model, compared with at most 5.50 points for MAGIC-Video. Ablations show that both agentic code search and the structured JSON records drive these gains, while adding hourly summaries, extra tools, or video access changes the average score by less than 1.5 points. In addition, fine-tuning Qwen-3.5-Flash on 64 VideoJSON trajectories from an unrelated 100-hour livestream improves its MM-Lifelong scores by up to 8.25 points. Code will be open-sourced after publication.

authors.name: Wenqi Marshall Guo, Kuan-Hao Huang, Junda Chen, Hao Zhang

papers.title: Med-Agentic: Distilling Agentic Medical Reasoning with Internalized Meta-Capabilities
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) in expert domains face a trade-off between agentic tool use, which externalizes expertise behind brittle multi-turn runtimes, and end-to-end specialization, which internalizes expertise only implicitly at task-level granularity. We propose internalized meta-capabilities: atomic, parametrically internalized, and composable reasoning units that an LLM can select and combine within a single chain-of-thought (CoT). We instantiate this idea as Med-Agentic for medical visual diagnosis, where the model emits a capability-tagged structured CoT in one forward pass, turning capability invocation into tagged token generation rather than external tool calls. For training, Med-OPD performs multi-teacher on-policy distillation with token-level dual-factor teacher routing conditioned on both the image and the active capability tag, strictly generalizing per-prompt teacher routing. We show that this routing gives an unbiased estimator of the same expected teacher-KL gradient. Across public medical imaging datasets spanning nine anatomies and eight modalities, Med-Agentic consistently improves in-distribution and out-of-distribution diagnostic accuracy over the strong competitors.

authors.name: Yucheng Zhou, Junwei Sheng, Jianbing Shen

papers.title: BReD: BEV Residual Diffusion for Feed-Forward Road Gaussian Reconstruction
papers.summary: Accurate road surface reconstruction is essential for autonomous-driving mapping and simulation, but existing methods trade reconstruction quality for cross-scene inference. Optimization-based methods recover detailed surfaces through costly per-scene optimization, while feed-forward methods lack road-specific constraints and often produce large elevation errors. We propose \textbf{BReD}, a feed-forward framework for reconstructing road elevation, appearance, and semantics from calibrated six-camera sequences. BReD first estimates coarse elevation through LiDAR-supervised depth learning and BEV lifting, using only cameras at inference. A lightweight BEV residual diffusion model then conditions elevation refinement on a camera-derived depth--elevation discrepancy and elevation-aware image features. Diffusion-indexed perturbations expose the model to different discrepancy corruption levels during training, while inference performs one deterministic refinement from the clean discrepancy. The refined elevations are temporally aggregated to anchor road-aligned Gaussians, whose attributes are predicted by a geometry-prior-guided decoder without test-time optimization. On four held-out nuScenes scenes, BReD achieves 7.34 cm elevation RMSE and 90.92\% semantic mIoU, compared with 14.43 cm for RoGS without test-time LiDAR and 8.88 cm for its test-time-LiDAR-assisted variant; both RoGS variants require per-scene optimization.

authors.name: Baizhi Wang

papers.title: DeFlowCritic: Dense Latent Reward Alignment for Text-to-Image Flow Matching Models
papers.summary: Online reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for aligning text-to-image flow matching models with complex user intent. However, existing methods typically rely on sparse rewards computed only from final decoded images. This delays credit assignment across the denoising trajectory and makes training computationally expensive. Moreover, simply combining multiple rewards does not reliably produce a Pareto trade-off, where gains in compositional accuracy often degrade aesthetic quality. In this work, we propose DeFlowCritic, an efficient online RL framework based on Dense Latent Reward Alignment. Unlike prior work, our method provides dense supervision on intermediate latents, enabling early-stage guidance for the denoising trajectory. To achieve this, we introduce an internal critic that evaluates noisy latents using features extracted directly from the diffusion model, a representation inherently better suited for latent-space reward estimation than standard image encoders. We construct a high-quality reward-modeling dataset with continuous scores for critic training, capturing compositional correctness on high-quality reference images. The resulting dense reward enables efficient online RL training and inference-time scaling. Experiments show that our method achieves a superior balance between prompt faithfulness and visual quality on GenEval2 and T2I-CompBench++ benchmarks. The approach also generalizes across text-to-image flow matching models, including SD3.5-Medium, SD3.5-Large, and FLUX.1-dev.

authors.name: Zeeshan Khan, Xin Yu, Shizhe Chen, Cordelia Schmid

papers.title: eSPG: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Event Speckle Plethysmography
papers.summary: Non-contact measurement of vital signs such as heart rate (HR) is valuable for patient monitoring and rescue operations. However, existing methods struggle with ambient illumination and motion, and have been demonstrated only at distances of tens of meters. Here we introduce event speckle plethysmography (eSPG), which illuminates a body part with a low-power (0.5-5 mW) laser and captures the resulting dynamic speckle pattern using an event camera. Event cameras, with their high dynamic range, temporal resolution, and sensitivity to intensity changes, are well-suited to capturing rapid speckle fluctuations that encode the physiological signal, even under challenging illumination and imaging conditions. We demonstrate HR estimation at 1 km with a mean absolute error of 5 beats per minute, and 90% of estimates satisfy an AAMI-defined HR estimation criterion. This distance exceeds previous remote plethysmography demonstrations by an order of magnitude and previous speckle plethysmography demonstrations by over three orders of magnitude. We also study and characterize robustness to motion and ambient illumination. Our theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that resolving dynamic speckle fluctuations enables accurate heart rate estimation even at kilometer-scale distances, establishing a new direction toward robust, non-contact physiological monitoring.

authors.name: Aniket Dashpute, Anirudh Bindiganavale Harish, Bhargav Ghanekar, Alankar Kotwal, Andrew Negrut, Syna Gupta, Pablo A. Valdes, Ashok Veeraraghavan

papers.title: Task-Agnostic Incremental Vision-Language Object Detection via Prompt Augmentation and Distribution-Aware Fusion
papers.summary: Incremental Vision-Language Object Detection (IVLOD) empowers pre-trained open-vocabulary detectors to continuously learn new visual concepts from sequential tasks without forgetting foundational knowledge. However, existing methods predominantly rely on oracle task identities during inference, severely limiting their open-world practicality. In this paper, we formalize Task-Agnostic IVLOD (TA-IVLOD), a more realistic setting where such priors are unavailable, requiring the model to simultaneously recognize classes from all learned tasks. This unconstrained setting exposes severe performance degradation due to cross-task semantic interference and parameter conflicts. To tackle these challenges, we propose TADA, a novel modular framework. Specifically, TADA introduces Stochastic Prompt Augmentation to mitigate semantic interference via training-time noise injection, and Test-Time Distribution-Aware Fusion to dynamically weight class-specific LoRA experts, effectively resolving parameter conflicts. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms baselines in standard IVLOD and yields substantial improvements in the rigorous TA-IVLOD setting on the ODinW-13 benchmark, while effectively preserving zero-shot generalization on the MS COCO dataset. The code is available at https://github.com/yonghanjiang/TADA.

authors.name: Yonghan Jiang, Zhengyuan Xie, Wenchu Liu, Linlan Huang, Fei Yang, Xialei Liu

papers.title: GlaucomaMarker - Biomarker-Grounded Glaucoma Vision-Language Model
papers.summary: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness. In the current clinical setting, glaucoma diagnosis is generally conducted by assessing optic disc cupping and asymmetry. Vision-language models (VLMs) have been utilized in recent years for glaucoma, mostly trained on fixed templates or AI-generated captions, as no public text describes the biomarkers. Our proposed framework, GlaucomaMarker, hypothesizes that retinal structural biomarkers can ground glaucoma-based VLMs. It converts public segmentation masks into sentences describing eleven biomarkers, to teach retinal foundation models to read them. We applied this framework to RETFound (GlaucomaMarker-R) and FLAIR (GlaucomaMarker-F), training on 9,778 images that yielded 45,190 image-text pairs. On a real-world clinical cohort, GlaucomaMarker-F detects glaucoma with an AUROC of 0.905, against 0.848 for FLAIR, and both read the biomarkers where baselines stay near random guessing. Since the biomarker text is computed from existing masks, it comes at no extra cost.

authors.name: Ahammed Sakir Nabil, Sadia Siraz, Nikita Chincholkar, Atalie C. Thompson, Jason Xiao, Theodore Leng, Jennifer I. Lim, Minhaj Nur Alam

papers.title: Alignment under Hard Negative Re-Pairing: Cross-Modal Similarity, Scale and Retrieval
papers.summary: Do vision and language models represent the world alike? That question hides three: what structure each modality has, whether the two modalities organize images and their captions alike, and whether a model ranks an image's own caption highly. Centered kernel alignment (CKA) and neighborhood agreement answer the second, yet matching and model selection use them as if they identified individual pairs and answered the third. To test this reading, we introduce hard negative re-pairing: every image receives the caption of a similar image, and nothing else changes. Although no image keeps its own caption and annotators judge a majority of the substituted captions wrong, CKA stays higher than under a random re-pairing that keeps 80% of the original pairs. In all 22 image-text models we test, neighborhood agreement loses far less than top-one retrieval, which collapses. The reason is scale: these diagnostics pool over many neighbors, matching and retrieval are decided among the nearest ones, and an exact decomposition shows that near-neighbor pairs contribute almost nothing to CKA. In the matching problems we test, an exact maximizer of CKA would not return the original pairing. On COCO and Flickr30k, the model with the highest diagnostic value retrieves worse on held-out data than the model chosen by validation recall, even where the two correlate positively. What re-pairing removes is the informative part: that share tracks retrieval on both datasets and ranks encoder pairs before alignment training. A diagnostic should be reported with its question and its scale, and tested against hard negative re-pairing.

authors.name: Charles Weng, Alexander Martin, Sandra Arcos-Holzinger, Andrew Yates, Dixin Zheng, Yue Zhang, Landi Zhou

papers.title: TOGO: Take One Image Editor, Get One Video Editor for Free
papers.summary: Instruction-based image editors are trained on millions of edit pairs and follow instructions far more reliably than current video editors. We show that this ability can be transferred to video editing without any training. Our key observation is that a growing number of image editors and video generators share the same latent space. Their velocity fields can therefore be combined at sampling time: the difference between the editor's velocity under the instruction and under a neutral prompt, which we call the \emph{edit velocity}, can be added to the sampler of a video model. Added naively, however, it blurs the video, alters the background and flickers. An analysis of the edit velocity explains why. It is small and reliable only at coarse scales and high noise levels, not concentrated on the edited object, and uncorrelated across frames. From these properties, we derive a simple guidance operator that amplifies the edit velocity and restricts it in noise level, space, and time. The video model then turns the incoherent per-frame signal into a temporally coherent edit. Our method, TOGO, combines Qwen-Image-Edit with the Wan2.1 video model without training or fine-tuning. On FiVE-Bench, it raises the edit success rate from 47.0\% (the same video model without the editor) to 65.6\%, above the best published method (59.2\%). At the same time, it maintains the background PSNR and obtains the best LPIPS and SSIM of all methods. Because the video editor is assembled at inference time, it can be upgraded to any newer image editor that shares the latent space with no cost.

authors.name: Yixuan Luo, Jose Caballero, Yanjing Li

papers.title: Plan Big, Paint Small: Semantic-Aware Computation Allocation for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.summary: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion streams a video chunk by chunk, but large AR models are too slow for real-time use. We ask where in an AR rollout a large model is actually needed. Pairing Krea-Realtime-14B with Self-Forcing-1.3B, which share their latent space and denoising schedule, we find that the order of the two models matters: when the 14B model generates only the first chunk and the 1.3B model continues, the rollout keeps 95\% of the 14B model's semantic advantage, whereas the reverse allocation keeps 16\% at about ten times the cost. The large model decides what the video shows; the small model only has to carry it forward. We turn this into BigSmall, a training-free planner--renderer sampler. The 14B model plans the opening chunk and sketches the chunks in which content changes, which preserves motion, and the 1.3B model renders the rest; a faster variant, BigSmall, plans only the opening chunk. A cross-model KV cache that is approximate, windowed and lazy lets the planner leave and re-enter the rollout at low cost. On VBench, BigSmall is $3.02\times$ faster than the 14B model at an unchanged semantic score and motion, and $1.55\times$ faster than SDVG, which lets the small model draft first; BigSmall reaches $3.77\times$ at the same semantic score, trading away 10\% of the motion. On minute-long videos (LoCoT2V-Bench), where the 14B model degrades when it reads its own long history, BigSmall is $3.14\times$ faster than the 14B model and scores higher ($+1.78$).`

authors.name: Yixuan Luo, Yanjing Li

papers.title: CAMA: Calibrated Anti-Collapse Marginal Alignment for Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models
papers.summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a model using unlabeled test data to help it handle distribution shifts. However, prior work has found that image corruption causes a vision-language model (VLM) to produce more similar features for different images, a phenomenon known as feature compression. Under compression, entropy minimization, the most common TTA objective, can cause the model to favor a few classes and perform worse than before adaptation. Despite these observations, a detailed analysis of how these failures are connected and an effective strategy for preventing them are still lacking. In this paper, we first analyze why entropy minimization fails for VLMs. We then propose CAMA, a new test-time adaptation objective that maximizes batch mutual information to encourage confident predictions for individual images while maintaining diverse predictions across the batch. CAMA also estimates a reference class distribution early in the test stream and aligns each batch's average prediction with this reference during adaptation. We prove that feature compression biases the predictions and that entropy minimization amplifies this bias into collapse, whereas CAMA is guaranteed to preserve every class. Across standard corruption benchmarks, we observe collapse on nearly every VLM backbone evaluated. CAMA prevents collapse in every observed case and, in turn, achieves the best accuracy on every backbone. Quantitative and qualitative analyses confirm that CAMA reverses the feature compression behind the collapse, and ablations show that each of its components contributes.

authors.name: Jinho Kang, Yunhui Guo

papers.title: VICA: Video Contextual Agreement for AIGC Video Detection and Localization
papers.summary: The rapid advancement of AI-generated content (AIGC) video generation and editing technologies has raised growing societal concerns about the authenticity and reliability of digital videos. Existing video detection methods primarily exploit temporal inconsistencies through holistic frame-level representations, whereas manipulation localization methods focus on artifacts within individual spatial regions. However, holistic representations may obscure localized artifacts through global feature aggregation, while region-centric approaches may overlook disagreements between individual regions and their surrounding spatiotemporal context. To address these limitations, we propose VIdeo Contextual Agreement (VICA), a unified framework that masks individual video regions and leverages a frozen V-JEPA model to predict their representations from the surrounding spatiotemporal context. Complementary masking ensures complete regional coverage, while context-conditioned predictions establish references for assessing regional agreement with the broader video context. By comparing predicted and observed representations, VICA derives spatial residuals that characterize intra-frame discrepancies and bidirectional temporal residuals that capture inconsistencies across preceding and subsequent frames. These residuals characterize contextual disagreements, providing a shared forensic representation for both tasks and shifting the focus from identifying isolated manipulation artifacts to assessing regional agreement with expectations inferred from the broader video context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VICA achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks across multiple benchmarks, with strong generalization to unseen video generators and editing methods.

authors.name: Runheng Lin, Jialiang Shen, Jiyang Zheng, Ruiqi Liu, Zonglin He, Yu Yao, Huajie Chen, Chris Russell, Runqi Lin

papers.title: Simple Baselines for Fetal Brain Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
papers.summary: Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) offers a promising approach to fetal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) analysis, where pathological data are scarce. Existing methods rely mainly on brain age prediction or image reconstruction, but are limited by noisy gestational age (GA) labels, lack of lesion localization, or poor cross-domain generalization. We propose FetalBUAD, a UAD framework based on voxel-level brain age estimation. A joint multi-task network predicts global brain age, voxel-level brain age maps, and brain segmentation to establish an internal biological brain age reference, reducing reliance on clinically recorded GA. Uncertainty-aware voxel-level brain age gap maps are then used for anomaly localization. Experiments on 1,317 internal fetal brain MRI volumes and an external benchmark demonstrate state-of-the-art anomaly detection performance and improved cross-domain generalization. FetalBUAD also generates anatomically interpretable maps that localize diverse fetal brain abnormalities. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/birthlab/FetalBUAD.

authors.name: Hongjia Yang, Mingxuan Liu, Yingqi Hao, Xiaotian Hu, Siyao Li, Xuguang Bai, Fenglin Jia, Yijin Li, Yifei Chen, Zihan Li, Juncheng Zhu, Jing Liu, Yi Liao, Ziyu Li, Haibo Qu, Qiyuan Tian

papers.title: VG3R: Video Generation Model for Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
papers.summary: Video generation models are widely used as 3D priors for novel view synthesis and 3D scene generation. Fine-tuned for perception, generation models also excel at dense prediction such as depth estimation. However, methods that apply video generation models to 3D reconstruction either predict depth without cameras or generate geometry and estimate cameras through many iterative denoising steps, which makes them slower. In this paper, we present $\textbf{VG3R}$, which turns a pretrained video generation model into a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model. Our key observation is that such a model already captures the depth and camera motion of a video, but not in the form required for reconstruction. We introduce two components: $\textit{clip-level shift prediction}$, which corrects depth distortion caused by the unknown shift in decoded inverse depth, and a $\textit{multi-layer camera head}$, which predicts per-frame cameras parameters by combining features across transformer blocks. Using Wan2.1 as its video backbone, VG3R reconstructs a scene and estimate the camera of every frame without iterative denoising. It achieves the lowest ATE and reconstruction errors among methods built on video generation models, runs about 4 and 14 times faster than Aether and Geo4D. VG3R also demonstrates competitive depth estimation and 3D reconstruction performance compared with geometry foundation models. Project page: https://github.com/KTH-RPL/VG3R

authors.name: Jingong Chen, Qingwen Zhang, Lin Lian, Xinxin Zuo, Yang Wang, Chulwoo Pack, Kyle Gao, Patric Jensfelt, Kwanghee Won

papers.title: Where the Image Sits: Vision-Text Order Bias in Jev
papers.summary: Jev-style system-1 decision models read a choice from a single prefill. They restrict the next-token distribution to the supplied option labels and return a distribution over the options, with no generation and no parsing. Recent work shows that generative vision-language models are sensitive to the relative order of image and text tokens. We ask whether that sensitivity reaches this Jev-style readout. The answer is always read at the end of the prompt, so moving the image changes the distance from the visual evidence to the decision, but never the position at which the decision is read. Using four placements---prefix, pre-question, pre-options, and suffix---and holding the option listing fixed, we measure argmax flips, total variation, accuracy, calibration, and label marginals. Suffix placement flips 41.0% of decisions and lowers accuracy by 18.6 points. Averaged over the four slots, the curve is monotone, not U-shaped. That shape differs from prior results on generative vision-language models. The effect survives a battery of controls. We also introduce prefix--question averaging (P+Q), a two-forward readout that averages the prefix and pre-question distributions. It is at least as accurate as prefix and outperforms the prior baselines. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/Youzhi333/Visual_Tex_Order_Bias_Jev.

authors.name: Youzhi Zhang

papers.title: Centerline-Guided Multi-Class Road Surface Segmentation
papers.summary: Road-surface extraction from satellite imagery supports geo- graphic mapping, but a binary mask leaves road axes, transverse extent, and junction structure implicit. Learning these proper- ties together is challenging because narrow corridors, merging roads, and occlusions require different geometric cues. We present a centerline-guided multi-class segmentation framework that makes these dependencies explicit. A hierarchical encoder sup- plies shared features, while predicted centerline features and soft probabilities condition specialized regular, intersection, and over- pass decoders. A two-component width branch supplies transverse geometry to regular-surface decoding, and learned feature fusion produces the complete road mask. Unlike independent prediction heads or a fixed union of component masks, this design exchanges geometric information during decoding while retaining separately inspectable outputs. Evaluation of the four-semantic-output con- figuration on CHN6-CUG achieves 65.53% complete-surface IoU, improving on a binary SegFormer-B4 baseline by 1.01 percentage points and reducing false-positive pixels by 11.94%. The results support geometry-aware surface refinement and a richer raster representation for road-map inspection.

authors.name: Xu Ouyang, Lin Gan, Di Ma, Sonnie Chen, Sanjay Boddhu

papers.title: Reconstruction-Guided Dual-Branch Learning for LiDAR Anomalous Object Detection
papers.summary: Detecting unexpected objects is essential for autonomous driving safety. Most existing LiDAR anomaly detectors rely on semantic discrimination, which primarily captures category-discriminative features but may overlook deviations from broader feature relationships in normal scenes. Reconstruction offers a complementary perspective by assessing consistency with learned normal patterns. However, pointwise reconstruction errors alone struggle to distinguish anomalies from normal variability in complex outdoor point clouds. We propose Structured Residual Reasoning (SRR) to extract additional anomaly evidence from residual structure across feature channels, time sequences, and geometric space. We further establish that semantic discrimination and normal-pattern reconstruction capture fundamentally different yet complementary anomaly evidence: category compatibility and consistency with learned normal patterns, respectively. At matched background false-positive rates, SRR recovers more objects missed entirely by the semantic branch while producing fewer false positives in normal-only scenes. Building on this finding, we propose Reconstruction-Guided Dual-Branch (RGDB) learning, in which SRR-derived normal-pattern consistency cues guide a semantic-conditioned anomaly decoder to complement reconstruction-based predictions during training. At inference, the two branches jointly exploit their complementary anomaly evidence. Experiments show that standalone SRR establishes a strong reconstruction-based baseline without semantic labels from the target-scene training data, while RGDB achieves state-of-the-art performance on the STU validation set.

authors.name: Guanyu Jiang, Junjie Cao, Jinshan Pan, Zhixun Su

papers.title: Analyzing Atypical Local Features in Museum Artifacts using Generative Image Inpainting
papers.summary: This study proposes a method for analyzing local visual features in museum artifacts that may appear atypical or unexpected. Objects in the same category often share a similar overall shape, while local details such as patterns, decorations, and facial expressions may reflect regional or cultural characteristics. We use the appearance distribution learned by an image generation model as a reference for what is generally expected within an artifact category. For each target region, we exclude images from that region and fine-tune a generative model using only images from the remaining regions. We then mask selected parts of artifact images from the target region and ask the region-excluded model to complete them. If the completed result differs greatly from the original image, the masked part may contain features that are difficult to predict from the appearance learned from other regions. We measure this difference using LPIPS and treat it as reconstruction difficulty for the generative model. We conduct experiments on images of kokeshi dolls, drums, and masks from the collection of the National Museum of Ethnology. For each category, we select several target regions, build region-excluded LoRA models, and perform inpainting on predefined local parts. The results show that typical shapes and simple decorations are often reconstructed consistently, whereas some region-specific colors, patterns, cord arrangements, and painted details are replaced with more common appearances. These results suggest that region-excluded inpainting can serve as an exploratory tool for finding region-specific local visual features in museum artifact images.

authors.name: Maho Kinoshita, Wakana Kuwata, Ryota Mibayashi, Hiroaki Ohshima

papers.title: WorldWeave: Rethinking Embodied Navigation through Cross-Task World Modeling
papers.summary: Mobile embodied agents continuously alter their observations through their own motion, while external dynamics further shape future interactions. Different mobile embodied tasks therefore capture complementary patterns of state evolution, yet jointly learning world dynamics across such interactions remains less explored. We investigate this problem through Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT), which respectively involve navigation toward a stationary goal and interaction with a moving target. We propose WorldWeave, a cross-task world model that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation.
