When marginalizing over glitches or massive black hole binary transients, estimation errors remain flat up to transient signal-to-noise ratios of several hundred, whereas ignoring them severely biases likelihood fits. Under time-varying spline noise levels, realistic glitch rates, and gaps up to one day long, posterior coverage remains nominal or conservative across $\sim 10^4$ simulations. We test coverage in the local neighborhood of a given observation by introducing a novel importance-weighted localized simulation-based calibration test. We find flow matching slightly better calibrated than diffusion in simpler regimes and observe modest gains from physics-aware template inputs. Finally, we outline how these networks can initialize the noise and stochastic blocks of a LISA global fit.

authors.name: Iuliu Cuceu, Nelson Christensen, Astrid Lamberts, Quentin Baghi, Coen Rondeel, Natalia Korsakova

papers.title: Simulating Episodic Like Memory in Octopus: Breaking the Rules
papers.summary: Episodic memory, which involves the recollection of past events, has been observed in several species including the invertebrate cuttlefish. In a subsequent experiment, episodic memory was not observed in the closely related octopus. Rather the octopus used simpler, cognitive rule-based strategies to gain access to food. Using a prior model of cuttlefish episodic-like memory, we replicated the octopus experiment. Under less challenging conditions, episodic memory and the simpler cognitive strategies all had positive gains. However, under more challenging conditions, which introduced the threat of predation, only the episodic memory model had positive gains. These results suggest that if challenged ecologically, it would be advantageous for octopus to use episodic-like memory. We discuss possible reasons for the behavioral discrepancies in these closely related cephalopods.

authors.name: Jeffrey L. Krichmar

papers.title: FastCREST: GPU-Accelerated CREST Conformer Searches with Consistent Energies and Gradients
papers.summary: CREST conformer searches with GFN2-xTB take days for large, flexible molecules: one search of a 274-atom gallium(III)--peptide complex with CREST 3.0.2 took 321.5~h on 32 CPU threads. FastCREST keeps CREST's algorithm and changes how a search uses the hardware. Its metadynamics (MTD) and molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories run with tuned OpenMP settings and one GPU, which solves the self-consistent-charge (SCC) eigenproblem and evaluates the three-body dispersion term. About 15,000 geometry optimizations per iteration run as Slurm array jobs on other CPU nodes, and checkpoints let a search continue on preemptible GPUs. On A100 nodes, the OpenMP settings and loop changes made an MTD step 2.4 times faster and the GPU another 2.3 times; array jobs made a batch of optimizations 39 times faster. For six more molecules of 24 to 339 atoms, a FastCREST step was 2.2 to 7.1 times faster than a conventional CREST step. A complete FastCREST search, which also lifts CREST~3's cap of 200 optimization cycles, took 54.3~h, evaluating energies and gradients 8.1 times as fast as the CREST 3.0.2 search (on different hardware) with fewer CPU-hours per evaluation. Two opt-in settings (a warm-started Jacobi eigensolver and GPU-resident SCC iterations), LLVM's OpenMP library and one CPU socket per trajectory made an MTD step 8.3 times faster than conventional CREST. Energies agree with CREST 3.0.2 within $1.01\times10^{-10}$ Eh and gradients within $8.2\times10^{-11}$Eh bohr$^{-1}$, and controlled MD runs passed a prespecified equivalence test. Most replicate FastCREST and conventional CREST searches ended in similar compact conformers, with no detectable difference in energy.

authors.name: Supantha Dey, Nilusha L Kariyawasam, Ratul Chowdhury

papers.title: From local competition to bump attractors:how excitation width sets capacity, interference and updating in recurrent models of visual working memory
papers.summary: On-centre off-surround (OCOS) networks and bump attractors, the two main recurrent models of visual working memory, differ chiefly in how far recurrent excitation spreads. We place them in one family parameterised by excitation width at fixed total excitation, and ask how stable each stored item is and what it costs the circuit to hold and change it. The answer is that excitation width sets the price of continuity. In the OCOS limit, which we solve exactly by completing the energy-function formalism of \citet{Sengupta2024}, an item occupies a single unit, relaxes quickly and never drifts, and capacity follows in closed form, exact over all stable states. As excitation widens towards a bump-like regime, items become continuous but costly: per item, the circuit uses 15--29 units instead of one and 6.5--11 times the activity, relaxes 35--60 times more slowly after a perturbation, needs a 35--230 times stronger cue to accept a second item, and holds 7--10 items instead of at least 40. Under noise, with background false alarms approximately matched, about a third of wide items drift, whereas narrow items never move. Yet even as an item's translation mode softens towards zero, items remain locked to the lattice. Locking is poorly predicted by energy differences between item positions, but strongly predicted by how far the unit just beyond an item's edge sits below threshold (rank correlation 0.91 across 40 parameter settings). Where that margin vanishes, a new input captures the stored item instead of being added to memory.

authors.name: Purvikalyani Prasannah, Rakesh Sengupta

papers.title: History-bearing thalamocortical signals reconstruct and redirect later decisions in a circuit model
papers.summary: Experience can guide an ambiguous choice or bias a choice despite strong current evidence. We asked how a thalamocortical circuit carries historical content forward and regulates its influence across successive decisions. In published data from adult male mice, suppressing posterior parietal cortex (PPC) or pulvinar (PUL) improved current judgments most when sensory history conflicted with the stimulus, reflecting reduced historical weighting. In trained thalamocortical circuit models, replaying recorded PUL input to PPC reconstructed a historical trace after equalizing complete recipient states across histories. Replaying the opposite history redirected the later choice, even after the circuit correctly judged an intervening strong stimulus. This historical message occupied a low-dimensional direction in thalamic output that remained broadly reachable under firing-rate bounds; redistributing the arriving current at matched energy showed that fine spatial organization, beyond total input strength, selectively shapes later history use without disrupting current choices. Strong sensory evidence suppressed historical output while preserving internal state differences, whereas ambiguity recruited neuronal rectification thresholds and readout alignment to express history. Small shifts in the cortical operating point modulated later historical influence, and partial attenuation of recurrent drive reduced it across all circuits while preserving current commitments; correspondingly, recurrent dynamics were essential for predicting post-stimulus trajectories in held-out histories. Together, these findings distinguish three operations in history-guided choice: returning thalamocortical input determines which past is reconstructed, recurrent dynamics carry its influence forward across intervening demands, and current sensory evidence gates how strongly it enters the decision.

authors.name: Yanzhe Zhao, Yongzhang Ji

papers.title: Linking vascular pathways to organ anatomical structures in the Human Reference Atlas
papers.summary: As part of the Human Reference Atlas (HRA) initiative, which brings together more than 25 international consortia to map the entire healthy adult body, we developed a multiscale Vasculature Common Coordinate Framework (VCCF). The VCCF uses vascular pathways to describe the location of organs, anatomical structures, and cells throughout the body. Here, we present the VCCF Blood Vasculature Organ Crosswalk, which links blood vessels to anatomical structures they supply or drain, and the Pathways Crosswalk, which lists relationships between blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and nerves. Blood Vasculature Organ Crosswalk Diagrams support the authoring and review of the crosswalk tables. In machine readable files, we catalog 349 blood vessels from these diagrams, with 663 linkages to 295 anatomical structures across 20 organs/body regions and 28 functional tissue units. The VCCF crosswalk tables and diagrams have been validated algorithmically and by 11 organ experts. They have brought together experts from different domains to document existing knowledge of the human vasculature and identify gaps where future research is needed.

authors.name: Katherine Gustilo, Quinlan Cuddy, Avinash Boppana, Bruce W. Herr II, Katy B\"orner, Griffin M Weber

papers.title: Introduced cases, spread of infection in a community and travel control measures
papers.summary: Travel restrictions, border screening and quarantine were widely used during the COVID-19 pandemic to prevent or delay the spatial spread of SARS-CoV-2, yet their effectiveness varied greatly across jurisdictions. To investigate how the timing and combination of border control measures interact with pathogen introductions and local transmission, we formulate a coupled Exporter--Importer epidemic model in both deterministic (ordinary differential equations) and stochastic (continuous-time Markov chain and multitype branching process approximation) frameworks. The model distinguishes latently infected, detected infectious and undetected infectious individuals, and explicitly separates recently arrived travellers in an introduction layer from the destination community. We derive analytical expressions for the control and basic reproduction numbers, final epidemic sizes and probabilities of outbreak extinction, and complement them with stochastic simulations. We show that pre-departure screening in the Exporter alone cannot prevent outbreaks in an Importer community with reproduction number larger than unity because latently infected travellers cross borders undetected. Post-arrival quarantine and screening in the introduction layer, as well as travel interruptions, can substantially reduce the attack rate in the Importer, but only when implemented with high stringency and triggered early. Triggering border interventions based on local detections in the Importer almost always acts too late because silent introductions precede local case detection, whereas triggers informed by surveillance in the Exporter provide a wider window of action. Effective protection of the Importer ultimately requires combining proactive, Exporter-informed border measures with local public health interventions that keep the community reproduction number near or below one.

authors.name: Julien Arino, Clotilde Djuikem, Amy Hurford

papers.title: Motoric signatures to detect original authorship versus cognitive effort in instructed motor responses of an emerging speaker with ASD
papers.summary: There is at present no objective, agnostic method to track levels of message authorship and agency in non-speakers who rely on assisted typing to communicate. Part of the problem is that nuances in spontaneous gestural movements of the typer transpire largely beneath awareness of both the typer and the communication-regulation-partner. Such spontaneous movements co-occur with the intentional ones producing the typed messages but are currently not considered part of the communication system. We introduce an assay that probes various levels of cognitive loads in an ecologically valid environment. Then, in collaboration with an emerging speaker-typer and his communication-regulation-partner, we empirically estimate motoric stochastic signatures during both independent and assisted typing. Under varying levels of cognitive loads, the assay and biometrics distinguish motoric patterns in spontaneous typing of phrases in response to open-ended questions from those in instructed typing of the same phrase. The non-dominant bodily motions, co-occurring with the dominant (typing) side reveal not only levels of cognitive mental effort and agency of the typer but also levels of creative thoughts through motoric preambles present only in open-ended mode. This level of semantic authorship is detectable in both the geodesic paths along the manifold representing the Gamma stochastic parameters of the motions fluctuations and those of the physical 3D spatial trajectories. The head and facial micro-motions capture these non-dominant-body nuances, offering a personalized motoric metric of cognitive effort, agency, authorship and a comprehensive suite of assays to open new research avenues for assisted typing with haptic support.

authors.name: Elizabeth B. Torres

papers.title: Topological Pharmacokinetics: A Model-Free Framework for Quantifying the Shape of Concentration-Time Curves
papers.summary: Pharmacokinetic analysis compresses concentration-time curves into scalar summaries (non-compartmental analysis, NCA) or pre-specified compartmental models, approaches that are either model-free but shape-blind or shape-sensitive but structure-dependent. We introduce Topological Pharmacokinetics (TPK), a framework that reads curve shape directly from data without committing to any model. TPK delay-embeds each curve into a state-space trajectory and applies persistent homology to extract a nine-component topological invariant: multi-scale shape descriptors (peak hierarchy, secondary-peak isolation, loop structure) with established perturbation-stability properties. We evaluate the framework on four layers of increasing realism. Monophasic linear systems generate no spurious cyclic signals, whereas double-site absorption and enterohepatic recirculation produce distinct loop signatures; 12 nonlinear scenarios resolve as curvature-without-cycles; a weak endogenous rhythm survives superposition with a large exogenous drug signal (inter-peak interval recovered at exactly 24 h); and loop detection stays stable to 10 percent of Cmax additive noise and to sampling thinned to 7 points. As clinical proof of concept, we apply the same pipeline to 15 mycophenolic acid profiles digitized from a published kidney-transplant study. The secondary-persistence ratio associates with ex vivo gut-microbiome reactivation at Spearman rho = 0.815 (p = 0.0002, q = 0.002), whereas the tested exposure metrics show weak, nonsignificant associations (rho <= 0.38). Analyses are fully automated and reproducible; code and data are public. TPK is proposed as a complementary, model-free, shape-sensitive layer alongside NCA and model-based methods.

authors.name: Hong-Can Ren, Ya-Xin Gu

papers.title: Active sensing as control over sensory acquisition
papers.summary: The term "active sensing" is used across neuroscience and engineering to describe a wide range of sensing behaviors, but there is no consensus on what makes sensing "active." We propose that the behaviors grouped under this label are better understood as forms of control over sensory acquisition and develop a framework that distinguishes three interacting forms of control. Mechanistic control physically structures sensory input, strategic control modulates sensing in closed loop through adaptive and attentional processes, and agentic control concerns the sensing policies available to an agent and its authority to choose among them. These forms of control can occur separately or in combination, and have distinct consequences for sensory input, perception, behavior, and performance. The framework clarifies active-passive comparisons and provides a common basis for analyzing biological, engineered, and hybrid sensing systems by asking what is controlled, how, and by whom.

authors.name: Neeli Tummala, Mitra J. Hartmann

papers.title: GABIF: An Adaptive Guided Graph Denoising Framework for Antibody Conditional Inverse Folding
papers.summary: Antibodies play a central role in the human immune system, and their design is critical for vaccine development, therapeutic intervention, and improving human longevity. However, the vast combinatorial search space of antibodies poses a fundamental challenge for de novo discovery. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly denoising diffusion models, have demonstrated strong potential in protein inverse folding. Nevertheless, existing approaches are largely constrained to learning from natural antibody repertoires, thereby generating sequences that closely resemble natural antibodies. Such similarity, however, does not necessarily translate into improved functional performance in downstream applications. In this work, we develop a novel generative protein design model that enables the generation and optimization of antibody sequences tailored to specific downstream tasks and target metrics. Besides training on given an antibody dataset, we guide the generative model by an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor for conditional discrete diffusion. The model is pre-trained on a given antibody dataset. Meanwhile, an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor is incorporated as a conditional signal in a discrete diffusion framework, where a regressor serves as the conditional probability to guide the learning of the amino acid probability distribution of sequences under the objective of affinity optimization. In silico experiments demonstrate that our antibody design model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches, while the proposed regressor effectively improves binding affinity, as validated by an independent external predictor. Furthermore, our results highlight that the combination of finetuning and supervised guidance provides a powerful paradigm for adapting pretrained models to downstream tasks.

authors.name: Mingwei Liu, Xiao Liu, Kai Yi, Feng Tan, Yu Guang Wang

papers.title: Interactions with hidden traits induce diversification and conceal its origin
papers.summary: Adaptive diversification is often inferred from a small number of measurable traits, even though evolutionary dynamics arise from many interacting phenotypic dimensions. Unmeasured traits may therefore do more than bias inference: through their interactions, they may determine whether diversification occurs at all. Here we develop a theory of the onset and attribution of adaptive diversification by partitioning phenotype space into focal and hidden sectors. Eliminating the hidden sector yields an exact effective operator. Coupling to hidden traits that are stabilizing in isolation can destabilize an otherwise stable phenotype and generate a diversifying composite mode: the interaction creates diversification rather than merely strengthening it. Conversely, when the hidden sector is itself diversifying, the focal traits diversify as a correlated response to a hidden-driven process: no effective description in the focal traits, not even the exact one obtained by eliminating the hidden sector, predicts the variation they display, and stabilizing the focal traits reduces it without removing it. These effects become strongest near the hidden sector's own threshold, so a weakly stabilized hidden trait can have a large effect even with modest coupling to the focal traits, and they can generate correlations between focal traits that have no direct interaction. Onset and observability are distinct: systems with the same leading eigenvalue can project very differently onto the measured traits, so the theory tracks both the full operator and the focal-hidden partition. Individual-based simulations recover the predicted threshold and variance law, coupling-induced trait splitting, and the reversal of induced correlations. Interactions with unmeasured traits can both create adaptive diversification and determine whether the diversification seen in measured phenotypes can be attributed to them.

authors.name: Vikas Kumar Jha, Praveen V, Suman Chakraborty, Vaibhav Madhok

papers.title: Pesticide mixtures may compromise ecosystem services provided by an egg parasitoid of soybean pest stink bugs: a comprehensive ecotoxicological risk assessment
papers.summary: Tank mixtures of crop protection products are widely used in agricultural systems, yet their integrated effects on biological control agents remain poorly understood. We evaluated the lethal, sublethal, and transgenerational effects of four synthetic insecticides, applied alone or in binary mixtures with three fungicides and two herbicides, on adults and pupae of Telenomus podisi (Hymenoptera: Scelionidae), an important egg parasitoid of pest stink bugs. In adult bioassays, LC50 values ranged from 28.26 mg a.i. L-1 for isocycloseram + lambda-cyhalothrin to 265.88 mg a.i. L-1 for acephate. Overall, mixtures increased adverse effects relative to the individual products, reducing survival, parasitism, and longevity. The lowest parasitism rates occurred with isocycloseram + lambda-cyhalothrin combined with chlorothalonil or glyphosate SL formulation. Transgenerational effects were also detected, including reduced F1 emergence and an increased proportion of males in some treatments. Following pupal exposure, several mixtures reduced F0 emergence, whereas ethiprole + fenpropimorph and acephate + bixafen + prothioconazole + trifloxystrobin also reduced parasitism and longevity of the emerged adults. Integration of lethal and sublethal responses using the reduction coefficient (Ex) revealed increased toxicity for several mixtures and shifts in IOBC risk classification; notably, all insecticide + glyphosate mixtures reached Ex = 100% after pupal exposure. These findings show that assessing pesticides individually may underestimate ecotoxicological risk to T. podisi and highlight the need to consider pesticide mixtures in integrated pest management programs.

authors.name: Matheus Rakes, Ma\'ira Chagas Morais, Gabriel Rodrigues Palma, Daniel Bernardi, Anderson Dionei Gr\"utzmacher, Leandro do Prado Ribeiro

papers.title: Beyond the Blueprint: The Continuing Evolution of Turing's Theory of Morphogenesis
papers.summary: Turing's article ``The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis'' has profoundly influenced conceptual views on the emergence of biological form across scales and species. It has also served as a foundational framework to guide experimental investigations into the mechanisms that underlie pattern formation. In this article, we trace the historical development of Turing's ideas and examine their integration into contemporary research programs. We critically assess the broad and often overlapping concepts that have derived from Turing's work, both highlighting value in productive applications of the theory and suggesting that skepticism should remain in overly simplistic validations. By clarifying these concepts and their intrinsic limitations, we rethink contemporary approaches aimed at understanding the essential principles that govern biological pattern formation. We pose some important challenges that will require interdisciplinary expertise to overcome, and which will necessitate fundamentally new paradigms to understand the physical origin of Darwin's ``endless forms most beautiful''.

authors.name: Andrew L. Krause, Kevin J. Painter, Denis J. Headon

papers.title: Comparison of 3D-DXA Measurements with QCT Software Solutions for Proximal Femur Bone Density Assessment
papers.summary: 3D-Shaper reconstructs proximal femur shape and density in 3D from a standard hip dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scan. In men and women aged 35-91 years, we compared 3D-Shaper integral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), trabecular vBMD, and cortical surface BMD (sBMD) with quantitative computed tomography (QCT) processed with three methods: an in-house pipeline, Stradview and QCTPro CTXA, which were used to derive bone measurements equivalent to those of 3D-Shaper. Agreement, including among QCT methods, was assessed with linear regression and Bland-Altman analysis (bias and limits of agreement, LoA). 3D-Shaper agreed strongly with the in-house pipeline and Stradview for integral vBMD (R=0.95-0.96; bias 1.5 to 4.2 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$39.7 to 41.4 mg/cm$^3$), trabecular vBMD (R=0.92-0.94; bias -11.8 to -7.8 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$33.3 to 39.4 mg/cm$^3$) and cortical sBMD (R=0.94; bias 5.6 to 38.2 mg/cm$^2$; LoA $\pm$23.6 to 26.4 mg/cm$^2$). The in-house pipeline and Stradview agreed for integral vBMD (R=1.00; bias -2.7 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$3.7 mg/cm$^3$), trabecular vBMD (R=0.96-1.00; bias -0.2 to 3.9 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$6.9 to 27.5 mg/cm$^3$) and cortical sBMD (R=0.98; bias 32.7 mg/cm$^2$; LoA $\pm$14.6 mg/cm$^2$). Compared with 3D-Shaper, QCTPro CTXA integral vBMD was systematically lower (R=0.90; bias -28.4 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$61.5 mg/cm$^3$) and trabecular vBMD showed a proportional bias (R=0.89; bias -44.1 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$61.3 mg/cm$^3$). The same pattern was observed against the other QCT methods, for integral vBMD (R=0.93; bias -32.6 to -29.9 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$49.6 to 50.0 mg/cm$^3$) and trabecular vBMD (R=0.94-0.96; bias -36.3 to -32.5 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$51.2 to 54.9 mg/cm$^3$). These findings support the agreement of 3D-Shaper with independent QCT approaches and show that 3D-Shaper-QCT differences must be interpreted in light of the QCT method used.

authors.name: Asier Mu\~noz, Luis del Rio, Jorge Malouf, Ludovic Humbert

papers.title: Big Tree Viewer: A high-performance browser-based phylogenetic tree viewer with agentic AI integration
papers.summary: Phylogenetic trees represent evolutionary history visually, and the ability to display and explore them is a key function in research across biological disciplines. Very large gene and species trees are becoming common with the increasing availability of low cost DNA sequencing, creating performance and informativeness challenges for display software originally designed for phylogenies with a few hundred to a few thousand tips. We discuss these limitations and introduce a browser-based Big Tree Viewer (BTV) highly optimized for fast display and biologically informative exploration of phylogenetic trees containing even a million tips. BTV can automatically map binomial species names to the NCBI or Catalogue of Life taxonomies and display colored ribbons to indicate taxonomic groups for enhanced exploration. Even without taxonomic mapping, BTV automatically labels groups of neighboring tips that share the first word of their names, such as a genus or gene family name, providing readable large-scale landmarks when individual tip labels are too dense to read. BTV supports metadata display, visual customization, tanglegram-like tree comparisons, statistics, figure export, and multiple tree layouts, including a new spiral form to display enormously large trees. BTV is also designed to integrate with common agentic AI tools, allowing agents to display, style, annotate, and inspect trees at the user's request. The BTV web app is freely available at https://BigTreeViewer.net and runs entirely in the user's browser, with no data uploads to any central server. Desktop versions of the BTV app for macOS, Windows, and Linux are also provided for download.

authors.name: John B. Allard, Sudhir Kumar

papers.title: SBTenv: A Literature-Validated Split-Belt Treadmill Simulation Environment
papers.summary: The split-belt treadmill is an important tool for studying human locomotor adaptation. Physics-based simulations complement such experiments by allowing hypotheses about the mechanisms of adaptation to be tested directly, and high-throughput simulation is increasingly needed as these models grow in complexity. However, no open-source split-belt treadmill environment exists in MuJoCo, a physics engine widely used for high-throughput simulation. Here, we present SBTenv, a split-belt treadmill environment built in MuJoCo and validated against published experimental data from a rimless wheel walking passively on a split-belt treadmill. By modeling compliant contacts at the spoke tips, SBTenv reproduces the experimental average steady velocity ($R^2=0.643$, RMSE $=0.0162$ m/s) without the empirical geometric correction required in prior simulations. We expect SBTenv, openly shared, to enable high-throughput simulation of musculoskeletal and robotic locomotion on a split-belt treadmill.

authors.name: Philip Byrne, John Drazan, Nidhi Seethapathi

papers.title: VEGA: A Scalable Software-Hardware Co-design for Genome Alignment using RVV Extension
papers.summary: Dynamic programming (DP)-based genome sequence analysis is fundamental to computational genomics, but it remains computationally intensive as genomic data volumes continue to outpace Moore's Law. Existing hardware accelerators often sacrifice programmability and scalability across diverse alignment algorithms. In this work, we present VEGA, a scalable software-hardware co-design that accelerates genome alignment using RISC-V Vector extensions. VEGA introduces specialized vector instructions and three key innovations: a Forefront Stationary dataflow that minimizes off-chip memory access, intersequence parallelism that maximizes SIMD lane utilization, and custom ISA extensions that accelerate core alignment operations. Evaluations show that VEGA achieves up to 15.1x and 9.7x speedups for Edit Distance and Smith-Waterman algorithms over the Ara2-RVV vector baseline, sustaining 10.2x and 6.7x gains for 10kbp sequences. Post-synthesis results indicate only 1.0% area overhead compared to a standard RISC-V core, with performance-per-area efficiency rivaling specialized ASICs. VEGA thus achieves a balanced advancement in efficiency, programmability, and scalability for genome sequence alignment.

authors.name: Weihong Xu, Shijie Xu, Qunyou Liu, Giovanni Ansaloni, Cheng Zhuo, David Atienza

papers.title: Motivo: A Motif-Based Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Fast and Energy-Efficient Graph-Based Genome Analysis
papers.summary: Read mapping, a key step of genome sequence analysis, matches each fragment of a sequenced genome (a read) to its location in a reference genome. A genome graph is a graph-based reference genome that represents the genetic diversity of a population as alternative paths, and thus improves read mapping accuracy. However, the size and complexity of a genome graph make sequence-to-graph (S2G) mapping a major bottleneck. Prior software and hardware approaches for S2G mapping perform redundant costly operations (e.g., graph traversals and dynamic programming) that do not lead to valid mappings. Our key observation is that a genome graph consists of small subgraphs that share a limited set of recurring topologies, which we call motifs. We propose Motivo, a topology-aware algorithm-architecture co-design for S2G mapping. Motivo's algorithm uses motifs in two ways. First, it stores the precomputed motifs of each node in a compact index, which replaces a graph traversal with a single memory lookup. Second, it uses the topology of a motif and the properties of its nodes to identify the few most suitable mapping paths with arithmetic operations. The algorithm enables high-performance execution on CPUs and GPUs and high-performance, low-energy execution on Motivo-ASIC, an accelerator we co-design with it. Motivo-CPU provides 2.1-18.4x, 2.8-343x, and 1.4-10.1x speedups over GraphAligner, vg, and minigraph, and Motivo-GPU provides 1.5-1.6x speedups over vg-giraffe. Motivo-ASIC provides 7.4-11.7x (138-274x) speedups over state-of-the-art CPU-based tools for short (long) reads. Compared to SeGraM (short reads) and HARP (long reads), Motivo-ASIC achieves 5.3x and 4.0-4.3x higher throughput per Watt and 1.7x and 2.7-3.0x higher throughput per mm$^2$, respectively. Motivo maintains equal or higher mapping accuracy than other tools (96.8%-99.7%) for short and long reads on two types of genome graphs.

authors.name: Eirini Maria Tzermpou, Konstantina Koliogeorgi, Konstantinos Kanellopoulos, Ataberk Olgun, Nisa Bostanc{\i}, Dimitrios Soudris, Nika Mansouri Ghiasi, Onur Mutlu

papers.title: Eight limit cycles in a three-dimensional competitive Lotka-Volterra system
papers.summary: Gyllenberg and Yan conjectured that a three-dimensional competitive Lotka-Volterra system can have at least five limit cycles. We prove the conjecture by constructing a strictly competitive system in which eight distinct limit cycles coexist near a single positive equilibrium. For each $m=5,6,7,8$, we construct a weak focus of order $m$ and identify parameter directions on the Hopf hypersurface that allow us to vary the first $m-1$ focus quantities independently. We choose these quantities so that the drift of a scalar amplitude function alternates in sign on $m$ nested level curves, forcing a limit cycle between each consecutive pair. A perturbation transverse to the Hopf hypersurface creates one additional cycle inside the others. The one-turn displacement map shows that both local counts are sharp. For each $m$, we give a rigorous computer-assisted proof that an explicit rational interaction matrix yields at least $m$ distinct hyperbolic limit cycles. We thank GPT-6 Astra for helping us compare earlier constructions, identify the main obstacle to extending them, and develop the present approach.

authors.name: Haoyu Albert Wang, Yuxiu Shao, Wei P. Dai

papers.title: A high-dimensional perspective of assortative mating: definition, dynamics, and limiting results
papers.summary: Assortative mating, or the systematic (dis)similarity of traits between mate pairs, has wide-ranging consequences. Chiefly, it modulates genetic variance in offspring due to the coupling of inherited trait-associated loci in parents. Over many generations, this buildup becomes appreciable at the trait level and may confound statistical genetics techniques, such as association analyses and heritability estimation. Theoretical characterisations of this effect are well-developed in the univariate case, where mates assort on a single trait pair. However, empirical studies increasingly show that assortment is not only multivariate, but high-dimensional, in that the correlation structure exhibited between mates cannot be represented by a single or few linear combinations of the constituent traits. In spite of this, the mathematical theory of assortment has not scaled with awareness of this fact. In this paper such a generalisation is developed. We begin by deriving sufficient conditions under which an estimator is invariant to assortment, followed by studying existence conditions and limiting behaviour of equilibria under assortment. Finally, univariate results involving trait heritability and consanguineal genetic correlation are generalised to the multivariate regime.

authors.name: K\'ari Hlynsson

papers.title: Gene ologs: a categorical framework for Gene Ontology
papers.summary: The Gene Ontology (GO) is the most widely used resource for the functional annotation of genes and gene products. It unifies biological knowledge across species through a dynamic, controlled vocabulary, and it is now primarily represented in the Web Ontology Language (OWL), a logic-based language that supports automated reasoning. Ologs (ontology logs), introduced by Spivak and Kent, offer a different language for knowledge representation, grounded in category theory: concepts are types, functional relationships are aspects, and declared equalities between paths are facts. Ologs come with features that are not part of the standard use of GO: path equations, universal constructions (products, coproducts, pullbacks and pushouts), a database reading in which instance data are set-valued functors, and functors with which ontologies can be compared and merged. In this work we take an initial step towards Gene ologs, i.e. ologs for GO. We fix conventions for reading GO terms as olog types, examine which GO relations can be represented as aspects and which must instead be represented as spans, illustrate each olog construction with GO examples, show that standard GO annotations and GO Causal Activity Models (GO-CAM) can be represented as olog instance data subject to checkable constraints, and describe how functors and pushouts can be used to compare and merge Gene ologs. We also discuss what ologs do not provide relative to OWL. We regard Gene ologs as complementary to, rather than a replacement for, the OWL representation of GO.

authors.name: Yanying Wu

papers.title: Fusion-pMT: Biological Sequence Modeling for Tri-Molecular Binding in Immunogenicity Prediction
papers.summary: Accurately modeling the tripartite interaction among peptides, major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules, and T cell receptors (TCRs) is essential for understanding T-cell-mediated immunity and informing immunogenicity prediction. A key challenge is to connect peptide-MHC binding knowledge with TCR specificity while retaining the residue-level context needed to model their interactions. In this paper, we propose Fusion-pMT, a biological sequence modeling framework that (1) learns representations of the three molecular inputs through a shared amino acid projection and molecule-specific encoders, and (2) combines peptide-MHC pretraining with two-stage cross-attention, retaining MHC-conditioned peptide tokens for subsequent interaction with TCR sequences. By aligning sequence fusion with the stepwise nature of immune recognition, Fusion-pMT effectively supports both pairwise and tripartite interaction modeling. To validate its effectiveness, we conduct comprehensive experiments covering both pairwise and tripartite interactions and demonstrate the advantages of Fusion-pMT over strong baselines while validating its core design choices.

authors.name: Jiahao Ma, Yujia Yin, Hongzong Li, Yunke Shi, Yifan Wu, Jian-Dong Huang, Ye-Fan Hu, Yifan Chen

papers.title: Emergent self-inhibition governs the landscape of stable states in complex ecosystems
papers.summary: Species-rich ecosystems often exhibit multiple stable states with distinct species compositions. Yet, the factors determining the likelihood of each state's occurrence remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize and explain the landscape of stable states in the random Generalized Lotka--Volterra (GLV) model, in which multistability is widespread. We focus on the regime of the model where interspecies interactions are predominantly competitive and nearly symmetric. We find that the same pool of species with random initial abundances can result in different stable states, whose likelihoods typically differ by orders of magnitude. A state's likelihood increases sharply with its total biomass, or inverse self-inhibition. We develop a simplified model to predict and explain this behavior, by coarse-graining ecological interactions so that each stable state behaves as a unit. In this setting, we can accurately predict the entire landscape of stable states using only two macroscopic properties: the biomass of each state and species diversity. Our analyses also provide insight into the biomass--likelihood relationship: High-biomass states have low self-inhibition and thus grow faster, outcompete others, and become much more likely. These results reveal emergent self-inhibition as a fundamental organizing principle for the attractor landscape of complex ecosystems---and provide a path to predict ecosystem outcomes without knowing microscopic interactions.

authors.name: Nitesh Kumar Patro, Washington Taylor, Akshit Goyal

papers.title: Modeling the Disjunction Effect within Classical Probability: A New Decision Process Model and Comparison with Quantum-like Models
papers.summary: In a Prisoner's Dilemma experiment, participants defected less often when the opponent's move was unknown than when they were told that the opponent had defected or that the opponent had cooperated. This disjunction effect has often been interpreted as a violation of the classical law of total probability and has motivated quantum-like models of decision making. We re-examine this interpretation and identify a strong assumption implicit in the conventional classical model. The conventional model uses the two informed conditions to represent the full range of participants' expectations and thus treats every participant as certain of the opponent's move even when that move is unknown. We relax this premise by introducing a continuous parameter for each participant's degree of expectation that the opponent will defect. Participants are grouped by expectation level, with the intermediate groups representing ambiguous expectations. A standard quantum-like model offers a different account of this same uncertainty about the opponent's move. In that model, ambiguity arises through superposition, and ambiguous pure states are generic (dense and of full unitarily invariant measure on the unit sphere), so certainty states are mathematically exceptional. Despite this difference in how ambiguity is represented, the proposed classical model can reproduce the observed strong disjunction effect while satisfying the classical law of total probability. More generally, we prove that it can exactly reproduce any triple of defection rates strictly between zero and one, including every such triple generated by the quantum-like model. The proposed model is therefore no less expressive than the quantum-like model for these three observable rates while remaining entirely within classical probability, and the substantive difference between the two lies in how they represent ambiguity and interpret events.

authors.name: Ryo Nasu, Yoshihiro Maruyama

papers.title: VCBench: Benchmarking virtual cell models for in-the-wild perturbation response
papers.summary: Virtual cell (VC) models aim to predict cellular responses to diverse perturbations in silico, offering great promise for drug discovery and precision medicine. However, although models routinely report strong performance on existing benchmarks, whether these predictions translate to practical biological utility remains unclear. Current evaluations often rely on overly simplified or inconsistent setups that fail to capture the complexity and variability of real biological systems. Here, we present a standardized, modular benchmarking framework that evaluates nine VC models under challenging, in-the-wild scenarios spanning unseen cell lines and donors, novel genetic and chemical perturbations, and cross-study transfer. Across these evaluations, complex models do not consistently surpass simple linear baselines on broad transcriptional trends, while fine-grained, perturbation-specific effects remain difficult to recover. Moreover, different evaluation metrics emphasize distinct biological properties, resulting in markedly different model rankings. Consequently, model selection and data integration strategies should be tailored to specific downstream tasks rather than applied uniformly. Together, this framework establishes a more biologically grounded benchmark to guide model development, evaluation, and deployment in real-world settings.

authors.name: Xinjie Mao, Songming Zhang, Qianhong Wen, Xiangyu Wen, Kedu Jin, Sheng Xu, Hao Wu, Lang Yu, Yuqiang Li, Lei Bai, Qi Liu, Ning Ding, Siqi Sun, Zhangyang Gao, Shuizhou Chen

papers.title: From Organization to Viability: A Multi-Level Analysis of Gait Dynamics Under Occlusal Constraint
papers.summary: Clinical interpretation often assumes that observable performance sufficiently reflects the organization of an adaptive system. The preceding Level 3 study showed that neither an aggregated scalar score nor a static exploratory UMAP embedding uniquely resolved the occlusal observational probes. This study introduces Level 4, centered on observed longitudinal viability. Using an exploratory single-case design in a participant with Parkinson's disease, gait was recorded with instrumented insoles under three probes: neutral natural occlusion (ONL), a nominal 2.5-degree increase in vertical dimension of occlusion (OC2.5), and a nominal 3-degree increase (OC3). Two sessions were conducted eleven weeks apart. A common PCA representation was used to compare M1-M2 centroid displacement. In the selected PC1-PC2 plane, OC3 showed the smallest Euclidean displacement, ONL an intermediate displacement, and OC2.5 the largest. This ordering was preserved in most bootstrap iterations but was not preserved after Mahalanobis covariance normalization, showing that within-condition dispersion contributes to the result. Level 4 therefore provides a retrospective, representation-dependent proxy for longitudinal reorganization when static representations remain non-identifying. The findings are exploratory and non-causal. They do not establish distinct physiological states, a causal occlusal effect, a validated viability threshold, a therapeutic optimum, or a covariance-independent ranking.

authors.name: Jacques Raynal, Pierre Slangen, Elsa Raynal, Jacques Margerit

papers.title: Stationary covariance spectra of discrete-time non-normal random recurrent dynamics
papers.summary: Principal component analysis is widely used to characterize structure in the dynamics of recurrent neural networks. For stationary noise-driven dynamics, the distribution of variance among the principal components is determined by the spectrum of the stationary covariance matrix. While the spectral properties of this matrix are well-understood for linear networks with normal synaptic weight matrices, our understanding of the stationary covariance spectrum for random non-normal dynamics remains incomplete. In this note, we use a free-probability approach to show almost-sure convergence of the stationary covariance spectrum of discrete-time dynamics with random non-normal Gaussian weights, and derive a closed functional equation characterizing its distribution. This characterization allows us to analyze the behavior of tail eigenvalues in the critical regime: they decay with the inverse-square of their rank. In contrast, applying the same approach to the analogous continuous-time dynamics leads to an infinite hierarchy of Schwinger-Dyson equations, rather than a closed scalar equation.

authors.name: Jacob A. Zavatone-Veth

papers.title: On the interpretation of the kinetics of ligand-receptor binding
papers.summary: When the rates of ligand binding are measured by methods such as surface plasmon resonance, it is common practice to use the observed rate constants for the onset and offset of binding to estimate an equilibrium constant for ligand binding. If this agrees with the equilibrium constant found as the EC50 for binding at equilibrium, this is taken as validation of the measured rates. This is correct only when binding produces no conformation change in the receptor, and ligand binding follows a single exponential time course. Here, we investigate a simple 3 state model in which binding is followed by a conformation change in the receptor. Three special cases of this model in which the time course of onset and offset of ligand binding are close to being single exponentials are analysed. These cases are (1) when binding is much faster than the conformation change, (2) when the conformation change is much faster than binding, and (3) when the rates of ligand dissociation and receptor activation are both fast. It is concluded that the measured rates will often yield an estimate of the equilibrium constant for ligand binding that is close to the effective, or macroscopic, equilibrium constant, the EC50 found by measuring binding at equilibrium, which depends on both of the underlying microscopic equilibrium constants describing ligand binding and the conformation change. The exception to this conclusion is the case when binding is much faster than the subsequent conformation change, though the estimate of the equilibrium constant for ligand binding still depends on both of the underlying microscopic equilibrium constants.

authors.name: David Colquhoun, James P Higham

papers.title: PlainMap: a lightweight, restartable mapping pipeline for ancient and modern DNA
papers.summary: Mapping sequencing reads to a reference genome requires preprocessing and alignment choices that can vary with library type, fragment length, sequencing platform, and reference genome. These considerations are particularly important for ancient and historical DNA, where short and damaged fragments complicate read mapping. We present PlainMap, a lightweight and restartable mapping pipeline for modern and degraded DNA sequencing data. PlainMap accepts a simple manifest of FASTQ files, identifies single-end and paired-end data from read headers, supports heterogeneous sequencing inputs, and provides alternative mapping strategies for modern and degraded DNA. Optional pilot subsampling allows users to rapidly compare mapped fragment recovery across different settings using identical subsets of raw data, without attempting to determine the most accurate mapping strategy. Chunking and checkpoint-based execution support processing large datasets and resuming interrupted analyses, allowing users to balance memory requirements, runtime, and restartability. PlainMap produces duplicate-filtered BAM files together with fragment-aware mapping and coverage statistics. Evaluation using heterogeneous Japanese sea lion and short-fragment cave hyena datasets demonstrated successful processing across mapping modes, consistent trimmed and merged read counts across chunk sizes, and recovery from interrupted analyses without repeating completed mapping steps. PlainMap is implemented as a single Bash script and is freely available at https://github.com/BiodiversityExtinction/PlainMap.

authors.name: Michael V. Westbury

papers.title: Trainable sparse dendritic networks reveal regime-dependent roles for shunting inhibition and morphology
papers.summary: Neural circuits must compute reliably despite noise and changes in context. We introduce DendriNet, a framework for training scalable rate-based networks with sparse excitatory and inhibitory contacts, controllable dendritic architecture and different synaptic integration rules. In image classification, shunting networks transmit and rely on distal dendritic signals more strongly than additive networks. Distributing limited contacts across compartments improves classification in small populations, whereas greater serial dendritic depth offers no clean-image benefit in resource-matched trees. Robustness depends on the perturbation. Deeper shunting trees better tolerate independent pixel noise, whereas additive trees better tolerate strong input scaling. On a contextual task with gain variation and noise, the primary shunting tree is more accurate than the separately tuned additive tree under the noise and gain conditions used during training, yet depends less on cue-specific inhibition. Learning dendritic leak conductances partly restores shunting accuracy on dim, noise-free inputs outside the training distribution. At AlexNet width, shunting integration and learned sparse connectivity support smaller deployed networks with accuracy comparable to the retrained dense layers they replace. These results relate dendritic organization and synaptic integration to noise tolerance and contextual computation, and suggest tests of dendritic function and design principles for brain-inspired networks.

authors.name: Houman Safaai, Maceo Richards, Ryan Whalen, Adithya Madduri, Naeem Khoshnevis, Bernardo L. Sabatini

papers.title: ShEPhERD-score: Fast, adaptable three-dimensional alignment of molecular features
papers.summary: Three-dimensional (3D) molecular similarity scoring and alignment are widely employed in ligand-based virtual screening and molecular design, and are increasingly used for training and evaluating machine learning models. Existing open-source methods utilize various molecular representations spanning shape, electrostatics, pharmacophores, and hybrid representations, but their implementations as independent software packages with distinct application programming interfaces (APIs), optimizers, and limited GPU support make them difficult to compare, combine, or extend. Here, we develop ShEPhERD-score into a unified, modular platform for differentiable 3D molecular similarity scoring and alignment by combining diverse molecular representations with high-performance Numba CPU and Triton GPU kernels to support both large-scale library screening and pairwise similarity workflows. In matched comparisons with open-source 3D similarity tools on the DUDE-Z virtual screening benchmark, ShEPhERD-score performed comparably or better in eight of nine cases. Across the scoring modes in ShEPhERD-score, throughput ranges from 17,800 to 1.03 million alignments/second for ten-million-conformer libraries using a single NVIDIA L40S GPU. Moreover, we found that the most effective scoring mode varied by protein target, indicating that target-specific calibration against validation data may be valuable before large-scale screening and underscoring the need for a unified platform that provides diverse molecular representations. Together, these capabilities establish ShEPhERD-score as a single, extensible toolkit for rapid virtual screening and machine learning workflows.

authors.name: Nate Somers, Kento A. Abeywardane, Connor W. Coley, Masha Elkin

papers.title: Fluctuating resource availability stabilizes coexistence beyond the oscillatory tragedy of the commons
papers.summary: Fluctuations in ambient conditions such as temperature and humidity can alter the effective availability of a shared resource at a given abundance. Standard evolutionary games with environmental feedback treat the payoff matrix as a deterministic function of resource abundance, leaving open how fluctuations in availability affect the oscillatory tragedy of the commons. Using noise-corrected replicator dynamics and individual-based birth-death simulations, we show that zero-mean fluctuations in resource availability can stabilize an interior equilibrium and suppress coupled strategy-resource oscillations. We derive an analytical criterion, in terms of the payoff structure and feedback dynamics, for when increasing noise favors local stability. These findings identify environmental variability as a mechanism that can promote strategy coexistence and help maintain shared resources in systems prone to recurrent depletion.

authors.name: Yi-Duo Chen, Jian-Yue Guan, Zhi-Xi Wu

papers.title: Old Matches, New Frames: Schedule-Gated Stereo Memory from Human Vision to Machine Matching
papers.summary: Human vision and video stereo networks both reuse disparity evidence across time, yet a refresh of the input can invalidate a match formed milliseconds earlier. What tells a system whether an old match still counts? We answer this from limited human data in three steps. First, nine temporal mechanisms share a frozen binocular-energy front end and an equal-capacity readout, so held-out behavior isolates the temporal selection rule: on 240 conditions from 10 observers, down-weighting aged evidence that has lost binocular support lowers subject RMSE from 12.6% to 10.3% and reproduces a period-dependent reversed-depth illusion, across all 59 readings of the unpublished protocol and 8 front-end perturbations. Second, four propositions establish what such data can identify: gating is identified at the level of the refresh schedule, and candidate binding is invisible to standard stimuli but exposed by a single-eye geometry flip that separates the readouts by up to 7.1%. Third, the identified rule becomes a two-field stereo memory that separates sample validity from hypothesis support. It removes a 50 ms recovery lag after geometry flips, and its regime analysis explains why plain integration stays preferable on MPI-Sintel, where 71.1% of pixels change appearance but not disparity.

authors.name: Ruiqi Liu, Yang Lu, Yanlan Kang

papers.title: State-selective dynamical freezing in driven Rydberg atom chains
papers.summary: Dynamical freezing, the near-complete suppression of dynamics at special drive frequencies, offers a route to mitigating Floquet heating in periodically driven quantum systems. In interacting systems, however, the energy cost of each transition depends on the many-body configuration, so that the freezing condition itself becomes state dependent. We study this dependence in periodically driven Rydberg atom chains under single- and bi-frequency driving. Using Floquet perturbation theory, we show that each spin flip is characterised by a single interference amplitude set by its local interaction shift, and that a state freezes only where the amplitudes of all its available flips vanish simultaneously. This picture accounts quantitatively for the shift and proliferation of freezing frequencies with interatomic spacing and for the response of entire families of initial states, which are sorted by a single local motif. Freezing is strong only within a window of spacings bounded by interaction tails on one side and nearest-neighbour excitation facilitation on the other, outside of which the advantage of bi-frequency driving is lost. In the regime of large detuning amplitude, where freezing points are numerous and the perturbative description is controlled, this window leaves almost no room for the PXP limit.

authors.name: Madhumita Sarkar, Sougato Bose, Roopayan Ghosh

papers.title: Foliated surface codes for optimal skip-gate leakage correction
papers.summary: Skip-gate leakage --- such as atom loss in neutral-atom arrays or trapped ions, or photon loss in superconducting dual-rail qubits --- takes a qubit out of its computational subspace and removes subsequent gates acting on it. If leakage is only detectable end-of-the-line at qubit measurement, error correction circuits must be designed to periodically measure all qubits, as in SWAP-based circuits and foliation. We show that the best SWAP-based surface code, although optimal against space-like skip-gate leakage errors, is suboptimal against time-like leakage errors. By optimal, we mean that the code corrects as many leakage errors as it can detect. Remarkably, we find that the foliated surface code is optimal against both space- and time-like error configurations. We support our findings with numerical simulations. Under two-qubit gate leakage with probability 0.5%, foliation suppresses time-like errors in a distance-4 rotated stability experiment by 1380(50) per two added rounds, compared to 63(1) for the best SWAP-based circuit. In memory, the two are comparable. Under an experimentally motivated neutral-atom noise model, we find that foliation outperforms SWAP-based circuits in stability for both rotated and unrotated code geometries. This holds true for a parameter sweep that takes the neutral-atom noise model from being dominated by computational errors to atom loss. Interestingly, a SWAP-based circuit for unrotated code memory performs best when computational noise dominates over loss. Our work motivates co-designing error correction circuits with logical operations: preferring foliation when time-like errors dominate and SWAP-based circuits when space-like errors dominate.

authors.name: Runjiang Bi, Nikita Astrakhantsev, Thomas B. Smith, Margaret Pavlovich, Ming Li, Shruti Puri

papers.title: Comment on phase vortex lattices in neutron interferometry
papers.summary: We present a phase-based theoretical description of the four-plate crystal neutron interferometer (LLLL geometry) originally introduced by Heinrich et al. [Z. Phys. B 72, 357 (1988)]. The LLLL interferometer can be interpreted as two coupled LLL interferometric loops that share partial beam paths, leading to characteristic interference phenomena beyond the standard three-plate configuration. Using a coherent beam-splitting model we derive the forward intensity in terms of loop phase sums and recover the cosine-sum structure reported in Refs.[1,2]. Based on these results we analyze the phase dependence of the forward beam in the presence of localized phase objects, such as wedges inserted into individual partial beams. In experiments presented in [2], the LLLL interferometer is used to generate a periodic array of intensity in two dimensions by which the authors claim to demonstrate a phase vortex grating of significant extrinsic orbital angular momentum (OAM). However, the same interference patterns are predicted by simulating a coherent superposition of {beam paths} along different interferometer loops and experiencing phase shifts in each loop due to two wedges that are perpendicular to each other, without assuming any neutron OAM.

authors.name: Wolfgang Treimer, Terrence Jach, Martin suda, Frank Hau{\ss}er

papers.title: Distant Bell States via Measured Spin Chain Dynamics
papers.summary: Preparing distant qubits in Bell states is a core requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum computation. The nonequilibrium unitary dynamics of spin chains have been envisaged as a convenient quantum channel for intra-chip communications. Typically it establishes mixed entangled states between its remote ends, to be purified by entanglement distillation after several uses of the channel to obtain Bell states. Here we show how the establishment of entanglement via spin chain dynamics can be (a) sped up and (b) made to yield a pure entangled state after a single usage of the channel, which is upgradable to a Bell-state without the complexity of purification. To this end, we intersperse unitary evolution for some period with measurements on intermediary spins. We explore two different measurements: a measurement that post-selects for a ground state; and local measurements in the computational basis. We illustrate the mechanism with qubits coupled to the ends of a 1D $XY$ spin chain.

authors.name: Ralph Jason Costales, Sougato Bose

papers.title: Tailored Magic States for Algorithmic Primitives
papers.summary: Algorithmic primitives such as adders, multipliers, and Boolean logic typically contain clusters of multi-qubit non-Clifford gates, whose decomposition into $T$ and $CCZ$ gates adds scheduling and spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computers. Synthillation addresses this difficulty for diagonal circuits at the third level of the Clifford hierarchy by jointly synthesizing and distilling their non-Clifford content. In this work, we develop a complementary, code-theoretic approach to synthillation. We introduce CSS-T-Product (CSS-TP) codes, whose transversal single-qubit phase gates implement multi-qubit logical diagonal gates, and give analytical rules that predict these logical gates from tensor-network operations. Using quantum LEGO, we generate code families with logical actions at the third and fourth levels of the Clifford hierarchy. We classify the resulting resource states as canonical (such as $T$ or $CCZ$), tensor products of canonical states, or irreducible, i.e., not reducible to a product of non-Clifford gates via Clifford operations and logical basis changes. Conversion into Encode-$T$-Decode factories built from these codes recover known synthillation resources and prepare magic states at higher levels of the Clifford hierarchy; we analyze them with a surface-code-based model for several algorithmic primitives. We demonstrate that tailored magic factories give significant latency improvements at similar or smaller occupied spacetime volume: at code distance $21$ with one factory per resource family, they reduce the latency of a $GF(2^{8})$ multiplier and a shared-addend carry-lookahead adder by up to $48\%$ and $38\%$, respectively, and the smallest tailored factory also lowers the occupied spacetime volume. CSS-TP codes thus connect code construction to resource factories for specific algorithmic primitives.

authors.name: Matthew Steinberg, Joseph Sullivan, Chunjun Cao, Michael Perlin

papers.title: Incompressible quantum information
papers.summary: For a small classical system correlated with a large one, it is always possible to compress the large system down to a size only dependent on the size of the smaller one, while preserving all correlations up to a given controllable error. Here, we show that such a statement does not hold at all when the large system is quantum mechanical. More precisely, we show that there are bipartite states such that any compression of the large system, by a non-trivial relative factor, will necessarily lead to the destruction of a significant amount of correlation, measured in mutual information. Our results therefore identify a limitation of information-bottleneck approaches to quantum machine learning, showing that a small system specifying the relevant features contained in a large quantum data set does not guarantee a compact encoding of the latter that preserves the relevant correlations.

authors.name: Lasse H. Wolff, Matthias Christandl, Bergfinnur Durhuus, Christoph Hirche, Andreas Winter

papers.title: Online Scheduling for Entanglement Distillation: Learning When to Wait
papers.summary: Entanglement distillation probabilistically increases the fidelity of entangled pairs at the cost of reducing their number. The outcome of each distillation operation takes time to communicate, during which the entangled pairs decohere while idle in their memories. This raises a dilemma: wait for the outcome before proceeding, or continue optimistically at the risk of needlessly consuming further pairs. We study online distillation scheduling, in which distillation trees are constructed dynamically to maximize the throughput of pairs that meet a required fidelity. A policy decides which pairs to distill together and, for each operation, whether to wait for its outcome. We derive an upper bound on the throughput of every scheduling policy and, by formulating the problem as a Markov decision process, train, with reinforcement learning, a policy that applies to any number of memories. Compared with two baselines that always or never wait, the learned policy delivers as many pairs of the required fidelity as the better one when one of these two extremes is the best choice, and more otherwise.

authors.name: Panagiotis Promponas, Spyros Tserkis, Leandros Tassiulas

papers.title: Verification and Evaluation of A Comprehensive Quantum Simulation Compiler
papers.summary: Hamiltonian simulation is a central application of quantum computing, yet most existing compilers offer no machine-checked guarantee that the circuits they produce approximate the intended evolution. The previous QBlue compiler verifies a Hamiltonian simulation compiler containing only Trotter-based algorithms. It takes a Hamiltonian written over Pauli strings, a simulation time, and an error bound, and produces a circuit or analog schedule that is proven, in the Rocq proof assistant, to approximate the ideal time evolution within that bound and proves a single end-to-end error bound that composes the errors of the individual stages; the compiler uses it to select, by resource estimation, the cheapest algorithm that meets the user's bound. This paper advances the verification efforts with two further steps. First, we extend QBlue to $\textsf{QBlue}_{\texttt{BE}}$ by verifying another important compilation method for Hamiltonian simulation: block-encoding-based (BE-based) algorithms. Second, we empirically evaluate 279 Hamiltonian simulation programs against the state-of-the-art BE-based compiler, PennyLane. For many programs, our compiler shows a $94\%$ gate reduction compared to PennyLane. Additionally, we also discover issues and bugs in PennyLane. We also compare Trotter- and BE-based algorithms, providing a practical comparison for the long-standing debate over which algorithms perform better. Our results surprisingly show that Trotter-based algorithms may gain a practical advantage, even though BE algorithms have a theoretical advantage.

authors.name: Bhuwan Joshi, Zoukarneini Difaizi Tagba, Zhi Xiang Chong, Liyi Li

papers.title: Froq: Safe Speculative Execution on Live Quantum States for FTQC
papers.summary: Reducing execution time is critical to fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) as longer executions expose logical qubits to more opportunities for failure. However, quantum processors could frequently stall due to slow classical error-correction decoders. Recent speculative decoding accelerates this process, but its speculation remains on the classical side, leaving quantum operations waiting for confirmed decoding results. Extending speculative execution to the quantum side is fundamentally challenging. Unlike classical processor states, quantum states cannot be arbitrarily copied or checkpointed for rollback, making recovery from mispredictions difficult. In this work, we propose Froq to enable safe speculative execution on live quantum states. Froq uses compiler-assisted recovery contracts to track how mispredictions propagate through quantum operations. It further employs a resource-aware runtime mechanism to reserve recovery workspace and dynamically balance the benefits of speculative execution against the expected costs of recovery. We evaluate Froq on eight FTQC programs across 88 configurations, building on an existing speculative window decoder. Froq reduces quantum-side time by 9.81% across all 88 configurations. The reduction reaches 18.34% across the 45 configurations allowing concurrent predictions, and peaks at 31.1% at code distance d=21, under limited resources.

authors.name: Yicheng Guang, Yueqi Chen

papers.title: Causal Consistency and Cost of Quantum Control
papers.summary: An unknown quantum state can supply the information needed to control a computation, but how much quantum data must be consumed to perform a prescribed action? We connect this resource question to causal consistency within the quantum state space. No-signaling requires identical observable predictions for remotely chosen ensemble preparations of the same complete input; quantum distinguishability then converts this requirement into finite-copy bounds. For amplitude amplification, we identify an exact low-copy obstruction and establish a dimension-independent, optimal quadratic dependence of the copy cost on angular gain at fixed accuracy, uniformly over arbitrary pure inputs. A coherent protocol attains this scaling without reconstructing a classical state description. Prior knowledge of a real two-level family additionally permits exponentially decreasing error with the copy budget at fixed gain. These results separate the resources needed to perform a specified quantum operation from those needed for universal state reconstruction. The central connection is operational: physical consistency restricts which distinctions a controller can expose, and the information carried by its complete input determines the cost of doing so. This links a causal requirement to quantitative limits on converting quantum data into computational control.

authors.name: Jeongho Bang, Kyoungho Cho, Jeongwoo Jae

papers.title: Subquantum Pilot-Wave System Theory: Structural and Amplitude Nonequilibrium under Source Fields
papers.summary: A source in the Schrodinger equation changes the norm of the guiding wave, apparently conflicting with the conservation of probability. In source-extended de Broglie-Bohm dynamics the conflict disappears: probability is carried by the particle ensemble, while the wavefunction guides its motion. The difficulty is then different. What does quantum equilibrium mean when the particle distribution remains normalized but the guiding density does not? We show that the departure has two independent components: a structural one, measured by the Kullback--Leibler divergence between the particle distribution and the normalized guiding density, and an amplitude one, measured by the Born weight. The Born rule holds precisely when both are equilibrated. Their evolution is governed by the complex source-to-wavefunction ratio; scale covariance further distinguishes an independently prescribed source, against which the amplitude of the wave matters, from state-dependent generators for which rescaling remains a symmetry. We develop a source-aware analytical--computational method, combining exact or semi-analytical guiding fields with Bohmian trajectory transport, ensemble quadrature and independent numerical checks. Free-space impulses expose the limits of global diagnostics and an exact jump rule; a driven ring has constant Born weight but either periodic or secular structural departure; oscillators show both source-generated structural change and amplitude-only evolution, including a finite-horizon weak-drive plateau far below its frozen-particle value; and a coupled two-body model exhibits nonlocal guidance and evolving particle entanglement. The source-free, initially equilibrated sector recovers standard quantum mechanics.

authors.name: Said Mikki

papers.title: Quantum nonclassicality as a marginal problem
papers.summary: Classical explanations of quantum statistics---local, noncontextual, or causal---fail for one and the same reason: the probability distributions observed in different contexts are not the marginals of a single joint distribution. Every single context admits a classical model. This is Boole's problem of the "conditions of possible experience." Garg and Mermin treated it as a linear problem and showed, via Farkas's lemma, that its solvability is equivalent to a finite list of Bell-type inequalities, one for each extreme ray of a convex polyhedral cone; Pitowsky gave it the form of correlation polytopes. We sketch this common structure and discuss two examples: Aerts's elastic-band model, which reproduces the quantum cosine in one context but obeys the classical bound when contexts are combined; and nonclassicality in causal data fusion, where the contexts are supplied by interventions on a causal structure.

authors.name: Karl Svozil

papers.title: Revealing the Hidden Symmetry of the Asymmetric Quantum Rabi Model
papers.summary: A longitudinal bias breaks ordinary parity in the asymmetric quantum Rabi model, yet exact crossings reappear when the bias equals an integer multiple $m$ of the oscillator energy spacing. We trace the hidden symmetry to exchange between equal-energy partners $m$ rungs apart on two displaced oscillator ladders. Tunneling to other rungs makes this exchange vary in time. We construct the exact symmetry operator by adding spin and oscillator coherences that cancel this variation. At nonzero coupling and tunneling, the resulting charge has no zero modes, and its sign divides the full Hilbert space into two generalized-parity sectors that cannot mix. Spin-resolved mirror interference probes coherence between the two opposite-parity states at a crossing. Its small-displacement exponent gives $m$, and its leading coefficient, together with the charge magnitude, predicts the mixing induced by a slight change in bias.

authors.name: Zi-Min Li, Zi-Cheng Liu, Long-Jie Li, Xuan Zou, Jin-Xiang Fu, Xilin Lu, Murray T. Batchelor

papers.title: Phase-dependent atomicity and PPT edge states for cyclic-sign covariant qutrit maps
papers.summary: Decomposable positive maps cannot detect entangled states with positive partial transpose (PPT). We obtain a necessary and sufficient criterion for decomposability in the entire seven-real-parameter class of Hermiticity-preserving cyclic-sign covariant maps on $M_3$. The criterion reduces to a one-variable inequality and, for positive maps in this class, characterizes indecomposability exactly. We apply it to a phase-dependent family obtained by adding a completely positive map to the Choi map. Every map in this family is positive, and we find the exact phase-dependent threshold for indecomposability and atomicity. At three phase values, the maps remain indecomposable for every finite deformation strength. Each indecomposable map gives an indecomposable entanglement witness through its Choi matrix. We construct PPT edge states of birank $(5,5)$ detected by these witnesses throughout the indecomposable region.

authors.name: Adam Rutkowski

papers.title: Many-Body Flux Selection in Chiral Quantum Batteries
papers.summary: We study an interacting quantum-battery chain in which a synthetic flux controls interference between hopping paths. Keeping the internal battery Hamiltonian fixed, we seek the flux that leaves the most extractable work. Even a Gaussian reconstruction supplied with exact one-body information can rank competing flux settings incorrectly. A reduced many-body model that retains correlations within a few battery-occupation sectors recovers the correct ranking and selects nearly optimal fluxes across the finite systems and parameter ranges studied. Strikingly, the model can make an accurate control choice even when it excludes configurations carrying substantial probability in the exact state. Thus, choosing a nearly optimal charging flux can require much less information than reconstructing the full many-body state.

authors.name: Borhan Ahmadi

papers.title: Sharp Purity Based Entropy Bounds and Machine Learning Assisted Entropy Estimation
papers.summary: Purity quantifies quantum-state mixedness, motivating the study of its role in controlling entropy variations. A sharp purity-based continuity bound is established for the von Neumann entropy of qubit states. The bound is attainable for every admissible purity difference and strictly improves the existing purity bound. In higher dimensions, an explicit sharp bound is derived within the family of pure states mixed with the maximally mixed state. Further continuity estimates are obtained for conditional entropy, quantum mutual information, quantum conditional mutual information, and squashed entanglement within specified bipartite and tripartite families. An application to machine learning assisted qubit entropy estimation illustrates how the sharp bound converts purity estimation errors into rigorous entropy error bounds.

authors.name: Komal Kumar, Shree Prakash

papers.title: Quantum Metrology With Quantum Limit Cycles
papers.summary: Beyond nonclassical states, emergent quantum phenomena offer new metrological resources. Quantum limit cycles, in particular, sustain long-lived oscillations that prolong coherent signal accumulation. However, quantum fluctuations may limit this advantage, leaving their metrological performance unclear. Here, we propose a quantum limit-cycle metrology protocol for collective spins by introducing nonlinear damping into the conventional collective-decay protocol. We develop a semiclassical phase-diffusion theory to characterize its metrological performance, in good agreement with numerical simulations. The limit-cycle protocol improves estimation precision and approaches Heisenberg scaling with system size. We further combine limit-cycle dynamics with spin squeezing, finding that squeezing improves short-time precision, but phase diffusion ultimately dominates, leaving the asymptotic scaling unchanged. Our results establish quantum limit cycles as a metrological resource and clarify the interplay between limit-cycle dynamics and squeezing in quantum sensing.

authors.name: Zhi-Hao Liu, Xiangyu Niu, Keren Li, Ran Liu, Xiao-Dong Yang, Jun Li

papers.title: Holevo-Bounded Total Information from Pair Distributions of Alternative Quantum Measurements
papers.summary: The accessible information of a quantum ensemble can be strictly smaller than its Holevo information because a single-copy measurement may discard part of the label--system correlation.
